text:
A Spanish police patrol car passes through one of Valencia’s largest parks and Lorena López, a 29-year-old Colombian woman, freezes and completely loses focus in her boxing class. She remembers the U.S. agents who held her for a year and a half at the Eloy Detention Center in Arizona and the officers from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) who deported her, handcuffed at hands and feet, to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on April 15, 2026. When she sees the officers, she also recalls the armed men she and 14 other Latin Americans encountered at the hotel where they were held in Kinshasa for two months. But then she immediately realizes that since she was able to leave that African country in June she is free and safe in Spain.

She knows that if the police ask her for documents she can take out her phone and show a photo of her receipt proving she applied for international protection in July. “Our lawyer has explained to us that they are denying asylum to Colombians,” she fears, “but we know a small percentage are approved. We cling to that hope.”

López agreed to speak to this newspaper about the ordeal she has endured as a result of the Trump administration’s policy of expelling migrants to third countries, but on the condition that her real name not be used. “Imagine always hiding from the police or immigration agents. There is this fear of being treated like cargo: ‘grab them and send them far away,’” says this woman, who says she was victim of gender-based violence. In 2025, Colombia recorded 118 femicides and more than 15,000 cases of domestic violence against women.

Sitting beside her, Carlos Rodelo, another Colombian national deported from the U.S. to the DRC, listens and nods. He gives his real name and agrees to be photographed because he is seeking help from Spain to have his international protection claim considered. “I want to make it clear that we are not here on a whim; it’s for our safety. We cannot return to Colombia,” says this 43-year-old from Barranquilla, who says he was a victim of extortion and death threats. Reports of extortion in Colombia rose 144% over the last decade to 13,417 cases in 2025.

By WhatsApp, Daniela, 31, born in Cúcuta, says she fled Colombia after being harassed and threatened by a police commander. “After everything that has happened to me, I have faith that things will get better and that someday I will be able to see my mother and my daughters again,” she says in a voice note from another city in the Valencia region. She asked that her surname be withheld for security reasons.

These three Colombians had received CAT protection in the U.S. (from the UN Convention Against Torture). But that protection was not a visa or a form of political asylum: it only prevented them from being returned to Colombia, but not to a third country. They ended up in the DRC against their will and are among more than 25,000 people Washington deported to third countries between January 20, 2025 and September 2026. According to data from Human Rights First and Refugees International, two NGOs that monitor these forced transfers, the U.S. government has signed agreements with more than 35 countries in Africa, Asia and the Americas. More than 300 detainees have been taken to 14 African countries, including the DRC, Eswatini, Liberia, the Central African Republic and South Sudan.

Among the group of 15 people who landed in Kinshasa on April 17 — after stopping in Senegal and Ghana — there were eight Colombian citizens. Three of them were able to leave the DRC by their own means and enter Spain, where the Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (Comisión Española de Ayuda al Refugiado, CEAR) provides legal support for their international protection applications.

I want to make it clear that we are not here on a whim; it’s for our safety. We cannot return to Colombia

Carlos Rodelo

The process will not be easy, says Jaume Durà, head of CEAR’s legal team in Valencia. Of the 40,512 Colombian applications decided in Spain in 2025, only 3% obtained some form of protection, according to the organization’s data. A year ago, the European Union placed Colombia on its list of countries considered “safe” despite the fact that some areas remain threatened by armed actors, drug trafficking or criminal groups and despite being the country where the most environmental defenders are killed.

“Violence in Colombia continues to be very high, with a lack of protection from the state [for victims of various crimes]. Spain grants a very low recognition rate to protection claims from people fleeing the country. That should not be the case; each case must be examined individually,” he says in a telephone interview.

Getting out of the DRC

The U.S. and the DRC signed a bilateral agreement in December for the African country to receive deportees. The deal, made public in April, established that people would be admitted with a short-term permit. The first and only group sent to the DRC to date was housed at the Venus Village hotel, about 30 minutes from Kinshasa airport. There, the International Organization for Migration (IOM), at the request of the DRC government, provided assistance.

“Although it was a hotel, it felt like a prison because we couldn’t go out,” Rodelo says. If they needed to buy food or go to a phone center to receive money their families had sent, he says, they had to request accompaniment. They also suffered daily power cuts and frequently ran out of water. “The food was unpleasant and everything was full of mosquitoes. One bit me and I got malaria,” he adds.

When there was internet service, Rodelo searched for information about the country he was in. “I had never heard of that place in my life,” he says. Browsing Google, he learned that in the eastern DRC, since early 2025, the war between the state and the rebel group March 23 Movement (M23) had intensified and had left thousands dead and 6.1 million displaced. “I also learned there is illegal mining, mafias and poverty. Imagine: it was going from bad to worse—danger in Colombia, danger in the U.S. and now danger in the Congo,” he recalls. With his phone he also managed to communicate with the hotel staff, who spoke Lingala and French.

López, for her part, connected online to speak with her lawyer and to look for ways to leave. “She explained to me that I had the right to go to another country and to seek a nearby alternative,” she recalls. They chose Spain and declined the assisted voluntary return to their country of origin that the IOM offered. They then contacted the Colombian consulate in Kenya to help issue new passports. Her lawyer confirms ICE had confiscated hers.

Then a race against time began because in mid-May the WHO declared a ‘public health emergency of international concern’ over an Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC. They feared travel or migration restrictions. When they obtained passports, they managed to raise the money to buy tickets to Madrid through online fundraisers or support from family.

Daniela was able to leave the DRC on June 1 bound for France. López and Rodelo flew to Spain on June 8. “I don’t feel anger toward Congo. I just don’t feel it can give me the security I seek,” López says, adding: “I’m angrier with the U.S.”

Lorena* had the chance to get a passport, the money to travel and to enter a large number of countries without a visa. Most people are forced to choose between returning to their country, where they may suffer violence, or finding a way to stay in a place that is not safe and where the government does not offer them permanent status.

Alma David, lawyer for Lorena López*

It is not easy for people deported by the Trump administration to leave these third countries. According to monitoring by Human Rights First and Refugees International, in addition to the DRC group, some deportees sent to Uganda have also managed to leave. Alma David, López’s lawyer, who handles other similar cases, says what happened to her client is “exceptional.” “She had the opportunity to get a passport, the money to travel and to enter many countries visa-free. Most people are forced to choose between returning to their country, where they may suffer violence, or finding a way to stay in an unsafe place where the government does not grant them permanent status,” she explains via WhatsApp messages.

In a press release, the IOM explains that since 2025 it has assisted and advised 800 people in this situation. “Some 300 of them later opted for voluntary return. The difference between that figure and the tens of thousands of people relocated is not an indicator of IOM’s effort but reflects the small number of governments that invited us to intervene or that met the conditions we demanded. Most relocated people have received no support.” If a person decides to leave on their own, the IOM supports them while they are in the country, but they do not receive the benefits of the assisted voluntary return program.

Others have been less fortunate. Some of those expelled to Eswatini more than a year ago remain confined in a maximum-security prison.

Starting over in Spain

López, Rodelo and Daniela reunited in Spain. They entered through Madrid as tourists because they feared applying for international protection at the border and being expelled or detained, as had already happened to them in the U.S. “We passed customs and we were so emotional we left a suitcase back at the airport,” López laughs. A few days later they went to Valencia. But no one would rent them a room and they couldn’t find beds in humanitarian shelters. “We slept in parks. But even so we were happy and free. Our lives depended on ourselves, not on other people,” she recalls.

One day they arrived at CEAR’s offices and received psychological and legal support to begin their international protection application. Once the process was underway, they obtained a Foreigner Identity Number (NIE) that allowed them to find rental housing, register their residency and access public healthcare. However, it does not grant work authorization. Rodelo, for example, is using the last of his U.S. savings to avoid asking his family in Colombia for help. He has not been able to send remittances for more than a year.

While their cases are being resolved, the three Colombians live with a mix of peace and fear. They have seen on the news that the new EU migration and asylum pact has come into force, speeding up but also tightening the procedures for resolving international protection claims. It also opens the door to creating deportation centers in third countries to expel migrants in an irregular situation. The Spanish government, however, has rejected that last measure. For that reason, despite everything, they say they have placed their hopes in Spain to regain the normality they lost in recent years.

López never managed to establish a life in the U.S. The first time she tried to enter and seek asylum, in January 2024, she was deported. After being threatened again by her ex-partner in Colombia, she tried again: she requested an appointment through CBP One, a U.S. government mobile app that allowed migrants to seek lawful entry or asylum. However, the day she was summoned to the checkpoint on the Mexico border, in September 2024, she was detained for a year and a half. Although she was released in February of this year, ICE detained her again in March and deported her to the DRC.

Rodelo, meanwhile, had arrived in the U.S. in May 2023 and obtained CAT protection in February 2025. With that document he obtained a work permit and made a living as a driver and courier until ICE detained him at its offices in August 2025 during a routine migration appointment. He spent eight months in a Louisiana correctional facility until, in mid-April, officers knocked on his cell. They took him to the airport and only there did he learn he was bound for the African continent.

Daniela crossed the Mexico border in December 2024 and surrendered to migration authorities. She was detained until February 2026 and after her release, with CAT protection and a work permit, she applied for authorization to settle in Dallas. “On April 2, ICE came to where I lived. They knocked on the door to verify my supervision order. They told me I had to accompany them. I agreed, they put me in handcuffs and once I was in their offices they told me they would send me to a third country,” she recounts.

The U.S. has defended its deportation policy despite criticism from international organizations and human rights NGOs. A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) document states that, before transfer, the government verifies whether the receiving country guarantees the person will not be sent to another destination where they could suffer torture. If the State Department deems those assurances credible, the deportation can proceed without additional procedures and without asking the person whether they fear for their safety in that country.

Nevertheless, the measure has been taken to several U.S. courts and is now in dispute. On September 18 a federal appeals court ruled that the expulsions were illegal and violated due process by failing to notify people with sufficient time of the decision to transfer them to a third country. Days later, the Trump administration filed an emergency appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court seeking to suspend that ruling and allow the procedures to continue.

text:
The judge instructs the baby and his mother, age 17, to apply for asylum. But the teenager can barely focus on what he is saying.

Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu, deputy director of a group that provides legal support for unaccompanied minors, described this scene, which she witnessed in August.

"This child is being expected to file her own application, also figure out how to file things for her one-year-old baby, while living through the distress of being a detained young mother," Avila-Cimpeanu told AFP.

President Donald Trump's administration has choked off funding for organizations that have years of experience assisting unaccompanied minors, bringing in substitutes that are under-equipped and unqualified, advocates say.

"We are gravely concerned that ORR would entrust a vulnerable population with firms so plainly unqualified for the task," Democratic lawmakers said in a letter to the Deportment of Health and Human Services this week.

ORR is the Office of Refugee Resettlement, an agency traditionally tasked with the care of unaccompanied minor migrants.

The category describes children who arrive in the United States without an adult, or whose parents were detained by immigration agents and are in shelters or government custody.

'Attack on children'

Since he returned to the White House for his second term in January 2025, President Donald Trump has a mounted an aggressive and sometimes violent operation to deport undocumented immigrants from the United States.

Last year the administration tried to cut off funding that ORR used to support a national network of organizations that have for years provided legal services to unaccompanied migrant minors.

Following a lawsuit, the measure was blocked by a federal judge who ordered that the services, which were mandated by a 2008 law, be maintained.

Months later, the government stopped making payments, and in July 2026, it allowed a contract with the Acacia Center for Justice -- which managed a network of about 100 organizations -- to expire.

Avila-Cimpeanu told AFP that in late 2025 that the government made funding contingent on the release of confidential information about some 20,000 children represented by the network -- "and we did not do so."

The government then announced plans to hand the cases over to the Burke Law Group, run by a former Trump administration official, but that firm withdrew its bid.

It then planned to deploy Our Rescue, an organization founded by a controversial anti-trafficking activist and led by a former investigator for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The contract was put on hold following questions raised in Congress, amid a review of federal funds allocated for this purpose.

"Children's legal protections should never be the currency Of political patronage," Democratic lawmakers said in their letter.

Avila-Cimpeanu says the administration is trying to complicate the defense of minors "in order to get to their goal of deporting as many children as quickly as possible."

"I have been doing this work for 10 years, and this is the worst time that I've ever seen with regard to the government's concerted attack on children," she said.

Babies in court

She said it is common for unaccompanied minors to appear in immigration courts. That is why a lawyer who understands the issue -- and even speaks the child's language if it is not English -- is necessary.

Avila-Cimpeanu recalled a case in 2018 when her organization was in court on behalf of a baby just months old.

"We had to say: this baby denies the allegations. This baby would like voluntary departure.

"It's ridiculous that children have to go through this process as if they were adults, but it is part of the proceeding."

This week, CNN reported that 25 migrant children, several without a lawyer, had a hearing in a Texas court.

In a statement to AFP, ORR said that in August it provided funding through the end of the year for the US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI) to appear at immigration hearings.

"USCRI is appearing at 100 percent of the hearings and has expanded to provide legal orientation, legal consultations and direct representation," it said.

Bilal Askaryar, a spokesman for Acacia, explained that USCRI is a small organization with about 50 attorneys, compared to the 800 in Acacia’s network.

"This isn't about a contract for us. This isn't about a dispute between an organization and the government. This is about 20,000 children who came to the United States seeking safety," he said.

text:
DODGE CITY — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrived in southwest Kansas on Sept. 22 and departed three days later, leaving fear, uncertainty and anger.

Many in the Hispanic and Latino communities in Dodge City, Garden City and Liberal, where most ICE activity was located, returned to work this week. But their fear persists and they aren’t yet leaving their homes or returning to regular activities, multiple immigrants said.

The fear was contagious. In Manhattan, about 225 miles east of Dodge City, social media posts blasted warnings of possible ICE agents on Thursday because of a large presence of law enforcement vehicles in a store parking lot. It turned out to be a training session for local police, according to a store employee.

Here are a handful of glimpses into the lives of Kansans affected by the raids.

Viridiana Boron, volunteer

Viridiana Boron spent several days last week delivering meals to Dodge City families whose members were scared to leave home because ICE was in the area.

Her mother and sister cooked meals for about 200 people, and Boron delivered them, she said.

“I was the one that was on the street and watching everything, watching all the suffer the families was having,” she said, pausing to apologize for her English. “I saw the reality, the truth. They were scared. They were sad. They were worried. I saw families with no water.”

Boron started crying.

“It was something that I’ve never seen in my life,” she said. “How can people not have heart and just do things like that? Because I mean, there I know could be a lot of immigrants over here that are like criminals, but a lot of people that I saw, they were not criminals. They were people working hard for their kids.”

This week, many people she knows have returned to work, but they aren’t eating out or shopping as the fear lingers, Boron said.

Boron came to the United States at age 24, receiving a visa because she and her family were threatened in Mexico. She has since married and is a legal permanent resident. Despite knowing she had the correct documentation, she was scared during the ICE operation.

Others who stayed home also had documentation, she said. But they have seen instances where it didn’t matter, and ICE agents stopped cars to check paperwork just because someone looked Hispanic or Latina, Boron said.

The affect on the community was “huge,” she said. It was difficult explaining to her 11-year-old son why people were scared because he didn’t understand the difference a paper could make, Boron said.

“We are all the same,” she said.

Julie Barraza, volunteer and activist

Julie Barraza smiled at everyone approaching the table she set up at a downtown Dodge City protest on Sept. 24. She patiently answered questions about a petition to reform the country’s immigration system.

“I was born and raised here, and I’ve never seen such a cloud over the town,” she said during a break. “The first morning, they (ICE) were waiting for me to get out of my car, and I didn’t know what was going on. I didn’t get out of my car.”

Barraza drove on to work at Rattlesnake Grill. She said ICE agents came in to eat but employees didn’t realize they were with ICE because they wore regular clothing.

“Once we figured out they were ICE agents, because a customer had alerted us, I stepped out and decided to tell them to leave, and they refused,” she recalled. “I was scared, but I still did it.”

The agents did get up and leave, Barraza said, adding that several restaurants in town refused to serve agents and others closed because there weren’t employees to work.

Patrick Lopez, immigrant and educator

Patrick Lopez stood in the midst of a Dodge City protest on Sept. 24, holding a sign and nodding to people he knew. He was there, he said, to “show solidarity with people who are being persecuted by ICE.”

“I’m here to defend my immigrant brothers and sisters. I’m here to stand up for them, and I hate that they have to live in fear right now,” Lopez said. “I can’t sleep last night. I’m offended as an American. I’m embarrassed as an American. I’m indignant. I can’t believe that this is happening right now.”

While acknowledging the economic costs to town — restaurants closed, businesses slowing or stopping work — Lopez said they weren’t what made him toss and turn at night.

“I also wish that people remembered the human rights effect,” he said. “People’s families should be protected. I don’t care what the issue is. You can’t destroy people’s families like that and hopefully get away with it.”

He tried unsuccessfully to reach a friend who drives a cab and worried that he was detained.

“He works every day, and that’s the thing. The people that ICE is after are hardworking people around town,” Lopez said. “Many of them are putting their kids through school. They’re just trying to make a living.”

Sarahí Aguilera, therapist and immigrant

Sarahí Aguilera is a licensed social worker, and she works as a mental health therapist. Advocating for the immigrant community, she said, is at the foundation of her personal and professional life.

She knows the challenges well. Aguilera is part of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, which allows young people who arrived during specific time periods to apply and work in the country.

DACA has been under fire during President Donald Trump’s administration, she said, but she was fortunate that her permit didn’t expire when the program was temporarily halted. Since then, it has been a “consistent uphill battle” to keep the program active, Aguilera said.

Other family members weren’t so lucky. Aguilera’s sister had just been to an immigration appointment after turning 15, which is the age that people can apply for the DACA program, Aguilera said.

“We had started her paperwork. She had been approved. She had gone to her biometrics. I lived at Wichita at the time because that’s where I was getting my education,” she said. “And she got approved. She just never received her work permit.”

It was frustrating because when the family looked her up in the system, it said she was approved, Aguilera said. But she never physically received the approval that would allow her to receive her driver’s license or continue her education.

Her sister eventually married and is in the process of acquiring her documentation, Aguilera said. The experience reminds her how difficult it is to go through the immigration process and how different it is for each person, she said.

“Especially seeing me and believing she was going to have the same opportunity,” Aguilera said. “It really impacted her mental health and her motivation to further her education and just work on herself.”

Aguilera volunteers with New Frontiers, a nonprofit organization that works with young people in southwest Kansas to create a grassroots movement focused on political, social and economic power.

The group has a rapid response team that becomes active when events like ICE raids in the area occur, she said. Volunteers watch for ICE agents and try to verify information before releasing it to the community.

“Fear already does a lot to someone,” Aguilera said. “So fear and the wrong information — we want to make sure that we’re just prepared and grounded with what information we’re trying to share.”

Fear of the unknown is a problem for southwest Kansas immigrants, Aguilera said, along with how overwhelming information coming out could be.

While ICE was in the area, she saw about four clients because most were afraid to go out. Typically, her schedule is full every day.

Aguilera said she understands why some people are critical of immigrants who don’t have documentation.

“There is so much misinformation. I believe as a society we need to do a better job of understanding what the immigration process looks like,” she said. “Of understanding what are the barriers, what are the circumstances? Because there is not a system that is going to work for all of us.”

DACA recipients, for instance, don’t have a pathway to citizenship unless they marry or their jobs petition for them, Aguilera said.

Whatever a person’s belief system, she said, she hopes people are careful with their words.

“I do think it’s important to be mindful of the comments and what they can do to the mental health of someone overall,” she said, adding that people are easily influenced by social media and political figures, who she believes often don’t understand the process either.

Does she think significant immigration reform is likely?

“My heart wants to say that it’s hopeful. My uncertainty and anxiety that I’ve experienced for the past 10 years wants me to have a different answer,” Aguilera said. “I do believe people are opening their eyes. I believe we are getting a lot more information and more attention. Although I think we are creating great awareness and sharing information and education, I don’t believe we will see the impact and the change we want to see until people get out and vote.”

text:
Quick Hits

A federal district court in California has blocked USCIS, CBP, and the State Department from enforcing or implementing policies related to the proclamation-based $100,000 H-1B payment requirement.

The California ruling represents another adverse federal district court decision involving the $100,000 payment, which is already blocked pursuant to a separate federal district court decision in Massachusetts that is currently on appeal.

The court order does not affect the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) separately proposed $103,265 fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions, which remains in the rulemaking process and is not currently in effect.

Background

The case, Global Nurse Force v. Trump, was brought by a coalition of employers, labor organizations, schools, healthcare providers, religious organizations, and individuals challenging the $100,000 H-1B payment requirement and the agencies’ implementation of it.

President Donald Trump established the payment requirement through Proclamation 10973, issued on September 19, 2025. As implemented by USCIS, CBP, and the State Department, the requirement primarily affected H-1B workers outside the United States who needed consular processing or admission at a U.S. port of entry.

On September 18, 2026, President Trump issued Proclamation 11069, extending the restriction through September 21, 2027.

On September 30, 2026, the federal district court in California blocked the agencies from enforcing or implementing the proclamation-based payment requirement unless and until they comply with the rulemaking requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act.

Impact on Employers

For employers, the practical impact is straightforward: the proclamation-based $100,000 H-1B payment is not currently being enforced. Employers filing H-1B petitions, including cases requiring consular processing or admission from abroad, are therefore not currently required to pay the $100,000 amount.

The September 30, 2026, California order is the second federal district court decision blocking the payment requirement. A federal district court in Massachusetts has also blocked the requirement, although that decision is currently on appeal before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit.

The litigation continues. The federal district court in California has scheduled a case management conference for October 27, 2026, with a joint case management statement due on October 20, 2026.

Employers should keep the $100,000 proclamation-based payment conceptually separate from DHS’s proposed $103,265 fee for certain H-1B cap-subject petitions. That proposed fee, part of a separate rulemaking process, is not affected by the September 30, 2026, order of court, though the $103,265 fee is not currently in effect. The comment period closed on September 24, 2026, and DHS has not yet issued a final rule.

text:
A major legal battle over the ability of asylum seekers to apply for refuge in the U.S. at ports of entry along the border with Mexico lands at the Supreme Court on Tuesday, as the Trump administration pushes for broad authority to turn migrants away regardless of their claims.

From the start of his second term, President Donald Trump has effectively blocked the entry of all noncitizens at the southern border, including those seeking safety and protection from credible fears of violence and persecution.

Immigrant advocates challenging the approach in multiple lawsuits allege it violates the Immigration and Nationality Act mandate that noncitizens who are "physically present in the U.S." or who "arrive in the U.S. ... at a designated port of arrival" must be allowed to apply for asylum.

The dispute largely turns on competing interpretations of what it means to "arrive in" the country.

"In ordinary English, a person 'arrives in' a country only when he comes within its borders," Trump Solicitor General John Sauer argues in a court filing. "A person does not 'arrive in the United States' if he is stopped in Mexico."

Nicole Ramos, border rights project director at Al Otro Lado, an immigrant rights group and plaintiff in the case, says Congress had a more nuanced view when it drafted the law following the U.S. failure to accept Jewish refugees from the Holocaust.

"The right to seek asylum at the border is a legal right and a moral right," Ramos said. "The stakes are not theoretical. They are measured in lives."

Trump has invoked multiple legal authorities to support his current border crackdown.

At issue in the case being argued Tuesday is the so-called "turn back" policy from Trump's first term that kept asylum seekers waiting in Mexico as a method of "metering" access at border crossings that faced overcrowding.

While the administration voluntarily discontinued the practice in 2021 after a lower court deemed it unlawful, the government insists it has broad discretion to regulate the border and now wants the justices to approve the ability to reinstate the policy if necessary.

"Administrations of both major parties have opposed the [ lower court ] decision, which deprives the Executive Branch of a critical tool for addressing border surges and preventing overcrowding at ports of entry," Sauer wrote. "This Court should reverse."

Melissa Crow, director of litigation at the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies, an immigrant rights group representing several asylum-seeker plaintiffs, said a ruling for the administration could have a major impact, even if not immediate.

"We have no doubt the administration is seeking a decision that will give them even more leeway to restrict the rights of people seeking asylum," Crow said.

Tens of thousands of asylum seekers who arrived at the U.S. southern border during Trump's first term were forced to remain in Mexico for weeks or months in sometimes harrowing conditions in hopes they might have a chance to be interviewed about their fears of persecution.

One of those migrants was Benito, a Mexican asylum seeker who declined to give his last name to protect his identity and spoke through a translator at an event hosted by Al Otro Lado.

"I was partially tortured, had a lot of lesions, and emotional harm, and traumas and I'm still healing from that," he said of the violence he was trying to escape. "I knew I could apply for asylum in that moment, on the side of Mexico, and so I did everything correctly. I came close; I told the [ U.S. ] immigration agents that I needed to apply for asylum because I was scared and thought I would be killed.

"I had scars on my body, on my face, and my head," he said, "but they said to me that they couldn't help me, couldn't accept me."

The court is expected to issue a decision on the Trump administration's bid to resurrect the "metering" and "turn back" policy by the end of June.

title: A Growing Movement Is Working to Evict ICE From Its Buffalo Command Center | Truthout
authors: Anton Woronczuk, Derek Seidman, Laura Hernández, Chris Walker, Shireen Akram-Boshar, Alex Nguyen, Uriel J. García, Alejandro Serrano, Neha Madhira, Thomas Kennedy
description:
“There can be no more business as usual at 250 Delaware Ave until the Montantes EVICT ICE.” ICE’s Command Center Buffalo is a border town — a city shaped by immigrants, past and present.
The Evict ICE campaign and numerous sources say 250 Delaware contains more than piles of paperwork and ringing phones.
The Evict ICE campaign formally launched on May Day of 2026 with a rally in front of 250 Delaware Avenue.
“Evict ICE!” Since its May Day launch, the Evict ICE campaign has organized a steady stream of activities and near-weekly demonstrations.
Amid loud chants of “Evict ICE!” at the July 25 protest, organizers stated their commitment to see the campaign through to victory.
text:
A glimmering 12-story building towers over the intersection where Delaware Avenue meets Chippewa Street in downtown Buffalo. The building is owned by Uniland Development, a major Buffalo real estate developer. Surrounded by coffee shops, luxury hotels, and boutique restaurants, the building’s facade is emblazoned with the corporate logo of its anchor tenant, Delaware North, one of the world’s largest concessions corporations, headquartered in Buffalo.

But amid the daily humdrum at 250 Delaware Avenue — paper shuffling inside, cars honking outside — is, to many Buffalonians, something more shocking: The building’s seventh floor serves as the operational hub of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) machinery of detention and deportation across much of New York State, and it is a “hold room” site used to detain immigrant neighbors, including children.

For years, ICE’s Buffalo field office has lived inside the Delaware North Building. Now, an escalating campaign, Evict ICE from 250 Delaware, is determined to pressure the building’s corporate owners — Uniland Development, owned by the Montantes, a prominent Buffalo area family — and its flagship renter — the Delaware North corporation, owned by the billionaire Jacobs family — to cut ties with ICE when its current lease expires on March 31, 2027.

Backed by a broad coalition of community organizations and immigrant rights groups, and driven by dozens of volunteers, the campaign is working actively — canvassing and petitioning, protesting weekly, staging direct actions — to not only shame and compel Buffalo’s corporate class into evicting ICE from its properties, but also to use the campaign’s momentum to advance the more sweeping movement goals of kicking ICE out of Buffalo and abolishing the agency altogether.

On September 26, eight people were arrested as they sat down and occupied the intersection in front of 250 Delaware — which the campaign is now calling the “Montante Detention Center” — to protest “the Montante family’s continued profiteering from deportation,” according to a press release.

“The people of Buffalo will not allow mass deportation profiteers to hide any longer,” the arrestees said in a statement. “There can be no more business as usual at 250 Delaware Ave until the Montantes EVICT ICE.”

ICE’s Command Center

Buffalo is a border town — a city shaped by immigrants, past and present. The region is a focal point for Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) operations, with raids, detentions, and deportations of immigrants a constant reality. Buffalo made national headlines in February after the death — ruled a homicide by the county medical examiner — of Nurul Amin Shah Alam, a blind Rohingya refugee who Border Patrol left at a downtown coffeeshop without notifying his family of his release.

The Evict ICE campaign describes ICE’s field office in 250 Delaware as the “command center” of the agency’s operations across most of New York State — essentially all areas upstate of New York City and its vicinity. Its purview also includes the nearby Batavia holding center, the state’s only ICE federal detention facility, which is expanding its capacity to hold detainees. In Buffalo, ICE arrests have soared over the past year.

“The masked men kidnapping people off the streets — that is orchestrated out of 250 Delaware,” Jennifer Connor, the executive director of Justice for Migrant Families, told Truthout.

Additionally, the building houses the Buffalo office for Homeland Security Investigations and Buffalo’s Office of the Principal Legal Advisor. Both are arms of DHS’s machinery across New York State.

The Evict ICE campaign and numerous sources say 250 Delaware contains more than piles of paperwork and ringing phones.

The campaign’s analysis of data from the Deportation Data Project found that 237 people were held at the “Buffalo Hold Room” on the 7th floor at 250 Delaware Avenue from February 2025 to March 2026, including 18 children under the age of 12. Many people were held for multiple days, exceeding ICE’s short-term holding policies, and in overcrowded conditions.

Connor says she’s spoken to multiple people who were held in 250 Delaware and that former detainees told her there are at least two holding cells in the building.

Truthout reached out to ICE’s Buffalo office for comment but did not receive a response.

For many Buffalonians, it is jarring to discover that the gleaming Delaware North Building is a place where immigrant neighbors, including children, are detained behind walls that are in plain view of passing drivers, latte sippers, and visiting tourists.

“At first I was like, ‘Oh, it’s just an office building,’” Lena Forti, an organizer with the Evict ICE campaign, told Truthout. “Now I understand that there’s so much power coming from this building. It’s directing all of ICE’s actions for New York State outside of New York City, and it’s holding people.”

Corporate Enablers of ICE

Local activists have been protesting ICE’s presence at 250 Delaware for nearly a decade. The current campaign began to take shape in 2025 among a core of local researchers and activists with mutual aid networks, immigrant rights groups, and progressive community organizations.

The Evict ICE campaign formally launched on May Day of 2026 with a rally in front of 250 Delaware Avenue. It has expanded to a coalition of nearly 60 organizations, small businesses, and elected officials, ranging from housing and environmental groups to labor unions and the Democratic Socialists of America, from bookstores and bike clubs to worker-owned bread co-ops.

The Evict ICE campaign has a clear and immediate goal: pressuring Buffalo’s corporate enablers of ICE to not renew the agency’s lease at 250 Delaware Avenue.

Two corporations — tied to two prominent Buffalo-area families — are at the center of the campaign. The first is Uniland Development, the owner and developer of the building at 250 Delaware North. Uniland is owned by the Montante family, which has a wide presence across Buffalo’s corporate structure and network of educational and cultural institutions.

Uniland rakes in over $2 million annually by renting to ICE at 250 Delaware, in addition to around $850,000 by renting to CBP at two other locations, and it has enjoyed millions in public subsidies.

The second is Delaware North, one of the world’s largest concessions corporations, which is privately owned by the billionaire Jacobs family. Delaware North is the anchor tenant at 250 Delaware Avenue, the company’s global headquarters.

The Jacobs’ have their hands all over the Buffalo area, from universities to banks to art museums. The Jacobs family has donated to politicians from Donald Trump to Kathy Hochul, whose husband, Bill Hochul, was Delaware North’s general counsel and senior vice president until 2023. Delaware North has also raked in public subsidies.

“We have to hold the Montantes and the Jacobs accountable,” said Connor. “The types of violence we’re seeing at the hands of ICE can’t happen without the support of the existing power structures.”

Uniland and Delaware North are just two of the most prominent examples of how Buffalo’s power structure — some of the city’s traditional elite families and leading names in real estate — are profiting from the machinery of detention and deportation through lease agreements with federal agencies.

“It’s really important for us to name names of people who have a responsibility to do better in the Buffalo community,” added Connor.

“Evict ICE!”

Since its May Day launch, the Evict ICE campaign has organized a steady stream of activities and near-weekly demonstrations.

In May and June, the campaign placed billboards across from the building shaming Uniland and Delaware North and calling for ICE’s eviction. During Mother’s Day brunch, protesters held signs in front of the building’s restaurant with names of mothers who have been detained and deported. Jeremy M. Jacobs Sr. is the recent former chairman of the NHL’s Board of Governors and owner of the Boston Bruins, so protestors crashed the National Hockey League draft in June, which took place in Buffalo.

There were around 80 people at a protest and vigil at the building that I attended on July 25, organized to honor the lives and memories of those who have been killed by ICE and DHS. Labor activists, faith leaders, poets, and representatives from refugee organizations all spoke. Dozens marched around downtown Buffalo after the rally.

“If you really care about Buffalo, you shouldn’t be putting the safety of your pocketbook over the safety of Buffalonians’ lives,” Alicia Huff, a community activist who co-facilitated the action, told Truthout.

The campaign says it has around 85 volunteers, including new organizers who have joined canvassing teams, led protests, and managed social media efforts. It has an ongoing petition that it says over 6,000 people have signed. It sent letters directly to Uniland asking it not to renew ICE’s lease and Delaware North asking it to advocate against the lease’s renewal. The campaign told Truthout it has not received any responses.

Organizers say that one indicator of the campaign’s influence came in August when the Erie County executive, Mark Poloncarz, cancelled a planned DHS job fair that was scheduled at a government-owned building. The city of Buffalo also recently ended free downtown parking for ICE officials.

Amid loud chants of “Evict ICE!” at the July 25 protest, organizers stated their commitment to see the campaign through to victory. “We’re going to show how much opposition the entire city of Buffalo has to ICE’s field office existing here,” said Tom Griffin, another rally co-facilitator.

“We’re going to continue standing in solidarity with all of Buffalo,” said Griffin.

Power Mapping

The Buffalo campaign can also be seen as one expression of a wider strategy being deployed by movements across the U.S.: attempting to isolate and ostracize ICE by driving a wedge between the agency and the public-facing corporations and billionaires that enable its operations.

Nationally, for example, organizers across the U.S. successfully pressured Avelo Airlines to end its contract with ICE to carry out deportation flights. Additionally, activists have targeted hotels like Hilton that house ICE agents who invade localities to carry out the Trump administration’s deportation agenda.

This corporate-focused strategy has a clear logic. While movements today lack the immediate capacity to compel the abolition of ICE at the federal level, they can create friction between the agency and businesses it depends upon.

Many corporations that work with ICE have vulnerabilities. They depend on a healthy brand image or desire public subsidies. Through their sponsorships, donations, and executive and board member connections, ICE-tied corporations often have a wide presence across local and regional philanthropic, educational, and cultural institutions — all of which widen the surface area for activists to protest and confront them locally.

In Buffalo, the use of “power mapping” — researching and visualizing the relationships of entities and individuals that undergird the local power structure — has been particularly important for campaign strategy. The Evict ICE website includes visual maps of the campaign’s main corporate targets, revealing their extensive imprint across Buffalo institutions and civic and cultural life.

“Montante Detention Center”

This power mapping, in turn, cracks open tactical possibilities for organizers to protest, shame, and isolate corporate targets.

Around 50 protesters gathered on the steps of the Montante Cultural Center at Canisius University on the afternoon of Friday, September 25, asking the Catholic and Jesuit institution, a flagship Buffalo school, to join the Evict ICE campaign, and demanding it use its longstanding relationship with the Montantes, a major university donor, to pressure the family to not renew ICE’s lease at Uniland’s 250 Delaware Avenue building.

Rush-hour traffic — insofar as it exists in Buffalo — whipped by as students and alumni spoke passionately about the need for Canisius to live up to its “social justice” Jesuit values.

“I am not here just to shame my school, but to ask them to do better,” Canisius alumnus Lauren Narbe told the crowd, adding that the Montantes “are profiting off of someone’s family being ripped apart.”

“We ask that Canisius be on the right side of history, even when their largest donor is the Montante family,” Narbe said.

Canisius told Truthout in a formal statement that “we are aware of the demonstration taking place near campus and understand people’s right to express their views peacefully.”

The campaign escalated the next day, on September 26, when eight campaign activists, supported by a hundred picketers, blocked the intersection in front of 250 Delaware for two hours.

The protesters staged the action to rechristen the 12-story building the “Montante Detention Center.”

“We are renaming the ‘Delaware North’ building to reflect its owners’ abuse and greed: Montante Detention Center,” the activists said in a statement.

The eight activists who sat down in the intersection were arrested on charges of “disorderly conduct.”

“I find it ironic that the Buffalo Police Department arrested us for ‘disorderly conduct’ for a peaceful protest, when ICE agents are allowed to brutalize and abduct our neighbors every day,” said one arrestee in the press release.

Truthout reached out to both Uniland and Delaware North for comment on this article but did not receive responses.

On September 27, the Buffalo News published a prepared statement from Uniland saying the company was “legally and contractually obligated to honor all lease agreements and abide by their terms, just as we do with every client” and that “as with all lease agreements, the lease renewal is governed by previously agreed upon contractual terms and conditions.”

From Eviction to Abolition

The Evict ICE campaign has a ticker atop its website counting down the days until ICE’s lease in the Delaware North Building expires.

In the meantime, organizers plan to continue to ramp up protests against ICE’s corporate enablers. In a place like Buffalo, the purported “City of Good Neighbors,” this means breaking through surface-level civility and forcing powerful people — who otherwise enjoy fine local repute in polite society — to make clear which side they’re on.

“It’s very easy for Uniland to not respond,” said Forti. “To get them to evict ICE, we need to be disrupting them more and make it impossible for them to ignore us.”

I asked Harper Bishop, a key leader in the campaign, what victory would look like.

“Victory would look like ICE no longer operating its regional headquarters in downtown Buffalo,” he said, adding that this would represent an “incremental win” toward ICE’s abolition.

“Having ICE leave one building isn’t enough,” Bishop added. “This campaign is giving people the feeling that their voices and actions matter and they have the power to change material conditions on the ground.”

“It’s bringing people into the place of fighting for what we ultimately need: ICE out of Buffalo and abolished completely,” he said.

text:
Trump administration is pushing more than $175 million of the State Department’s flagship human rights fund toward conservative and far-right initiatives abroad just before funding expired on September 30. Approximately $176.9 million out of $205 million appropriated for the HRDF was moved into 43 specific awards.

Among the awards were a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund support led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC). Another was for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a $1 million campaign against Brazil’s Supreme Court. The Trump administration has clashed with the Lula government and has imposed sanctions on Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes.

A third is focused on Nigeria, where the administration has alleged “mass slaughter” of Christians. Millions earmarked to build a “western civilizational norms” in Europe, fund right-wing media consortiums, and document what the administration terms "democratic backsliding" tied to mass migration and supranational regulations. The new slate includes opposition to regulation, Brexit, immigration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.

Add WION as a Preferred Source

Also Read: Diesel crisis deepens as global supplies shrink, crack spreads hit record highs

“The President promised to combat the destructive woke agenda that has done so much damage to our country and to the world,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said. “We will never apologise for defending Western civilisation, opposing censorship, ending the era of mass migration, and taking action against government-sponsored race-based discrimination in South Africa.”

The funding allocation marks a major shift in US foreign policy, moving away from traditional human rights and democracy support in repressive or authoritarian nations to fund ideological allies and causes in established democracies. It is consistent with the US National Security Strategy, where it had mentioned prioritising the protection of Western civilisation in Europe, which the US think is facing a “civilisational erasure”.

text:
The future of the H-1B temporary visa program remains in limbo, with Vice President JD Vance signaling he would support eliminating the system entirely — a program designed to allow American companies to employ skilled foreign workers.

The program has become a frequent target of the Trump administration as part of its broader immigration crackdown, with officials arguing the system has allowed companies to bypass qualified American workers in favor of cheaper foreign labor. (TNND)

My view is the H-1B program is completely broken. And I'd be very supportive of just eliminating it. But while we have it, what we have to do is protect American workers. So I understand people are annoyed. What I would say is tell your congressman to fix this program," Vance said.

The program has become a frequent target of the Trump administration as part of its broader immigration crackdown, with officials arguing the system has allowed companies to bypass qualified American workers in favor of cheaper foreign labor. In 2025, President Trump signed an executive order imposing a $100,000 fee on H-1B visa applications, a dramatic increase from the previous cost of roughly $2,500 to $5,000.

"The whole idea is no more will these big tech companies or other big companies train foreign workers. They have to pay the government $100,000. Then they have to pay the employee. So it's just non-economic," Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said in September 2025. "If you're going to train somebody, you're going to train one of the recent graduates from one of the great universities across our land. Train Americans. Stop bringing in people to take our jobs."

Trump extended the fee for another year this September, but the policy has since become tied up in legal challenges, with federal judges in both Massachusetts and California ruling against it. The fight is far from over, and the program's ultimate fate may ultimately be decided in the courts rather than through legislation or executive action alone.

Tech companies have largely pushed back against the added barrier, arguing that access to top global talent is essential to their operations. "From my standpoint, I'm like, 'We have a lot of difficulty finding enough talented people to get these difficult tasks done. And so more talented people would be good,'" SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in November 2025. "Some of the outsourcing companies have kind of gamed the system on the H-1B front. And we need to stop the gaming of the system, you know? But I'm certainly not in the school of thought that we should shut down the H-1B program."

The executive order specifically targeted hiring from outside the United States, a category that saw roughly 35,000 to 40,000 visas awarded annually before the new fee took effect. According to the White House, that number has plummeted to around 700 over the past year, a dramatic drop that supporters see as evidence the policy is working as intended, while critics warn it could cost American companies access to talent they need to remain competitive globally.

text:
A judge ruled that a federal law banning noncitizen voting is unconstitutional, dismissing a case against an illegal immigrant who allegedly voted in the 2020 election.

U.S. District Judge David Leibowitz for the Southern District of Florida, a Biden appointee, on Thursday threw out a federal charge of illegal voting against Chelsea Michelle Ann Cox, a Jamaican national who allegedly cast a ballot in the 2020 presidential election, Reuters reported.

Federal prosecutors alleged that Cox knowingly voted in Broward County, Fla., on Oct. 29, 2020, in a misdemeanor charge filed against her last year. Cox allegedly overstayed a tourist visa, using a fake U.S. Virgin Islands birth certificate to obtain identification and register to vote.

Leibowitz wrote in his 31-page opinion that a federal ban on noncitizen voting couldn’t be used to support Cox’s prosecution since the U.S. Constitution says that states generally determine voter eligibility.

The case focused on a 1996 federal law that generally prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, Florida Politics reported. Violating the law is punishable by up to a year in prison, a fine, or both.

In his ruling, Leibowitz cited Article I, Article II, and the 17th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which he interpreted as reserving authority for the states to determine who is eligible to vote in federal elections.

“When you’re prosecuted based on a law that Congress did not have the authority to pass, the prosecution cannot stand,” Leibowitz wrote.

He said that Congress can regulate election procedures, but that authority does not generally extend to determining the electorate.

“To hold otherwise would allow Congress to establish and modify the parameters of its own special electorate, entirely divorced from what Florida or any other State may decide,” Leibowitz said. “That result is precisely what our federal constitutional republic does not allow.”

Leibowitz rejected prosecutors’ arguments that the federal law was valid because of congressional powers over immigration, foreign affairs, and election administration.

The ruling ended Cox’s federal prosecution for now, but left Florida’s citizenship requirement for voting intact and did not resolve her potential deportation by the federal government.

Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival posted on X on Friday regarding the ruling, mocking politicians who have denied that noncitizens have voted in elections.

"A Biden appointed judge in Florida says that federal bans on noncitizen voting are unconstitutional. The thing that never happens is now 'constitutionally protected activity!'" Percival wrote.

The Florida ruling comes after the Supreme Court last week cleared the way for the Trump administration to use its revamped federal voter eligibility database to ensure that noncitizens do not vote in elections.

Hans von Spakovsky, Senior Legal Fellow at Advancing American Freedom, said in a statement on Friday regarding the ruling, "Judge David Leibowitz’s opinion that the federal law barring aliens from voting is unconstitutional is patently wrong. It is true that states have the constitutional authority to set the qualifications of citizens who are eligible as voters in federal elections. But he ignores the fact that in Article I, Section 8, Congress is given 100% authority over naturalization.

"In other words, Congress has plenary authority over the admittance of aliens and the standards under which they are allowed to be in the U.S. That gives the federal government the authority to ban aliens from voting or otherwise in any way participating in the democratic process," he continued, later adding, "This is an obviously wrong decision that will be squashed by the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals."

“All flow from the mistaken conclusion that there is a special property or legal interest in access to the White House,” they wrote.
The White House has also continued to block CNN from performing its duties as part of the five-network television pool that shares resources to broadcast coverage of the president.

Circuit court precedent says the White House may not arbitrarily deny a journalist a press credential because press access to the White House is protected by the First Amendment and may not be revoked without due process.
text:
The Trump administration on Friday insisted that it has a right to ban journalists from three national news organizations from accessing the White House as a federal judge weighs whether to restore access to the journalists indefinitely while the legal battle continues.

In a new court filing, the Department of Justice argued against a court order that would reverse President Donald Trump’s press ban and restore access to MS NOW, CNN and Politico. The government has maintained that the president’s ban is lawful.

The administration maintained that its actions are lawful under the First Amendment, and are not retaliatory or viewpoint discrimination.

They also alleged that due process was given, pointing to the letters the White House sent to the news organizations after the ban went into effect. Those letters purported to give the news organizations the opportunity to respond to the expulsion.

“Plaintiffs declined to submit any response, request any extension, or otherwise defend their conduct. Accordingly, at 5:00pm last Friday, the President’s preliminary decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ continued access to the White House, though temporarily enjoined from continuing in effect, became final,” they wrote in the filing.

The government’s attorneys said the news organizations’ main arguments are flawed. “All flow from the mistaken conclusion that there is a special property or legal interest in access to the White House,” they wrote. “There is not.”

Theodore Boutrous, attorney for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, responded to Friday’s filing in a statement: “The White House’s filing tonight shows the President’s ‘ban on the free press’ is indefensible. The law is absolutely clear. The harm to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. It is critical that the White House is enjoined to keep this unconstitutional ban on the free press out of commission.”

Kelly will hear arguments on the media organizations’ request for a longer-term block on the administration’s access ban on Thursday– the same day his current order is set to expire. But he indicated he intends to hear arguments and “rule expeditiously.”

On Monday, lawyers representing the three affected news organizations asked U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly to block Trump’s ban while litigation continues. If granted, that order would extend the emergency relief Kelly handed down last week when he blocked the ban for two weeks.

Lawyers for the three news organizations again argued the ban violated both the First Amendment and the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment. They said without longer-term relief, the Trump administration would revive the ban.

“The White House’s words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstate a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity,” lawyers for the news organizations wrote. “Because the ban is an unlawful assault on the most fundamental First Amendment freedoms and will inflict irreparable harm on Plaintiffs and the public if not restrained.”

More articles

It took the White House nearly 12 hours to reinstate the journalists’ press credentials after Kelly issued his ruling. The White House has also continued to block CNN from performing its duties as part of the five-network television pool that shares resources to broadcast coverage of the president.

Kelly has not yet addressed the news organizations’ First Amendment claims. When he blocked the ban last week, he only ruled on due process grounds. He found the Trump administration had not given the journalists appropriate due process before enacting the ban and confiscating press credentials.

“The record is bereft of any relevant ‘formally articulated standards’ in place before any of the conduct for which the Defendants revoked their hard passes,” Kelly wrote. “One standard Defendants appear to offer – reflected in letters they sent to plaintiffs on September 22, 2026, identifying their objectionable reporting– is so vague it hardly does the trick.”

“Moreover, Defendants renewed Plaintiff Betsy Klein’s hard pass several months after she published some of the identified reporting, undercutting any argument that she or her employer, for example, had the requisite notice that the conduct at issue violated a relevant standard,” Kelly added.

Kelly issued a similar ruling in 2018 when he oversaw a legal challenge after the White House revoked then-CNN correspondent Jim Acosta’s credentials. Kelly found the White House had not given Acosta due process and ordered the Trump administration to restore the credential. Acosta chose to voluntarily dismiss the case before Kelly had the opportunity to address the First Amendment claims.

Circuit court precedent says the White House may not arbitrarily deny a journalist a press credential because press access to the White House is protected by the First Amendment and may not be revoked without due process.

The First Amendment issues in this case remain unsettled, as the news organizations continue to argue Trump’s ban was both retaliatory and blatant viewpoint discrimination.

text:
The Trump administration announced an immediate appeal Friday, a day after a federal judge issued a startling ruling finding that Congress doesn’t have the power to outlaw noncitizens casting ballots in federal elections.

Judge David Leibowitz’s decision applies, for now, only to the single criminal case before him. But his reasoning, if it stands, could undercut dozens of criminal cases the Trump administration has brought against noncitizens in recent months for casting ballots.

Judge Leibowitz, a Biden appointee to the court in southern Florida, said the Constitution gives states the role of determining voters’ qualifications — and states do generally bar noncitizens from voting.

But he said that leaves no room for Congress, so a law barring noncitizens from voting stretches beyond Capitol Hill’s purview.

“Congress has no power to say who can vote or who cannot vote in federal elections,” he wrote. “Some legal principles are so fundamental that they form American constitutional bedrock, and this case reveals a big one: When you’re prosecuted based on a law that Congress did not have the authority to pass, the prosecution cannot stand.”

He tossed the federal misdemeanor case against Chelsea Cox, an illegal immigrant who had been charged in October 2025 with voting in the 2020 election.

Hans von Spakovsky, senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, said he expects Judge Leibowitz’s ruling “will be squashed” by the appeals court.

He said while states get to set voters’ qualifications, Congress has power over immigration matters — and what flows from that.

“That gives the federal government the authority to ban aliens from voting or otherwise in any way participating in the democratic process,” he said.

Mr. von Spakovsky pointed to a 2011 decision authored by future Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh who ruled noncitizens with temporary status didn’t have the right to make contributions to political campaigns. Justice Kavanaugh said the Supreme Court has “long held that the government … may exclude foreign citizens from activities that are part of democratic self-government in the United States.”

That, Justice Kavanaugh said, included ruling “that the government may bar aliens from voting.”

The federal law criminalizing noncitizen voting is actually relatively new, dating back to 1996.

Judge Leibowitz said no federal court had been asked to rule on its constitutionality until recently.

He said the Constitution does give Congress the power to regulate the times, places and manner of federal elections, but that can’t be stretched to allow barring an entire category of people.

Judge Leibowitz said states are still free to bar noncitizens from casting ballots. Some are explicit in preventing it for all elections, while others only bar it for statewide offices and allow localities to make their own decisions.

That has spawned a recent rush of jurisdictions attempting to allow noncitizens to vote in local matters.

The District of Columbia explicitly allows noncitizens, including illegal immigrants, to vote on city issues, but not federal offices.

And a number of small cities in Maryland have adopted noncitizen voting for local matters.

Judge Leibowitz said Congress may have the power to prescribe immigration consequences, such as deportation, for noncitizens who vote. Indeed, such a law exists, and has recently been flexed by the Trump administration.

The judge said he wasn’t deciding on that law’s constitutionality in the Cox case.

In the early days of the republic noncitizen voting was common. Judge Leibowitz noted that all 13 original states allowed noncitizen voting in some fashion.

That began to change in the early 19th century, though the last state to bar noncitizen voting was Arkansas in 1926.

President Trump has claimed that noncitizen voting is rampant and is skewing U.S. elections. Voting rights groups challenge that idea, saying there’s scant evidence of the practice.

The Justice Department, seeking to bolster Mr. Trump’s claim, has initiated more than 60 cases since January 2025.

Ms. Cox, a citizen of Jamaica, came to the U.S. in 1999 on a tourist visa but never left.

Authorities said she used a bogus birth certificate to obtain a Florida driver’s license, then registered to vote in the state in 2012.

She falsely claimed to have been born in the U.S. Virgin Islands, prosecutors said.

She voted in 2012, 2016, 2018 and 2020 — though only the last of those was charged. The others fell outside the statute of limitations.

Ms. Cox had fought her case on several fronts, including accusing prosecutors of racism. She said she was being singled out because she was a Black immigrant.
