title: ICE contract reveals network infrastructure behind HSI surveillance operations
description:
HSI’s Technical Operations arm manages the agency’s Title III and linguistics programs.
These connections allow investigative data to flow from the providers into the TechOps network and then to Title III investigative equipment.
Connectivity is one layer of a larger interception system The Spectrum contract is only one layer of HSI’s communications interception infrastructure.
ICE says the services support nationwide Title III operations “in support of Executive Order 14385,” signed February 6.
A review by Biometric Update found no other public DHS or ICE document specifically connecting the order to Title III operations.
text:
An inadvertent change to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations’ internet service provider caused months of downtime for HSI wiretaps in 2025, according to a procurement document that provides an unusually detailed look at the network infrastructure supporting the agency’s communications interception system.

ICE disclosed the disruption in justifying a new sole-source contract with Cox Virginia Telcom LLC, now part of Charter Communications operating under the Spectrum brand, to maintain dedicated Internet circuits for HSI’s Title III and Linguistics Unit.

The September 25 award has a potential value of about $702,885 over a base year and two option years.

Title III is the federal framework governing court-authorized interception of wire, oral and electronic communications. HSI’s Technical Operations arm manages the agency’s Title III and linguistics programs.

Federal contracting records say the circuits are “vital to the resilience and effectiveness” of the program.

Static IP addresses connect HSI to telecom providers

The sole-source justification shows how much of the resulting interception infrastructure depends on comparatively mundane networking technology.

HSI says its main site in Lorton, Virginia, and regional core sites act as routing hubs for Title III wiretaps and another capability ICE redacted from the document.

Intercept data arrives from telecommunications and electronic communications providers over connections tied to static internet Protocol addresses supplied by Cox. Those addresses are then provided to telecommunications companies so they can establish secure tunnels between their networks and HSI TechOps.

These connections allow investigative data to flow from the providers into the TechOps network and then to Title III investigative equipment.

ICE says its current static IP addresses are tied into connections with roughly 50 telecommunications providers.

That architecture became a problem in April 2025.

According to ICE, an inadvertent change to HSI’s internet service provider resulted in a new IP address, which in turn caused “months of downtime for wiretaps” and another redacted capability while the connections were painstakingly rebuilt.

ICE says the experience represents the worst-case scenario it is trying to avoid by retaining its current provider. Changing carriers now, it says, would again require HSI to obtain new static IP addresses and re-establish connections with roughly 50 providers, many of which will not pre-negotiate or pre-configure the replacement connections.

The procurement document does not identify the investigations affected by the 2025 outage or specify how many interceptions were unavailable.

ICE warns that losing Title III capabilities for weeks or months could disrupt criminal investigations and potentially affect the safety of undercover agents, officers and the public.

Spectrum currently provides connectivity to seven HSI sites. Two regional core locations are being relocated without changing the total number of sites.

A separate HSI procurement in Puerto Rico further underscores the importance of persistent IP addressing for interception systems. An August solicitation for internet service at HSI facilities in San Juan requires a static IP address at the Miramar office specifically “to maintain connectivity” of a Telephone Intercept Server.

Connectivity is one layer of a larger interception system

The Spectrum contract is only one layer of HSI’s communications interception infrastructure.

DHS describes ICE’s Title III Digital Collection System as supporting the interception, recording, and monitoring of telephone calls, emails, and other wire, oral, and electronic communications for ICE investigations, interagency task force cases, and investigations conducted by other federal agencies.

ICE awarded the Ottawa, Ontario, Canada-based JSI Telecom a sole-source contract in March 2025 to operate and maintain that Digital Collection System.

Federal award data show about $14.1 million obligated under that contract, which ICE describes as supporting HSI’s Cyber and Operational Technology Division and a system used for court-ordered interception of electronic communications.

JSI’s role in the system is longstanding. A 2011 ICE procurement sought JSI support for the VoiceBox Unified Collection Management system, which is used in the Title III Digital Collection System, indicating that the company’s interception technology has been embedded in the program for well over a decade.

ICE is also spending heavily on the software and personnel surrounding the collection system.

On the same day as the Spectrum award, ICE awarded Herndon, Virginia-based Procentrix a contract potentially worth about $35.4 million for operations, maintenance, enhancements, and releases of what contracting records call the agency’s “current T-III applications” supporting the Title III and Linguistics Unit.

ICE says those applications facilitate investigations and operations that use intercepts to dismantle complex criminal organizations. The competed order received two bids.

Separately, the Ashburn, Virginia-based KACE Company holds a five-year ICE order now valued at up to $126.9 million for monitoring, transcription, and translation services supporting HSI criminal investigations nationwide.

Together, the contracting records describe different pieces of the same operational environment: Spectrum provides dedicated connectivity between HSI locations and external providers, JSI maintains the digital collection system, Procentrix supports applications for the Title III and Linguistics Unit, and KACE provides large-scale monitoring, transcription, and translation services.

The infrastructure sits alongside other communications surveillance technologies used by HSI. Biometric Update reported earlier this year on ICE’s long-running relationship with PenLink, whose technology is used to collect and analyze court-authorized wiretap data, as well as other communications and location information. Lawmakers have also scrutinized ICE’s use of PenLink commercial cellphone location tools, warning that such data purchases may allow location surveillance without the judicial process associated with traditional wiretaps.

The Spectrum justification also makes a less obvious connection to a recent White House directive. ICE says the services support nationwide Title III operations “in support of Executive Order 14385,” signed February 6. The order itself does not mention Title III, wiretaps or communications interception. Its operative provisions focus on giving DHS access to criminal history information for screening and vetting and allowing certain exchanges of that information with foreign governments.

The procurement record does not explain the connection. The underlying wiretap infrastructure also predates the order: the previous Spectrum purchase order was awarded in August 2025, while the network failure ICE cites occurred in April 2025.

What the new filing establishes is narrower: ICE now describes an existing nationwide Title III capability as operating in support of the executive order, even though the public directive itself concerns criminal-history information and screening rather than electronic interception. A review by Biometric Update found no other public DHS or ICE document specifically connecting the order to Title III operations.

authors: Morgan Chilson, Baya Burgess, Anna Kaminski

text:
DODGE CITY — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrived in southwest Kansas on Sept. 22 and departed three days later, leaving fear, uncertainty and anger.

Many in the Hispanic and Latino communities in Dodge City, Garden City and Liberal, where most ICE activity was located, returned to work this week. But their fear persists and they aren’t yet leaving their homes or returning to regular activities, multiple immigrants said.

The fear was contagious. In Manhattan, about 225 miles east of Dodge City, social media posts blasted warnings of possible ICE agents on Thursday because of a large presence of law enforcement vehicles in a store parking lot. It turned out to be a training session for local police, according to a store employee.

Here are a handful of glimpses into the lives of Kansans affected by the raids.

Viridiana Boron, volunteer

Viridiana Boron spent several days last week delivering meals to Dodge City families whose members were scared to leave home because ICE was in the area.

Her mother and sister cooked meals for about 200 people, and Boron delivered them, she said.

“I was the one that was on the street and watching everything, watching all the suffer the families was having,” she said, pausing to apologize for her English. “I saw the reality, the truth. They were scared. They were sad. They were worried. I saw families with no water.”

Boron started crying.

“It was something that I’ve never seen in my life,” she said. “How can people not have heart and just do things like that? Because I mean, there I know could be a lot of immigrants over here that are like criminals, but a lot of people that I saw, they were not criminals. They were people working hard for their kids.”

This week, many people she knows have returned to work, but they aren’t eating out or shopping as the fear lingers, Boron said.

Boron came to the United States at age 24, receiving a visa because she and her family were threatened in Mexico. She has since married and is a legal permanent resident. Despite knowing she had the correct documentation, she was scared during the ICE operation.

Others who stayed home also had documentation, she said. But they have seen instances where it didn’t matter, and ICE agents stopped cars to check paperwork just because someone looked Hispanic or Latina, Boron said.

The affect on the community was “huge,” she said. It was difficult explaining to her 11-year-old son why people were scared because he didn’t understand the difference a paper could make, Boron said.

“We are all the same,” she said.

Julie Barraza, volunteer and activist

Julie Barraza smiled at everyone approaching the table she set up at a downtown Dodge City protest on Sept. 24. She patiently answered questions about a petition to reform the country’s immigration system.

“I was born and raised here, and I’ve never seen such a cloud over the town,” she said during a break. “The first morning, they (ICE) were waiting for me to get out of my car, and I didn’t know what was going on. I didn’t get out of my car.”

Barraza drove on to work at Rattlesnake Grill. She said ICE agents came in to eat but employees didn’t realize they were with ICE because they wore regular clothing.

“Once we figured out they were ICE agents, because a customer had alerted us, I stepped out and decided to tell them to leave, and they refused,” she recalled. “I was scared, but I still did it.”

The agents did get up and leave, Barraza said, adding that several restaurants in town refused to serve agents and others closed because there weren’t employees to work.

Patrick Lopez, immigrant and educator

Patrick Lopez stood in the midst of a Dodge City protest on Sept. 24, holding a sign and nodding to people he knew. He was there, he said, to “show solidarity with people who are being persecuted by ICE.”

“I’m here to defend my immigrant brothers and sisters. I’m here to stand up for them, and I hate that they have to live in fear right now,” Lopez said. “I can’t sleep last night. I’m offended as an American. I’m embarrassed as an American. I’m indignant. I can’t believe that this is happening right now.”

While acknowledging the economic costs to town — restaurants closed, businesses slowing or stopping work — Lopez said they weren’t what made him toss and turn at night.

“I also wish that people remembered the human rights effect,” he said. “People’s families should be protected. I don’t care what the issue is. You can’t destroy people’s families like that and hopefully get away with it.”

He tried unsuccessfully to reach a friend who drives a cab and worried that he was detained.

“He works every day, and that’s the thing. The people that ICE is after are hardworking people around town,” Lopez said. “Many of them are putting their kids through school. They’re just trying to make a living.”

Sarahí Aguilera, therapist and immigrant

Sarahí Aguilera is a licensed social worker, and she works as a mental health therapist. Advocating for the immigrant community, she said, is at the foundation of her personal and professional life.

She knows the challenges well. Aguilera is part of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, which allows young people who arrived during specific time periods to apply and work in the country.

DACA has been under fire during President Donald Trump’s administration, she said, but she was fortunate that her permit didn’t expire when the program was temporarily halted. Since then, it has been a “consistent uphill battle” to keep the program active, Aguilera said.

Other family members weren’t so lucky. Aguilera’s sister had just been to an immigration appointment after turning 15, which is the age that people can apply for the DACA program, Aguilera said.

“We had started her paperwork. She had been approved. She had gone to her biometrics. I lived at Wichita at the time because that’s where I was getting my education,” she said. “And she got approved. She just never received her work permit.”

It was frustrating because when the family looked her up in the system, it said she was approved, Aguilera said. But she never physically received the approval that would allow her to receive her driver’s license or continue her education.

Her sister eventually married and is in the process of acquiring her documentation, Aguilera said. The experience reminds her how difficult it is to go through the immigration process and how different it is for each person, she said.

“Especially seeing me and believing she was going to have the same opportunity,” Aguilera said. “It really impacted her mental health and her motivation to further her education and just work on herself.”

Aguilera volunteers with New Frontiers, a nonprofit organization that works with young people in southwest Kansas to create a grassroots movement focused on political, social and economic power.

The group has a rapid response team that becomes active when events like ICE raids in the area occur, she said. Volunteers watch for ICE agents and try to verify information before releasing it to the community.

“Fear already does a lot to someone,” Aguilera said. “So fear and the wrong information — we want to make sure that we’re just prepared and grounded with what information we’re trying to share.”

Fear of the unknown is a problem for southwest Kansas immigrants, Aguilera said, along with how overwhelming information coming out could be.

While ICE was in the area, she saw about four clients because most were afraid to go out. Typically, her schedule is full every day.

Aguilera said she understands why some people are critical of immigrants who don’t have documentation.

“There is so much misinformation. I believe as a society we need to do a better job of understanding what the immigration process looks like,” she said. “Of understanding what are the barriers, what are the circumstances? Because there is not a system that is going to work for all of us.”

DACA recipients, for instance, don’t have a pathway to citizenship unless they marry or their jobs petition for them, Aguilera said.

Whatever a person’s belief system, she said, she hopes people are careful with their words.

“I do think it’s important to be mindful of the comments and what they can do to the mental health of someone overall,” she said, adding that people are easily influenced by social media and political figures, who she believes often don’t understand the process either.

Does she think significant immigration reform is likely?

“My heart wants to say that it’s hopeful. My uncertainty and anxiety that I’ve experienced for the past 10 years wants me to have a different answer,” Aguilera said. “I do believe people are opening their eyes. I believe we are getting a lot more information and more attention. Although I think we are creating great awareness and sharing information and education, I don’t believe we will see the impact and the change we want to see until people get out and vote.”

title: US: Victims Of Nicaraguan Government Risk Deportation, HRW Says - Eurasia Review
authors: Eurasia Review, Dr. Sahibzada Muhammad Usman, Dan Steinbock, Dr. Fr. John Singarayar, Robert Reich
description:
People with knowledge of their cases told Human Rights Watch that at least four had pending asylum claims.
In September 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed the legal representative of two of the detainees and the wife of a third.
The detention of another has been reported by news outlets, but Human Rights Watch was unable to independently verify his case.
Deporting Nicaraguan exiles to Honduras or other neighboring countries may place them within reach of the Nicaraguan authorities they fled, Human Rights Watch said.
US authorities should not deport anyone to Nicaragua who faces a risk of persecution or torture there, Human Rights Watch said.
text:
Key Takeaways:

Human Rights Watch says ICE has detained at least eight Nicaraguan exiles stripped of citizenship by Ortega and Murillo, seven of them among the 222 political prisoners expelled to the U.S. on Feb. 9, 2023, and given two-year humanitarian parole; at least four had pending asylum claims.

As of the report, five appeared still detained; journalist Luis Galeano was released on bond Sept. 26 after arrest Sept. 14, and Marvin Castellón Ubilla was released in July. HRW cites non-refoulement rules and warns of third-country transfers (over 1,100 Nicaraguans since Jan. 2025) that could put critics within Managua’s reach.

HRW’s ICE-data analysis says U.S. deportations to Nicaragua reached over 6,300 from January–July 2026, nearly double the same months in 2025, and asks Congress for a count of stateless Nicaraguans in custody and their removal destinations.

US immigration authorities have detained at least eight Nicaraguan exiles whom the Ortega-Murillo government has stripped of their nationality, including some with pending asylum claims, Human Rights Watch said today.

Seven of the people detained were among 222 political prisoners whom the Nicaraguan government expelled to the United States, declared “traitors,” and stripped of their nationality on February 9, 2023. The US government granted them humanitarian parole for two years. The eighth, Luis Galeano, a journalist, was stripped of his nationality on February 15, 2023, along with 93 other government critics. People with knowledge of their cases told Human Rights Watch that at least four had pending asylum claims.

“After offering refuge to these critics of the Nicaraguan government just three years ago, the United States is now detaining and threatening to deport them,” said Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch. “International law prohibits the United States from returning anyone to face the threat of persecution or torture. US authorities should not be trying to send these men back into danger.”

At least two of the eight were arrested during a court appointment or asylum interview between April and September 2026.

It appears that five of the eight men are still in detention. In September 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed the legal representative of two of the detainees and the wife of a third. Human Rights Watch also confirmed through the Online Detainee Locator System, maintained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), that four of the men are currently in ICE custody and reviewed the status of their cases in the Executive Office for Immigration Review’s automated case information system.

The detention of another has been reported by news outlets, but Human Rights Watch was unable to independently verify his case.

Two others have since been released. Galeano was released on bond on September 26. Marvin Castellón Ubilla was released in July after more than two months in ICE custody.

Two of the men had been convicted in Nicaragua on drug charges in cases that Nicaraguan human rights groups describe as politically motivated. One was charged with illegal possession of a regulated firearm in the United States and placed on probation, according to a court order reviewed by Human Rights Watch.

ICE detained Galeano, 48, on September 14. An immigration judge granted him bond on September 23, and he was released on September 26 after being held for several days at the Krome immigration detention center in Miami. His family told Human Rights Watch that he applied for asylum in June 2019, holds a work permit, and has no criminal record in the United States. He has an immigration court hearing scheduled for October 27.

Human Rights Watch has documented abusive conditions at Krome, detainees being held for days in overcrowded and freezing intake cells without bedding, practices that amount to inhuman and degrading treatment. On September 11, the Department of Homeland Security Office of the Inspector General published findings from an unannounced May 2025 inspection of Krome. It documented violations of medical and use-of-force standards, including the improper use of a chokehold on a detainee.

Under Co-Presidents Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo, Nicaragua has become one of the most authoritarian countries in the Western Hemisphere, Human Rights Watch said. Those who criticize the government face prison, exile, and/or the loss of their nationality. The Mechanism for the Recognition of Political Prisoners, a Nicaraguan human rights group, registered at least 68 political prisoners, 31 of whom it considered victims of enforced disappearance, as of September 2026. Between February 2023 and September 2024, the Nicaraguan government stripped 452 Nicaraguans of their nationality and confiscated their property, including the 222 people it expelled to the United States.

The Trump administration has imposed sanctions on numerous Nicaraguan officials for their role in repression.

The US government has sharply increased deportations to Nicaragua. Based on a Human Rights Watch analysis of Immigration and Customs Enforcement data, the government deported over 6,300 Nicaraguans between January and July 2026, nearly twice the 3,323 for the same period in 2025. According to media reports, many Nicaraguan deportees face surveillance upon return.

US authorities are also increasingly deporting Nicaraguans to third countries. Since January 2025, over 1,100 Nicaraguans, including 400 through July 2026, have been sent to third countries, including 864 to Mexico, 63 to El Salvador, 50 to Guatemala, 49 to Honduras, and 26 to Panama, Human Rights Watch analysis of ICE data has found.

In November 2025, the US deported Juan Barilla to Honduras. He is a peasant who had spent over two years in prison and was among the 222 people expelled to the United States in 2023.

In March 2026, the UN Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua reported that the government runs a transnational “surveillance and intelligence network … to identify, monitor and target exiled Nicaraguans.” It documented at least a dozen killings or attempted killings of exiled critics, including the June 2025 murder in San José, Costa Rica, of retired army major Roberto Samcam. Deporting Nicaraguan exiles to Honduras or other neighboring countries may place them within reach of the Nicaraguan authorities they fled, Human Rights Watch said.

The Convention against Torture prohibits the US government from returning anyone to a country where they would face a real risk of torture. The 1967 Protocol relating to the Status of Refugees also bars returning refugees to face the threat of persecution. This can include indirect returns, in the form of chain deportations from third countries.

US authorities should not deport anyone to Nicaragua who faces a risk of persecution or torture there, Human Rights Watch said. Nor should it deport people to third countries where they face such risks, including through onward deportation to Nicaragua. Anyone facing removal to a third country should receive adequate notice and a meaningful opportunity to challenge it before an immigration judge. While people remain in detention, US authorities should guarantee humane treatment, adequate medical care, and access to their lawyers.

Congress should require the Department of Homeland Security to report how many Nicaraguans who have been stripped of citizenship are in ICE custody, how long they have been detained, and which countries have been designated for their removal.

text:
The Supreme Court temporarily cleared the Trump administration to continue its third-country deportation policy this week, as DHS’ top lawyer mounts a public defense of an immigration authority the administration says previous presidents largely left dormant.

DHS has increasingly used so-called "third-country" removals when a removable alien cannot be returned to their home country or that country refuses to take them back — part of what agency General Counsel James Percival describes as a broader Trump strategy of reviving immigration authorities already on the books.

"Imagine going to a country and saying, hey, we've got a guy, he's not your guy, and he's a rapist, but can he please live there?" Percival told Fox News Digital.

"That's not an easy ask. It requires significant diplomatic energy… Norway is not taking a rapist from Cuba."

TRUMP’S SPECIAL STRATEGY TO DEPORT ILLEGALS GIVES HIM ANOTHER TOOL FOR ENFORCEMENT

The justices on Tuesday stayed a lower-court judgment restricting DHS’s policy, allowing the administration’s guidance to remain in effect while the Court considers the case on the merits. Arguments are set for December over whether agency procedures comply with federal immigration law, due process and safeguards against torture.

The case does not squarely challenge DHS’s underlying authority to conduct third-country removals, but rather the procedures it must follow beforehand.

"It’s in the statute expressly that we can do this," he said. "If you go back and read most of the immigration laws, there's a lot of really good tools in there that people just haven't used."

The third-country provision was included in a major immigration reform package passed by Congress and signed by President Bill Clinton in 1996: the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA).

"A lot of people in government sort of treat their authority like fine china," Percival remarked.

"They're afraid if they ever actually use it, someone will take it away. And if you've ever owned fine china, it's like you can find yourself at the end of your life and you were so afraid you would break it you never used it."

TRUMP’S FIGHT OVER RARELY USED 18TH-CENTURY DEPORTATION LAW LIVES ON IN LATEST COURT CLASH

But Percival’s strategy has not come without blowback from human rights advocates, who pointed most recently to allegations that deportees were beaten by authorities in Equatorial Guinea, a tiny nation on Africa’s Atlantic coast that has been under the control of President Teodoro Obiang since 1979.

Obiang's government received $7.5 million from Washington as part of an agreement with Malabo to accept third-country deportations.

"I’d rather live in the United States than Equatorial Guinea too, but I’m an American citizen and I haven’t killed anybody," Percival said.

The detention issue traces in part to the Supreme Court’s 2001 decision in a case involving a stateless legal resident whom the government ordered deported due to his criminal record. Kestutis Zadvydas was born to Lithuanian parents in a German displaced- persons camp, but neither Lithuania nor Germany would accept him.

The court held that six months of post-removal detention is presumptively reasonable, after which continued detention can be challenged if removal is not reasonably foreseeable.

Percival is making that case publicly through his "Daily Deportee" series on X, highlighting criminal deportees whose home countries will not accept them.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"If the person is a child rapist and serves 20 years, we have two choices: Find a third country — or let the child rapist go live in an American community," he said, adding that the effort is intended to shape public understanding of the issue and highlight its stakes.

Percival cited Burmese national Kyaw Mya, whose home country won’t take him back.

"[He] tried to kill somebody, the gun misfired, so he pistol-whipped them instead. He served time for that. He got out," Percival explained.

authors: Jarvis DeBerry, Cedric Alexander, Clarissa-Jan Lim, Jillian Frankel, The Associated Press

text:
The lawsuits filed this week by the survivors of Renee Good, who was shot dead Jan. 7 by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Jonathan Ross in Minneapolis, make the general claim that Ross had no reason for killing the 37-year-old mother of three. But plaintiffs make two more specific allegations that particularly trouble me as a 40-year law enforcement veteran who trained other officers.

The lawsuits say at least one ICE agent told Good, who was in the driver’s seat of an SUV, that she could leave the scene where ICE agents were working at about the same time other agents were ordering her out of her car. The lawsuits also allege that agents at the scene not only failed to provide aid to Good after she was shot but also stopped a doctor from trying to help her.

These are but allegations. The government has claimed Ross fired in self-defense because he feared she was about to run over him with her vehicle, and a court may eventually decide whether he was justified. But the allegations that Good was given conflicting orders and denied medical aid after she’d been shot describe failures I’ve seen before and know have no place in professional policing.

As someone who has led police officers, I have defended them when they are right. I know a vehicle can kill an officer as surely as a gun can, and agents are right to respect that. But that’s why sound training tells officers to step out of a vehicle’s path rather than fire into it. The Department of Homeland Security’s own policy bars deadly force used simply to stop someone from driving away. Video taken at the scene suggests Ross got in front of Good’s car when he didn’t have to.

According to the Good survivors’ lawsuit, in the incident in question, “ICE agents got out of their vehicle, with one instructing: ‘Out of the car. Get out of the f—ing car.’ On information and belief, another ICE agent gave Renee an instruction to leave the scene.”

Put yourself in Good’s seat. One officer says go. Another says get out. A third has a hand on your door. Whatever you do, you are disobeying someone. And whatever you do can later be called resistance. Good trainers teach one rule for this: one voice. When several officers approach a subject, one gives commands and the others cover. That is not courtesy. It is tactical. A person given conflicting orders cannot comply, and officers who give them cannot predict what happens next. Confusion breeds fear. Fear breeds gunfire.

Minnesota is familiar with allegations of conflicting commands. In 2016, a St. Anthony police officer pulled over motorist Philando Castile who answered affirmatively when the officer asked him if he was armed. (Castile had a permit to carry a handgun.) Seconds later, the officer fired seven shots into Castile’s car and shouted, “I told him not to reach for it.” Castile’s girlfriend, who was in the passenger seat, responded, “You told him to get his ID, sir, his driver’s license.” The police officer was later acquitted of manslaughter, but St. Anthony, without admitting blame, settled with Castile’s family for nearly $3 million to avoid a federal wrongful death lawsuit.

When commands cannot be obeyed, they stop being commands. They become a pretext. I don’t believe most officers set such a trap on purpose. But the person in the car pays the same price either way.

The allegation that agents denied Good medical aid after she was shot and prevented others from helping is even harder to stomach, but it is supported by bystander video that was reported by newsrooms in January. Included in that video was a person asking if he could help Good and telling the ICE agent he was a physician. The agent responded, “I don’t care.”

I’ll be candid. One of Ross’ bullets entered Good’s temple and exited the other side of her head. It is unlikely any doctor on that street could have saved her. But that grim fact changes absolutely nothing about the duty to aid. No one at that scene knew the wound was fatal.

More articles

At the time, a DHS spokesperson defended the agents’ lack of aid by saying Good did not have a pulse. But officers are neither physicians nor coroners. Duty requires them to begin aid, or allow it, until someone qualified takes over. DHS own use-of-force policy calls for medical assistance for people injured by force.

Again, this is an issue Minneapolis already knows a lot about. In 2020, as Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin kept his knee planted on George Floyd’s neck, an off-duty Minneapolis firefighter begged officers to let her check Floyd’s pulse. They refused to let her do so. Her testimony helped convict Chauvin.

There is a deeper point. What officers do after force is used tells the public who they are. An officer who fires and then rushes to stop the bleeding shows that force was used to end a threat, not to punish a person. Officers who wave off a doctor send the opposite message.

Nearly nine months later, no one has been charged in Good’s death. The Department of Justice declined to open a criminal investigation, and Minnesota officials have accused federal agencies of withholding evidence. DHS said it launched an investigation into the shooting, but no details or updates have been released, and the status of that investigation is unclear. DHS did not immediately respond to MS NOW’s questions about the probe.

Civil court is the one door still open to this family. Good’s brother Brent Ganger summed it up: “No accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy.”

The fixes are not radical. Federal agents should be trained and required to use one designated voice for commands. They should render aid or let qualified bystanders do it once a scene is secure. Supervisors should answer when either rule is broken. Every well-run police department I know already works this way.

Being firm and being humane are not opposites. Law enforcement officers are expected to be both. Renee Good deserved clear instructions and a fighting chance. According to her family, she got neither. That is not law and order. It is only force.

title: Newsom signs bill banning forced marriage in California - TheCenterSquare.com
authors: Bethany Blankley, The Center Square contributor
description: (The Center Square) - Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed another bill that advocates hope will end human rights abuses in marriage.
text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom discusses his revised budget during a news conference in Sacramento, May 14, 2026. Photo: Madeline Shannon / The Center Square

(The Center Square) - Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed another bill that advocates hope will end human rights abuses in marriage.

On the same day that Newsom signed a bill to end child marriage in California, he signed a bill to end forced marriage.

Newsom, a Democrat, signed into law Assembly Bill 2534 , introduced by Assemblymember Ash Kalra, D-San Jose - "Domestic Violence Prevention Act: forced marriage."

With the new law, California becomes the first state to create a legal restraining order specifically to protect victims of a forced marriage. The law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Advocates are hoping it is replicated in other states.

Forced marriage is a form of gender-based violence that primarily impacts women and girls. It is classified as a human rights violation and can be part of human trafficking. It is also often linked to child marriage, where girls are the majority of victims.

Many may believe forced marriage is a phenomenon in third world countries. But advocates of AB 2534 argue the practice is widespread, with cases in the U.S., where it's difficult for those in forced marriages to pursue legal protections available for survivors of other forms of domestic violence because of the way the law and restraining orders are written.

AB 2534 amends state law to recognize forced marriage as a form of domestic violence and enables anyone in California, child or adult, to seek a restraining order to prevent a forced marriage before it happens. This includes a marriage in the civil legal system or through a religious or cultural ceremony. The law also applies to anyone already in a forced marriage.

“In creating the country’s first Forced Marriage Restraining Order, California has set itself apart as a leader in the movement to end forced marriage in the United States. This law provides survivors with a critical new tool to protect themselves before a forced marriage occurs and sets an example for similar action across the country,” Tahirih Justice Center public policy manager Alex Goyette said.

“California closed a gap in the law that left survivors of forced marriage without clear civil protections when they needed them most,” said Sadia Khan, policy advocate at Family Violence Law Center and a forced marriage survivor. “For more than 12 years, my own story showed where California law fell short.”

She described in gruesome detail her experience of a forced marriage when testifying in support of the bill before a California Assembly committee.

"I know what it feels like to have your choices taken from you, to believe no one can stop what’s happening, and to discover that the law doesn’t have a clear answer for your situation," Khan told The Center Square in an email. "The right to choose if, when, and whom you marry is one of the most fundamental freedoms a person has. California has now recognized that survivors deserve protection before irreversible harm occurs, not after.”

Khan said she had to get her restraining order from the United Kingdom, which has had this type of protection on the books for some time, because there was no such protection under California law.

California's new law changes this by giving courts a clear authority to intervene before someone is forced onto a plane, their passport is confiscated or they are pulled out of school to be forced into a marriage, advocacy groups argue.

In the U.S., the practice is predominantly found in immigrant communities.

In 2011, the Tahirih Justice Center published a report stating that its staff had noticed an “increasing number of forced marriage cases involving young women and girls — some as young as 13 — from traditional immigrant communities in the United States. By force, fraud, or coercion, they were being compelled to marry men from their families’ countries or regions of origin, and — if the young woman was a U.S. citizen — she might then be forced to sponsor a fiancé or spouse visa to enable the groom to come to the United States.”

The center also surveyed more than 500 social service agencies nationwide that reported encountering 3,000 suspected and confirmed forced marriage cases. Among them, 67% of services providers said that forced marriage cases weren’t being properly identified in their caseload. As a result, it believed at the time that the number was much higher.

Forced marriages were identified in immigrant communities from 56 countries, impacting people of different backgrounds and faiths, according to the report.

The Tahirih Justice Center has published a range of resources to help those trapped in a force marriage.

title: Faith Leaders Embark on an Eight-Day Pilgrimage to Protest ICE Detentions
description:
Left: Rabbi Goldberg, an organizer of the pilgrimage, places a flower in front of the Adelanto ICE Processing Center.
Right: Flowers are laid out in front of the entrance to the Adelanto ICE Processing Center.
Faith leaders and activists begin their pilgrimage to Los Angeles from Adelanto, dwarfed by the pylons and powerlines that stretch across the Mojave Desert.

text:
The Trump administration’s aggressive crackdown on immigrants has prompted boisterous street protests in Minneapolis, New York and Chicago, as well as quieter acts of resistance, including, most recently, an eight-day pilgrimage led by faith-based groups from an immigration detention center in California’s high desert to the downtown Los Angeles Federal Building.

Capital & Main documented the first morning of their journey, which began at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in San Bernardino County, where about 1,800 people were being held as of April. The 96.5-mile trek, which began on Sept. 29 and is expected to wrap up on Tuesday, was organized by the faith-based social justice coalition Clergy and Laity United for Economic Justice (CLUE), Nefesh, a progressive Jewish nonprofit, and Sacred Resistance, the advocacy ministry of the Episcopal Diocese of Los Angeles.

With the sun still low in the sky, dozens of attendees listened to faith leaders deliver speeches about the spiritual significance of resistance. CLUE Executive Director the Rev. Jennifer Gutierrez led the group in prayer before participants placed flowers in front of the detention center’s gates. Then began their long walk to Los Angeles. Organizers said they plan to walk 12 to 16 miles a day, resting at various congregations along the way.

In an interview before the pilgrimage, Gutierrez said the journey was designed to raise awareness about the Trump administration’s treatment of immigrants, who have been “hunted down and kidnapped by ICE,” and the squalid conditions inside the federal detention center in Adelanto.

“People are eating rotten food and don’t have clean water to drink and are existing in terrible temperatures without air conditioning out in the desert,” she said, adding that the journey is also a way “to call one another to be closer to what God wants for us in terms of loving each other.”

At sunrise, attendees begin signing in for the pilgrimage event across the street from the Adelanto ICE Processing Center.

A participant stretches in preparation for the long walk ahead. A cloth with the image of a monarch butterfly — a symbol used by protesters to represent what Nefesh founder Rabbi Susan Goldberg described as the “beauty of migration” — is draped over a sign.

CLUE organizer Sithy Bin — who was arrested by immigration authorities in 2020 and held in Mesa Verde Detention Center — speaks about his personal connection to the fight for immigrants’ rights.

Left: CLUE Executive Director the Rev. Jennifer Gutierrez leads faith leaders and activists in prayer.

Right: Victorville City Council candidate Derek Marshall (seen here wearing a white shirt and tie), stands among protesters while holding a placard honoring Luis Beltran Yanez-Cruz, who died while in ICE custody in California earlier this year.

The Rev. Sam Pullen — an ordained minister in the United Church of Christ — stands in the middle of the street, arms outstretched so as to stop traffic and allow pilgrimage participants to safely cross the street and reach the Adelanto ICE Processing Center. Rabbi Jason van Leeuwen (seen here wearing a tallit, or Jewish prayer shawl) holds a lulav and etrog, sacred plants associated with the Jewish pilgrimage holiday of Sukkot, which happened to overlap with the protest action.

Left: Rabbi Goldberg, an organizer of the pilgrimage, places a flower in front of the Adelanto ICE Processing Center. The rabbi said she got the idea for the event during a fellowship when she learned about the central role pilgrimages play in various ancient faiths.

Right: Flowers are laid out in front of the entrance to the Adelanto ICE Processing Center.

Faith leaders and activists begin their pilgrimage to Los Angeles from Adelanto, dwarfed by the pylons and powerlines that stretch across the Mojave Desert.

Left: Kevin Kang, pastor at Tujunga United Methodist Church, walks eastward away from the Adelanto ICE Processing Center. His church has provided shelter for refugees released from Adelanto after CLUE posted bond for them.

Right: The Rev. Andy Schwiebert, pastor at Immanuel Presbyterian Church in Koreatown, said he was participating in the pilgrimage because “our faith calls us to welcome strangers and this country is a nation of immigrants.” He said a member of his church’s community was detained at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in the fall of 2025.

Less than two miles into the pilgrimage, Angelica Salas (left), the executive director of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, and Gutierrez (right) stop the crowd to announce the breaking news that Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of bills intended to protect immigrant communities in the crosshairs of the Trump administration’s crackdown. Those bills included a ban on shock gloves, which ICE recently announced it would provide officers, and a 25% tax on private detention centers, including the Adelanto ICE Processing Center, which is operated by Boca Raton, Florida-based GEO Group.

Steve Doutt, who is 74, joined the first day of the pilgrimage to “show solidarity for those currently detained in America’s concentration camps” and to affirm the inherent dignity of “all eight billion of us on the planet who were created in the image of God.”

Sacred Resistance’s the Rev. Canon Jaime Edward-Acton (left) points at Scott Shulman, who provided the pilgrims with snacks and beverages on their first planned break of the journey.

Shulman, who left the country to avoid being drafted to fight in the Vietnam War, reminisced about the political protests of his youth. “Back then, we were organized. We protested all the time. People felt like we were facing life or death,” he said. “I think people are too complacent today. … I’ve been telling my friends this is my fuck ICE pilgrimage because I’m angry. I’m angry at our government, our treasonous administration.”

A protester holds up a butterfly cutout as the group continued its march toward Los Angeles.

text:
PHARR, Texas (Border Report) — An analysis of government data by a think tank finds the Trump administration has cut legal immigration by 96% for those coming from majority-Muslim countries this second term.

The analysis by the Cato Institute, released this week, says data from the State Department shows monthly immigrant visa issuances and permanent lawful refugee admissions from the 45 majority-Muslim countries fell from 21,096 in December 2024 to just 808 in February.

The drop is not attributed to season trends, the analysis notes.

Immigrant visas issued to family members dropped by 95%. And refugee resettlements — immigrants admitted lawfully based on threats of persecution abroad — was completely ended for majority-Muslim countries, dropping from 5,157 admissions in December 2024 to zero in February, the analysis found.

“The decline has affected nearly every majority-Muslim nationality in the world,” the report says.

Only nine Afghan people were allowed legally into the United States in February, down from 5,563, the report says.

Only three countries saw increases: Qatar, Indonesia and the United Arab Emirates.

The analysis estimates that if this trend continues then Fiscal Year 2026 “would see the fewest immigrants and refugees from majority-Muslim countries in at least 30 years.”

Spouses and minor children of U.S. citizens and other close family members make up half of immigrants blocked by immigration restrictions from coming to the United States.

When President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, he issued a presidential proclamation that suspended refugee admissions for 120 days. In December, he issued a proclamation that bars entry to the United States by immigrants from 40 countries, of which 10 are majority-Muslim.

Since taking office, the president has issued several directives that freeze legal entry for immigrants into the United States for various reasons.

“Although these policies have affected immigrants from most countries in the world, the cuts for majority-Muslim countries have been far more severe, falling 96 percent compared to 36 percent for other countries,” the report says. “The administration has shown particular contempt for immigrants from Muslim-majority countries.”

Sandra Sanchez can be reached at SSanchez@BorderReport.com.

text:
EL PASO, Texas (Border Report) — Opponents of border construction in the Big Bend region brought their fight to federal court Friday, and they came out with a victory that stops work they say threatens private property, wildlife and historic sites along the Rio Grande.

U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone granted a preliminary injunction blocking the construction of border wall and other border security infrastructure in the Big Bend region.

In the order granting the injunction, Cardone wrote, “The Court finds that Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of at least one of the claims in suit, that there is a likelihood that they will suffer serious, irreparable harm without an injunction, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest weigh in their favor.”

The order says that, effective immediately, the defendants — the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Secretary Markwayne Mullin and U.S. Customs and Border Protection — “SHALL NOT build border barrier or related infrastructure, or engage in any construction or ground disturbing activities, in the Big Bend Sector until and unless Defendants comply with all applicable laws.

The Center for Biological Diversity, one of the plaintiffs, called Cardone’s ruling a “massive, historic victory.”

“This is a historic victory for Big Bend and everyone who loves this wild corner of Texas,” said Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity. “No administration has the right to destroy a crown-jewel national park for political theater. With a federal court ordering the bulldozers to stop, Big Bend gets to breathe. But this fight is far from over. We won’t rest until Big Bend’s environmental protections are fully restored and the illegal waiver that allowed so much destruction is gone for good.”

Cardone had scheduled the hearing to consider a preliminary injunction that would halt border infrastructure construction in Big Bend National Park and the surrounding region while a lawsuit proceeds. The plaintiffs include the Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church and Big Bend-area river guide and landowner Danny William Miller Jr.

Jordahl said opponents wanted both an immediate stop to construction and a broader ruling against the federal government’s use of legal waivers.

“We are here finally having our day in court to argue for a permanent stop to border wall barrier road construction in the Big Bend region, and hopefully to invalidate the waiver authority that’s being used to strip away legal protections from border residents, from wildlife,” Jordahl told Border Report before the hearing.

Friday’s request for a preliminary injunction concerned whether construction can continue during the litigation. The lawsuit separately seeks a permanent injunction and a declaration that the challenged waivers violate the Constitution.

The plaintiffs argue that the Department of Homeland Security has exceeded its constitutional authority by setting aside environmental and historic preservation requirements to expedite border projects. Their amended complaint alleges that the government’s actions threaten river access, recreation, livelihoods and cultural resources.

DHS offers a different rationale. In its June 9 waiver notice, the department said additional barriers and roads would help prevent unlawful entry and smuggling. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin cited authority Congress granted under Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 to waive legal requirements for expedited construction.

The waiver sets aside requirements under laws including the National Environmental Policy Act, Endangered Species Act, Clean Water Act and National Historic Preservation Act for the designated project area.

Jordahl accused DHS of damaging national park land and pursuing Texans’ properties for construction. He said opposition crosses political lines.

“It’s completely nonpartisan. We’ve got conservative sheriffs. We’ve got conservative ranchers on our side,” he said. “They have picked a fight with the toughest part of Texas in Big Bend.”

Jordahl said he hoped the court would conclude that DHS had overstepped its authority and stop further damage.

“Our message is that Big Bend is the wild heart of Texas, and we will do everything in our power to protect this place, this national park, this amazing river,” he said.

Former state Rep. Norma Chavez, who attended in support of opponents, said the dispute carries implications for people concerned about border construction near Mount Cristo Rey.

“Every American should be concerned at what’s happening,” Chavez told Border Report.

Chavez said she fears an unfavorable outcome in the Big Bend challenge could make efforts to protect Cristo Rey more difficult. She also argued that border infrastructure threatens ecosystems that extend across international boundaries.

“It’s a big land grab,” Chavez said. “It’s a violation of ecosystems that pass internationally.”

Her comments connected the Big Bend dispute to broader concerns about border construction around El Paso. The lawsuit reviewed for this story challenges projects in the Big Bend region.

The center initially filed the lawsuit with its fellow plaintiffs in April and later expanded the challenge to cover additional waivers. Attorneys from the Center for Biological Diversity and Texas Civil Rights Project represent the plaintiffs.

For Jordahl, the fight centers on preserving the landscape and the communities that depend on it.

“Everybody who lives in the Big Bend region has such a deep love for the land,” he said. “And without Big Bend, Texas is so much less wild.”

Aracely Lazcano can be reached at alazcano@borderreport.com

text:
Five European Union countries are pushing ahead with plans to start deporting asylum seekers whose applications are rejected to third countries outside the bloc, potentially in Africa, after the EU approved new rules this week that clear the way for the practice.

Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands have agreed on a common framework to establish "return hubs" outside the EU to which people who have exhausted their legal options to remain in Europe could be transferred if they cannot be sent back to their own countries of origin.

"When it comes to return hubs, it's progressing very well," Danish Interior Minister Morten Bødskov told reporters Thursday, according to AFP. "We are moving in the right direction."

He previously said Denmark expected "to be ready to transfer the first irregular migrants to a partner country outside the EU within 2027."

Greek Migration Minister Thanos Plevris told Politico that Greece expects to have a pilot project in place in the first half of next year.

No potential destinations for EU return hubs have been confirmed, although Rwanda has been reported as a possible partner in the project. A Greek government statement on the plans said the hubs would be established in safe third countries, "particularly on the African continent."

The EU itself has presented the idea of return hubs as a potential deterrent to irregular immigration. A discussion paper published by the EU's governing European Council in October 2025 said the hubs could "incentivize voluntary returns," because migrants who fail to comply with a deportation order could face transfer to a hub instead.

It said the policy could also discourage people without a valid asylum claim from making dangerous journeys to Europe.

The rules adopted this week by the EU establish a bloc-wide legal framework for returns and allow member states to conclude bilateral or unilateral agreements with countries outside the bloc, but with stipulations.

Under the rules, "any such agreement or arrangement may only be concluded with a non-EU country that respects international human rights standards and principles of international law, including the principle of non-refoulement," which guarantees that no individual can be sent back to a country where they would face torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, punishment or other irreparable harm.

EU follows U.S. and U.K. examples

The Trump administration has enthusiastically embraced the use of third-country deportations to remove undocumented migrants from the United States. More than 100 deportees were sent to eight African countries over a 10-day period in August, according to internal U.S. government documents obtained by CBS News.

The deportees were sent to destinations including the African nations of Liberia, Rwanda, Eswatini and Sierra Leone.

Plevris, Greece's migration minister, has praised the Trump administration's approach.

"I am a fan of President Trump," he told Breitbart in August. "But if you ask me what was the best thing he did, it was change the migration policy of the USA, because now we have a new migration policy also in Europe."

Other European governments have experimented with deportations to third nations before, however, with mixed results.

"No shortcut around the difficult parts of migration policy"

Britain's former Conservative Party government sought to send asylum seekers who arrived through irregular routes to Rwanda to have their claims processed there. The U.K. Supreme Court ruled the scheme unlawful in 2023, before it ever got going, over the risk that refugees could ultimately be returned to countries where they faced persecution.

The following year, the policy was formally abandoned by the new Labour Party government after the Conservatives were voted out of power. The British Home Office said £715 million (almost $950 million) had been spent on the Rwanda program by June 2024, and no asylum seekers were forcibly relocated. Four people traveled voluntarily to Rwanda under the program.

"One lesson may be that European governments should expect litigation, even where the third country looks considerably less controversial than Rwanda," Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory, told CBS News on Friday.

"These policies are often justified as deterrence measures, and that assumes a sufficiently large share of people believe there is a realistic chance they will actually be transferred," Walsh said. "If only a very small proportion can be moved, the deterrent may be much less credible."

"The broader lesson from Rwanda is that externalization is not a shortcut around the difficult parts of migration policy," he said. "It may relocate some of those difficulties geographically, but governments still have to deal with courts, individual rights, administrative capacity, countries that may not cooperate with returns, and substantial costs"

The push for return hubs is part of a broader effort by European nations to tighten their immigration policies amid intense pressure on governments to increase the number of people without a legal right to remain who are actually removed.

Jacob Reynolds, policy director at the Freedom and Sovereignty Initiative Europe, a right-wing think tank based in Brussels, called the EU decision to embrace these hubs a "welcome step towards gaining control of our borders and removing those who have no right to be here."

But he added that "outsourcing the problem of illegal migration to third countries — as the EU has long done — risks avoiding the broader problem: the lack of control over EU countries' borders."

He called for "much more fundamental action" to address "the generous regimes available to asylum seekers in Europe," and said until that happened, "the problem will not be solved."

text:
Republicans are struggling with how to thread the needle on immigration ahead of what is expected to be a bruising midterm season in which many voters have soured on the Trump administration’s aggressive enforcement.

But the party has spent two years championing policies that resulted from President Trump running on “securing” the border, including a pledge to carry out the largest mass deportation operation in history.

Two back-to-back statements from Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) illustrate the problem.

In an interview with Politico on Tuesday, the lawmaker said immigration officers have been “dragging people away that have lived on your street corner for 15 years.”

“I don’t know that we need to be doing that stuff,” he told the outlet.

“To get better, the first thing you got to do is admit you’re doing something wrong,” he added, nodding to the need to “step back.”

But the next day, he walked the comments back.

“Let me be crystal clear: I support President Trump’s immigration strategy, full stop,” he wrote on the social platform X.

Trump has also acknowledged the issue.

“Frankly, it’s the hardest job that I’ve had,” Trump said during a Hispanic Heritage Month event at the White House on Wednesday. “They’ll say you’re too tough or you’re too soft. Get tougher, get softer. No matter what you do, it’s always tough.”

The president’s comments come as a Thursday AP-NORC poll found Trump had a 39 percent approval rating on immigration, while recent Politico polling found divides in how the GOP rated Trump on the issue. Thirty-one percent of those polled who did not identify as MAGA said Trump’s deportation campaign is too aggressive.

Republicans are also struggling with the Hispanic voting bloc, which boosted Trump and the GOP in 2024. Signs of disapproval among Hispanic and Latino voters are particularly noticeable in Texas and Florida, as the GOP looks to keep control of Congress in November.

Twenty percent of Hispanic voters in Florida who supported Trump in 2024 said they would not repeat their vote, according to a UnidosUS survey from this spring. Meanwhile, a September Cook Political Report and TelevisaUnivision poll found that 18 percent of Texan Latinos who voted for Trump said they no longer back him.

Several conservative voices have grumbled about impacts.

Paul LePage, a former Republican governor of Maine who is now running for Congress, has bragged about being “Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular.” But he revealed recently that his son’s father-in-law, who he has said was living in the U.S. legally, was “being deported because he came from a country that’s not liked by certain people in Washington. That’s not right.”

LePage, however, has largely refused to answer additional questions after his comments garnered headlines, saying earlier this week it was a “personal matter.”

In Florida, Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R) saw that her district, which has one of the largest foreign-born populations of any in the country, was so disenchanted with Trump’s immigration policies that she campaigned on it.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said in a September ad. In the ad, she stands in front of the White House, addressing Trump.

She faced some pushback for her comments, including from constituents and Trump himself, who criticized the congresswoman in a dozen social media posts after the ad aired. Border czar Tom Homan also dismissed Salazar’s take.

“Give me an example where we went too far. That’s a pretty bold statement to make,” Homan told CBS News in a recent interview.

Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R), also a vocal proponent of Trump’s immigration policies, offered tepid criticism after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers conducted enforcement operations in his home state, saying they did not sufficiently coordinate with police.

“Law enforcement officers were not given advance notice or the level of cooperation we would expect from ICE’s enforcement and removal operations. As a result, there have been mass disruptions to local communities and businesses,” he said in a statement late last month.

ICE has made changes to shift the optics around their immigration enforcement, moving away from aggressive raids that were advertised in advance on social media.

But many of the tactics remain the same. ICE officers are operating in unmarked cars and donning plainclothes — details that have prompted some migrants to flee amid confusion.

Arrests, however, are still ticking up and are increasingly likely to be carried out against those who have no criminal record and who even have immigration petitions in processing.

ICE arrested about 50,000 migrants in both July and August — record-breaking figures.

Meanwhile, internal Justice Department data obtained by The Hill shows cases handled by the Office of Immigration Litigation have soared, with cases jumping from roughly 7,700 to nearly 9,500 since the start of Trump’s second term. Many of those are habeas petitions from the nearly 70,000 people currently held in immigration detention.

Other Republican senators said they’re hearing less from constituents about ICE now that the operations are quieter.

“Generally speaking, people want to see folks that commit violent crimes and, you know, removed from that aren’t supposed to be here, under deportation, be … taken out of the country,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.). “There’s been scrutiny on methods, and certain incidences have had some very sad results, obviously, with a couple deaths.”

“I feel like it’s calmed down in terms of what ICE is doing, and they’ve upped their training.”

Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) said he had also heard fewer concerns about ICE, although the Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association joined trade groups in Kansas and Texas in a letter last week describing the disruption recent raids have had on the industry.

Lankford said the complaints that come to him are “fewer than I used to hear about that.”

“But yes, I mean, we’ve always heard that.”

Democrats, however, believe Republicans will suffer on Election Day given the unpopularity of Trump’s immigration enforcement and deportations after several fatal shootings this year.

“They’re no longer going after ‘the worst of the worst’ — they are acting like the worst of the worst,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said during a recent hearing on Trump immigration efforts.

“Trump’s poll numbers have sunk like a stone, and the majority of Americans have rejected their authoritarian police-state tactics.”

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (Wash.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary subcommittee on immigration, said the Trump administration’s focus on meeting arrest quotas has backfired.

“They are continuing this strategy quietly now because it was unpopular when it was loud,” she told The Hill last month after the release of record-setting arrest figures.

“But they’re going to find out in November that it’s unpopular when it’s quiet as well.”

title: Five Great Reads: ICE 2.0, millennial motherhood, and skinny-dipping with Christine Baranski
description:
Grab a coffee and dig in, digest, and reflect on harrowing accounts of Trump’s immigration crackdown, investigations into modern motherhood and masculinity, and for a bit of weekend fun, we leave you with some celebrity gossip.
Inside Trump’s new immigration dragnet At the peak of Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, armoured vehicles occupied neighbourhoods, while masked agents violently pulled people from the streets.
In this series, ICE 2.0, Guardian reporters track how, despite the administration’s change of tactics, ICE is everywhere.
Further reading: All the stories from the series ICE 2.0: inside Trump’s new immigration dragnet.
Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatre Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant have stories to tell.
text:
Hello and welcome to the weekend.

The Guardian’s range was on display this week across these five very different stories. Grab a coffee and dig in, digest, and reflect on harrowing accounts of Trump’s immigration crackdown, investigations into modern motherhood and masculinity, and for a bit of weekend fun, we leave you with some celebrity gossip.

Enjoy.

1. Inside Trump’s new immigration dragnet

At the peak of Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, armoured vehicles occupied neighbourhoods, while masked agents violently pulled people from the streets. After officers killed two US citizens during the raids in Minneapolis, public backlash prompted Trump to try a new approach. Now, ICE arrests have hit record levels. In this series, ICE 2.0, Guardian reporters track how, despite the administration’s change of tactics, ICE is everywhere.

Notable quote: “Before, they were storming around, making a lot of noise Now, they are moving more quietly.”

The violence continues: People are arrested while pumping gas, leaving behind their empty cars. They are arrested on their way to work, or on their way home. Recently, an ICE agent shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in Texas. That same day, in Grand Rapids, Michigan, a Guatemalan man died in a fiery crash while fleeing federal immigration agents. ICE is now detaining more immigrants than ever before, despite the new secretary of homeland security, Markwayne Mullin, promising to avoid negative headlines by cutting the flash and fanfare.

How long will it take to read: Under four minutes.

Further reading: All the stories from the series ICE 2.0: inside Trump’s new immigration dragnet.

2. Why does millennial motherhood feel so impossible?

Women today are more educated, more employed and more engaged in childcare arrangements than ever before. But research shows that the expectations facing modern mothers continue to grow. In Australia, the statistics illuminate a global phenomenon. New research shows that the cost for Australian families of raising two or more children has risen to at least $36,500 a year. The cost of keeping a family afloat has increased by 134% in two decades, while household income has grown by only 102% in the same period.

Between juggling rising costs and managing careers, is there any way out of the total overwhelm?

A problem with no solution: In this personal piece, Kate Lyons writes that millennial women no longer feel trapped in their homes like generations before, but rather, by the impossible juggle of managing their career, relationships and children. Lyons recounts a friend reaching out for advice late one night after their five-year-old had a meltdown before bed. Another woman Lyons spoke to got so desperate she turned towards ChatGPT, asking the AI chatbot how to make her life work. But solutions are not easy to come by. After Lyons assessed the state of her living room, which, “looks as though someone has taken the contents of a laundry basket, a toy box and a nappy bag and Jackson Pollocked the floor with them”, all she could offer was solidarity.

Notable quote: “It’s not that I want to be at home five days a week. I don’t want to be exactly like my mum was. But I want to pick them up from school and take them home and calmly wind down the day with them. There’s absolutely no way I can do that.”

How long will it take to read: Just under six minutes.

Further reading: Why birthrates are plummeting, and why workplaces were built for men.

3. Trump’s testosterone culture war

Polls show that Donald Trump is losing support with the bros that got him elected. As the midterms approach, the cost of living and the war on Iran have left male voters increasingly disillusioned. So how does one win them back? The health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, and the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, seem to think the hormone testosterone, often known simply as “T”, is the answer. Or as Sam Wolfson explains, Trump is hoping that “the male populace will vote not with their heads or their hearts, but with their hogs”.

The testosterone dog-whistle: Testosterone is found in the bodies of men and women, with a low amount all that is needed for normal function. But the hormone has emerged on the frontlines of the Trump administration’s many culture wars. While the war in Iran causes problems for Trump back home, Hegseth has shifted the military message to one of machismo. On the campaign trail, he said, “We’re reminding our warriors that their sole purpose is to be the most lethal fighting force on the planet. Full stop. We’re not here to do social engineering, or social justice, or gender-bending, or DEI, or dudes and dresses.” But Wolfson writes that Hegseth’s testosterone push is a “sciencey” way to dog-whistle his sexist message.

Notable quote: “Everything has been politicized in the United States. Vaccines are liberal and TRT is Maga. The needle is apolitical but the content of the syringe is decided by who you vote for.”

How long will it take to read: eight minutes.

Further reading: The Pentagon and “incel” slang, plus RFK Jr’s “peptide wild west”.

4. Exposing the world’s biggest porn bosses

Patricia Nilsson was determined to bring porn industry leaders out of the shadows. For five years, she subjected the adult industry to forensic analysis in an effort to reveal who was getting rich through porn and how they were doing it. For decades, the owners of these companies have escaped scrutiny, and they have often enjoyed relative anonymity. But porn is everywhere, and for many young men and women, adult content can be their default sex education. Nilsson argues the owners of businesses that are recalibrating our sexual culture deserve further investigation.

Notable quote: “My argument is not that we should be neutral towards porn, but that we need to accept and understand it as a real industry, and ask what its growth and popularity says about the state of our economy and the world of work.”

The story of porn is the story of the internet: Nilsson argues that even if you do not consume explicit content online, the industry has shaped the way you interact with the digital world. We have porn to thank, she says, for high-quality video streaming and the way influencers sell their online personas. “Staring at content that is algorithmically engineered to arouse you is a perfect metaphor for our relationship with our devices and the internet and social media,” Nilsson says.

How long will it take to read: About five minutes.

Further reading: The malignant rise of OnlyFans managers and the rise of deepfake pornography in schools.

5. Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatre

Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant have stories to tell. The actors have joined forces for the first time in a London production of Noël Coward’s comedic play Hay Fever. The Guardian sat down with the actors to get a glimpse of the tall tales told backstage.

Notable quote: When asked if she has ever worked with Grant before, Baranski wryly says: “Regrettably not. We could have had some good fun a few decades ago. A girl could have got into some real trouble. But here we are, and now we’re the veterans.”

Skinny dipping in the dark: Recalling her “marvellous house” on a lake in Connecticut, Baranski recounts an evening spent with Mark Rylance when the pair went skinny-dipping and ended up howling at the moon till four in the morning. Pressed on whether taking your clothes off is a prerequisite for visiting, Baranski says: “I encourage people only if they’re comfortable and if it’s pitch dark.”

How long will it take to read: five minutes of gossipy joy.

Further reading: How Richard E Grant ended up on Celebrity Traitors.
