text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s harsh criticisms may still be ringing in the ears of Supreme Court justices when they return to the bench for a new nine-month term next week.

In the final months of its previous term and over its summer break, the conservative-majority court, which includes three Trump appointees, ruled against Trump on some of the issues he holds most dear.

The justices blocked his sweeping tariffs, ended his plan to curb birthright citizenship, prevented him from firing a member of the Federal Reserve and blocked his plan to exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of this fall’s election.

The Supreme Court has “let our country down,” Trump said in a Truth Social post after the mail-in ballots ruling. The very justices he appointed — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — are “a shell of their previous selves,” he added. The president made similar claims in a Time magazine interview published Thursday, saying: “I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often.”

The president still desperately needs justices’ votes when key parts of his agenda come before the court in the coming months, in particular multiple cases arising from his hard-line immigration crackdown.

The court could also weigh in on his administration’s ban on transgender people in the military, which the justices in a previous decision allowed to go into effect. Another appeal is pending in Trump’s effort to overturn a defamation verdict against him in a case brought by writer E. Jean Carroll, who accused him of sexual abuse. The court in June rejected an earlier Trump appeal concerning a separate case that Carroll won.

Trump’s complaints about the court mask the fact that the administration has had plenty of wins, in particular in emergency cases that reach the court via what is known colloquially as the “shadow docket.”

The court’s interim rulings have allowed the administration to move forward with immigration enforcement, restructuring of the federal government and even construction of a ballroom at the White House in emergency rulings while litigation continues.

Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that overall “the administration’s policies have been consistently upheld as lawful.”

“President Trump will not stop implementing the America First agenda that he was elected on,” she added.

The court resumes oral arguments Monday as it formally opens the new session, which runs until June, by hearing a major case about whether cities and counties can sue oil companies for the impacts of climate change.

Those who regularly challenge Trump policies in court say their recent wins have them hopeful about this term, showing that even though the court has a 6-3 conservative majority, it is not a rubber stamp for the president.

“Even with this court, you can go too far beyond the bounds,” said Norm Eisen, co-founder of Democracy Defenders Fund, which has challenged Trump on multiple fronts. The justices would not, for example, “allow Trump to hijack mail-in voting,” he added.

Cecillia Wang, national legal director of the American Civil Liberties Union, was similarly relieved by some of the court’s recent decisions.

“I think the court has proved it is willing to stand up to the Trump administration’s excesses. And that gives us confidence going into this term,” she said.

Two key parts of Trump’s immigration policy are already lined up for Supreme Court review. In one, the justices will consider the administration’s ongoing efforts to deport immigrants to “third countries” they have no previous connection to if they cannot be returned to their home nations. The Supreme Court already allowed the policy to go ahead twice, suggesting the administration has a good chance of prevailing.

The other case concerns the administration’s attempt to detain indefinitely thousands of people in deportation proceedings, a break from previous administrations, which would release those immigrants while their cases were adjudicated.

Other Trump-related cases are likely to be added to the docket in time to be ruled on by next summer, with several appeals already pending.

Among them is another potentially significant immigration case arising from the Trump administration’s shutdown of asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border. Lower courts ruled against the administration, although the policy currently remains in effect.

Robert Luther III, who served in the White House during the first Trump term and is now a professor at Antonin Scalia Law School at George Mason University, said that, as with the previous term, much of the focus will be on Trump’s broad interpretation of executive power.

“He’s always staked out an aggressive view of executive power. The court’s relationship with that view continues to unfold. Some of those cases he is winning and some he is losing,” he added.

Although the court has been on its customary summer recess since the end of June, the justices have remained busy dealing with cases brought on the shadow docket. Such cases are typically dealt with swiftly, with no oral arguments or detailed written opinions.

The shadow docket has increasingly become a key part of the court’s operations in recent years, with some of the rulings proving more consequential than those on the court’s traditional docket, in which the justices hear arguments and spend months deliberating before issuing long rulings.

During the summer, the Trump administration filed seven shadow docket requests on a variety of issues. The court ruled for Trump on four of them and against him once, while one was withdrawn and one is pending.

The administration’s most high-profile win of the summer recess allowed Trump to continue with his construction of a ballroom at the White House.

But his single loss on his mail-in ballots executive order was a significant one, prompting some of his strongest criticism of the justices to date.

Luther said the justices are likely able to put the president’s colorful rhetoric to one side.

“I think the justices know the president is a politician,” he added. “I don’t think they take it personally.”

This week we cover Justice Henry Baldwin, who served on the court from 1830 until 1844.
Baldwin fell out of love with the court in his very first year, telling Jackson he wanted to resign, but Jackson convinced him to stay.
In 1831 alone, he dissented seven times, more than any other justice on the Marshall court.
Upon returning, Baldwin apparently wrote a series of incoherent legal opinions, deliberately ignored grammar in his writing, and had violent outbursts.
A court reporter also noted that five different people had called the justice “crazy” on the same day.
text:
Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice Henry Baldwin, who served on the court from 1830 until 1844.

Justice Henry Baldwin caused trouble both early and late in his life. At Yale, he “found the lectures droll and misbehaved frequently,” while on the Supreme Court he grew so erratic that his colleague Justice Joseph Story deemed him “partially deranged at all times.” (This is not to mention his near-death duel or unprecedented number of dissents while on the often-unanimous Marshall court.)

Baldwin was born in New Haven, Connecticut, in January 1780. One of his half-brothers signed the Constitution and later represented Georgia in the House for the first through fifth Congresses and in the Senate during the sixth through ninth. Baldwin graduated from Yale in 1797, although one of his classmates described him as a “lightheaded boy, who neither aimed at, nor attained to, much distinction as a scholar,” before attending Litchfield Law School. He then clerked for Alexander Dallas, the Supreme Court’s first unofficial reporter of decisions. (The court was then located in Philadelphia.)

In 1799, Baldwin went to Pittsburgh (originally on his way to visit his brother), and there founded a law practice and came to co-own a newspaper. Reportedly spurred by politics, Baldwin fought a duel and almost died – according to Oyez, he was saved by a “silver dollar in his jacket pocket” that deflected the bullet. During the War of 1812, Baldwin sat on Pittsburgh’s Public Safety Council and by 1816, he had been dubbed “the Pride of Pittsburgh.” He then won a House seat for Pennsylvania, where he chaired the Committee on Manufactures and was a proponent of high tariffs (these protectionist views won him another nickname, “Father of the American System”). But Baldwin’s career was most aided by his defense of then-Gen. Andrew Jackson’s conduct in the Seminole War; Baldwin argued that the men Jackson had killed “were not our citizens, not bound by our laws, [and] not entitled to our protection.”

Baldwin then campaigned for Jackson in 1828 and expected to be made Secretary of the Treasury in return but did not receive the position. He refused the three foreign missions Jackson offered instead and wrote to an editor that he was valued about as much as “a candle-snuffer at a court-house,” or “a mere passing post, against which every puppy of the party raises his leg.” After Justice Bushrod Washington died in 1829, Jackson nominated Baldwin to the court. The Senate confirmed him 41-2 two days later, with both “no” votes cast by South Carolinians. (South Carolina was generally against Baldwin’s pro-tariff position.)

Baldwin fell out of love with the court in his very first year, telling Jackson he wanted to resign, but Jackson convinced him to stay. In 1831 alone, he dissented seven times, more than any other justice on the Marshall court. One of the seven was his “spirited dissent” in Ex parte Crane, where he argued that the Supreme Court did not have the power to issue writs ordering lower federal courts to take a specific action.

In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, which held that the court did not have jurisdiction to hear the case since the Cherokee Nation was a “domestic dependent nation[]” and as such could not sue Georgia, Baldwin also wrote separately, stating that “the judicial power cannot divest the States of rights of sovereignty,” a position that sided with Georgia and Jackson’s push for Indian removal. (That said, Baldwin wasn’t entirely in Jackson’s pocket; he repeatedly urged Attorney General Roger Taney to advise the president against vetoing the national bank’s rechartering bill.)

On slavery, Baldwin was the lone dissenter in United States v. The Amistad (where the court held that because a group of Africans had been illegally abducted, they were free and entitled to their liberty), and in 1841’s Groves v. Slaughter, he argued that the Constitution regarded slaves as property rather than persons.

In 1833, Baldwin was hospitalized for “incurable lunacy” and absent for that term. In May 1833, his colleague Story wrote to a circuit judge that “I am sure he cannot be sane.” Despite this, Baldwin returned the following year and served 11 more years on the court until his death in 1844. Upon returning, Baldwin apparently wrote a series of incoherent legal opinions, deliberately ignored grammar in his writing, and had violent outbursts. A court reporter also noted that five different people had called the justice “crazy” on the same day. Friends further reported financial issues (Baldwin had filed for bankruptcy early in his tenure) and that he appeared overworked.

title: New ICE facility to hold families, unaccompanied minors could open in Louisiana next week
description:

text:
A new facility in Alexandria, Louisiana, may begin receiving undocumented families with children, local officials and immigrant rights advocates say.

The 528-bed facility will house families with children, unaccompanied minors, and single adult females as they await removal inside renovated former Air Force barracks at England Airpark, a former military base that now houses the Alexandria International Airport and an immigration detention facility, according to a draft agreement between ICE and the England Economic and Industrial Development District (EEIDD) reviewed by ABC News.

A communications manager for EEIDD told ABC News the facility could start receiving people "within the next week or two."

The facility would be the second constructed to house children since President Donald Trump's second term began but is the first to hold unaccompanied minors who are usually held in shelters under the custody of the Department of Health and Human Services before deportation or release.

A board of commissioners that governs the airpark approved the facility in February amid protests from local residents.

The facility will be managed by LaSalle Family Foundation, a nonprofit arm of LaSalle Corrections, a private prison company that manages several immigration detention centers across the country. Daily operations will be run by Anovaeon, which describes itself as a humanitarian response company. The operators are calling the facility the Alexandria Family Staging Center and say it will house people who are voluntarily self-deporting or voluntarily leaving the country, for an average stay of under 48 hours.

Last week, Robert Hagen, the project manager for LaSalle Family Foundation told commissioners the facility was 95% completed.

During board meetings that have at times become contentious with police having to remove opponents of the plans, operators of the facility have attempted to push back against the notion that it's a detention center.

"This project right over here is not a detention center, it's a staging center for families who are voluntarily departing this country, admittedly through pretty crappy circumstances on their end. I acknowledge that," Anovaeon CEO Eric Fritz said at a commissioner board meeting last week.

Fritz said the facility will provide medical care, mental health care, "quality meals," soccer fields and free international calling, among other resources.

A pamphlet distributed during one of the board meetings and obtained by ABC News said migrant families will be held in a "non-detained" setting at the facility. However, during last week's board meeting, Anovaeon Senior Director of Operations Jeffrey Lynch acknowledged operators would have to alert ICE if someone attempted to leave the facility.

"I think what we would do is, we would approach the individual, say 'Look, you're part of this program. It's in your best interest to follow through with the program,'" Lynch said. "If they were adamant about it, I think we would open the gate but at the same time we would be in communication with ICE, letting them know what's happening."

There's an ICE office "literally steps away" from the facility, Lynch added.

"They're literally steps away and they would be there to either intervene, convince them to come back in, or take whatever steps they would take as part of their case management practices," Lynch said.

A draft of the Intergovernmental Service Agreement between DHS and the EEIDD obtained by the advocacy group National Immigration Project and reviewed by ABC News said one of the purposes of the agreement is to provide "ICE alien detention in a secure environment under the authority of the Immigration and Nationality Act."

A communications manager for the EEIDD said she could not share the final agreement with ABC News, noting that ICE had to sign off before it could be shared.

At a press conference on Wednesday, immigrant rights groups and attorneys denounced the facility and raised concerns that the property was contaminated with PFAS.

"There can be no hiding what this is, this is a detention center. People are not free to leave," said Stephanie Alvarez-Jones, Southeast Regional Attorney for the National Immigration Project.

DHS, EEIDD and Anovaeon did not respond when asked to address concerns about possible contamination, or whether people would be restrained at any point during their stay or during removal.

DHS did not provide an estimate of when the facility would open.

In a statement, an ICE spokesperson called it a "staging facility for deportations"

"A staging facility is where illegal aliens await their deportation flight to their destination country or transfer to a detention facility," the spokesperson said.

ABC News' Ely Brown and Laura Romero contributed to this report.

Sign up to receive the Early Edition in your inbox here.

A curated weekday guide to major news and developments over the last 24 hours. Here’s today’s news:

IRAN WAR

Senior Iranian commanders are reviewing plans to expand potential targets beyond U.S. linked assets if the United States resumes large-scale military attacks, according to sources. The planning reflects a conviction within Iran’s leadership that any renewed U.S. campaign must be met with a stronger response than before, even as Iran seeks to avoid escalation through talks. Parisa Hafezi reports for Reuters.

A U.S. official yesterday said the U.S. military is dispatching around 9,000 troops and a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East. Konstantin Toropin, Michelle L. Price, and Aamer Madhani report for AP News.

President Trump yesterday said Iran would be struck “very hard” if links to the copilot who tried to crash an Israel-bound flight are confirmed. Trump added that based on what he heard, Iran likely was involved. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu yesterday said the initial investigation into the attempted hijacking found that the co-pilot went through religious Islamic radicalization, and his remarks were confirmed by an Israeli intelligence official. Melanie Lidman, Samy Magdy, Michelle L. Price, and Cara Anna report for AP News; Barak Ravid reports for Axios.

IRAN WAR – YEMEN

The military spokesperson for Yemen’s internationally recognized government today said that warplanes carried out 20 strikes targeting Iran-aligned Houthi movement, personnel, vehicles, and military equipment in Taiz province. Saudi Arabia yesterday said the Houthis attacked a power distribution station in Medina that supplies electricity to the Prophet’s Mosque. A Houthi military source denied the claim and said it was intended to cover up Saudi’s failure to substantiate an earlier accusation that the Houthis had targeted the holy city of Mecca. Tala Ramadan and Mohammed Ghobari report for Reuters.

IRAN WAR – OTHER DEVELOPMENTS

The U.S. military in recent weeks sent two additional Patriot missile batteries to protect oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, according to sources. The sources added that lobbying efforts by Saudi Arabia and Qatar against U.S. bombing of Iran in August was a key reason Trump decided to pursue an economic pressure campaign instead. Barak Ravid reports for Axios.

U.S. Central Command headquarters will hold a daylong conference this month to discuss ways to limit civilian casualties during combat operations, according to a former Pentagon official. Other attendees will include former staff members from a Pentagon initiative created to limit civilian harm that U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth shut down early in his term. John Ismay, Malachy Browne, and Christiaan Triebert report for the New York Times.

The U.S. State Department yesterday said it has waived human rights conditions for more than $300 million of military aid to Egypt in light of Egypt’s “helpful role” since the Iran war began. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio “has made a determination to waive the certification requirement with respect to $320 million in FY 2025 Foreign Military Financing for Egypt,” according to a letter addressed to various congressional committees dated Sep. 21, seen by Reuters. Alexander Dziadosz, Patricia Zengerle, and Humeyra Pamuk report.

U.K. counter-terror police yesterday said a 25-year-old U.K.-Iranian national was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with the incident at Royal Air Force Fairford. Henry Moore reports for BBC News.

LEBANON

The Turkish Presidency’s communications directorate yesterday denied Reuters’ report that Turkey last month hosted a meeting between Syrian government representatives and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah. The Syrian government on social media also called the claims “false.” Feras Delatey, Laila Bassam, and Timour Azhari report.

WEST BANK VIOLENCE

Israeli militant settlers yesterday shot two Palestinians, killing one and injuring the other, in an attack on Yasuf village in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, according to Village Council Head Jumaa Abdel Fattah. Mashour Yassin was killed during an attack on his home. Ali Sawafta and Pesha Magid report for Reuters.

RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR

Kyiv officials today said Russian airstrikes killed one and injured two in the capital, and forced the closure of two bridges across the Dnipro River. Kyiv’s Mayor Vitalii Klitschko yesterday said a Russian drone struck a school. No casualties were reported as children and staff were in shelters when the drone hit. Jekaterīna Golubkova reports for Reuters; Susie Blann and Barry Hatton report for AP News.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy yesterday said Ukraine had launched a FP-7 ballistic missile at a Russian target for the first time in combat. Alistair MacDonald reports for the Wall Street Journal.

The U.S. Treasury Department yesterday issued economic sanctions against Russian company A7. A department statement described how A7 had developed a web of companies to help businesses, people, and governments subject to sanctions buy domestic and military goods from around the world, and labelled the company a “significant transnational criminal organization.” Aaron Krolik reports for the New York Times.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung today threatened unspecified measures against Ukraine unless Ukraine acknowledged a confidentiality agreement that South Korea says covered the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers, and issued an apology for reporting on it. Lee also expressed “grave regret” over what he described as Ukrainian remarks about an imminent military clash between North and South Korea. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha yesterday said Ukraine is working to heal tensions with South Korea, and described the situation as a “diplomatic misunderstanding” rather than an incident. Kyu-Seok Shim reports for Reuters; Ron Popeski reports for Reuters.

OTHER GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTS

The Ethiopian government yesterday severed diplomatic relations with Eritrea. Eritrean diplomats were given 48 hours to leave, raising fears that the conflict in Ethiopia might become a direct war with Eritrea. Nicholas Bariyo reports for the Wall Street Journal.

Egyptian authorities yesterday arrested the entire editorial team of independent media outlet Matsadaash, accusing them of belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood. The six journalists are alleged to have produced fabricated news for an online outlet in exchange for foreign funding. Matsadaash co-founder Abedlrahman Mansour denied the allegations and said he and the arrested individual’s families have no idea where those who were arrested are. AP News reports.

Bolivian Interior Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo yesterday said Bolivia’s Attorney Gen. Roger Mariaca on Wednesday was arrested, two days after the United States revoked his visa and accused him of accepting bribes to facilitate drug trafficking. Mariaca was arrested alongside 13 other people as part of an operation targeting what authorities described as a “criminal organization” embedded within the judiciary and the Public Prosecutor’s Office. Daniel Ramos reports for Reuters.

An International Criminal Court spokesperson yesterday said the Hague-based court ended its contract with French life and health insurer Axa and will now be using a new health insurance provider. The spokesperson gave no reason for the decision. Kanjyik Ghosh and Chandni Shah report for Reuters.

CLIMATE DEVELOPMENTS

The EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service today said 52% of Europe experienced “very strong” levels of heat stress at times this summer, exposing people in a record-high share of the continent to the health risks of extreme heat. Western Europe experienced its hottest summer since records began, recording “very strong” heat stress on 13 days. Kate Abnett reports for Reuters.

A coalition of 21 U.S. states and four cities yesterday sued the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency over its move to erase all limits on planet-warming emissions from powerplants. The suit alleges that the EPA acted unlawfully when it repealed regulations on carbon dioxide emissions from power plants that burn gas and coal. Brad Plumer reports for the New York Times.

AI DEVELOPMENTS

A Tokyo court on Wednesday awarded legal protection to the human voice in a case in which voice actor Kenjiro Tsuda demanded that TikTok close an account over its unauthorized use of an AI clone of his trademark baritone. The ruling was the first acknowledgement of the right of one’s voice in Japan. The judge said the human voice is “symbolic of individual personality, just like one’s portrait,” according to a court document seen by AP News. Mari Yamaguchi reports.

U.S. AI DEVELOPMENTS

OpenAI has fired three researchers on its safety team for alleged misconduct, including sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI-safety organization, sources told the Wall Street Journal. An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed the firings “for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information.” Keach Hagey, Maxwell Zeff, and Berber Jin report.

The Justice Department yesterday said a California man was arrested on federal charges alleging he smuggled more than $300 million worth of export-controlled computer servers containing U.S. manufactured graphics processing units, commonly used for AI applications, to China. Greg Lui was charged with one count of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act and the Export Administration Regulations, one count of outbound smuggling, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. Kanishka Singh reports for Reuters.

U.S. cybersecurity firm Proofpoint yesterday said suspected Chinese hackers impersonated an Anthropic employee and ex U.S. officials in an espionage campaign aimed at gaining insights into U.S. AI developments. The hackers targeted the email accounts of experts in AI export controls and military applications of AI, among other topics. Sean Lyngaas reports for CNN.

U.S. CHINA DEVELOPMENTS

The Commerce Department has been taking steps to turn China’s dependence on U.S. aviation suppliers into leverage for trade negotiations, sources told Reuters. The department slowed export licensing for airplane parts bound for China in recent weeks, among other efforts to position itself to increase pressure on China should the Trump administration call upon it to do so. Karen Freifeld and Allison Lampert report.

U.S. FOREIGN AFFAIRS

Israeli President Isaac Herzog yesterday called Trump Israel’s “No. 1 friend,” downplaying strains between Israel and the United States over the Iran war. Herzog accused the United Kingdom of intervening in Israel’s elections through sanctions he called “unfair and politically motivated.” Jalen Beckford reports for POLITICO; Jalen Beckford reports for POLITICO.

The Korean government yesterday denied that it has finalized an investment for an Alaskan natural gas project, a day after Trump tried to use the investment to boost Sen. Dan Sullivan’s re-election prospects. Lee and other members of South Korea’s government said their investment in the pipeline remains conditional on its commercial viability and its compliance with the legal procedures of South Korea. Daniel Desrochers reports for POLITICO.

The State Department yesterday said Rubio will visit Iceland, Greece, and Portugal next week to discuss economic and security cooperation, among other issues. Rubio will lead the U.S. delegation for the sixth session of the U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue. Simon Lewis and Jonathan Landay report for Reuters.

Democrats in the Senate and House foreign affairs committees yesterday urged the State Department to review the conduct of U.S. ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a Wall Street Journal investigation into her efforts to promote gas deals with a Greek company across southeastern Europe. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) sent a letter to Rubio about Guilfoyle’s “inappropriate uses of an official position.” Dana Mattioli, Rebecca Ballhaus, Joe Parkinson, and Drew Hinshaw report.

The State Department has stripped tens of millions of dollars in U.S. military assistance from European and Middle Eastern countries and will give the funds to Latin American conservative governments instead, sources told the Washington Post. The department notified Congress of its intentions in September, but Democrat lawmakers placed a hold on the diversion. On Wednesday, the Trump administration notified Congress it was defying the hold and moving ahead. John Hudson reports.

U.S. IMMIGRATION DEVELOPMENTS

The relatives of Renee Good, who was killed by an ICE agent on Jan. 7, 2026, yesterday filed two federal lawsuits. The first suit accused ICE agent Jonathan Ross of having placed himself at risk by standing in front of Good’s car during a confrontation and unjustifiably using deadly force. The same suit also names former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem and White House Border Czar Thomas D. Homan, amongst others, as defendants, and argues that Good’s death was the result of an immigration operation in Minnesota that was driven by unconstitutional racial animus against Somali and Hispanic people. The second suit names the U.S. government as a defendant, and is filed under a 1964 law that allows plaintiffs to seek redress for deaths caused by negligence. Ernesto Londono reports for the New York Times.

The Department of Homeland Security pays local agencies as much as $2 million for each arrest in a nationwide task force, according to a Wall Street Journal report released yesterday. The DHS task force program enlists local police as paid partners in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, and departments qualify to receive $60,000 a year for each deputized officer, regardless of additional immigration arrests. Brenna T. Smith, Marianne LeVine, and Jack Gillum report.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez yesterday had surgery to remove the bullet shot into his back during an ICE operation nearly two weeks ago. A spokesperson for Garces Perez’s legal team said he is recovering in the custody of the U.S. Marshalls. In light of recent escalated vehicle stops, ICE officers on Wednesday were ordered to not engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training, according to an internal memo obtained by AP News. The memo said that officers should instead take down the vehicles’ information for further investigation. AP News reports; Ryan J. Foley reports.

U.S. DOMESTIC DEVELOPMENTS

The State Department directed millions of dollars, originally set to promote human rights, to promote far-right causes, a source told CNN. The department defied a hold by Congress on the diversion, and the funds were due to lapse on Wednesday. Jennifer Hansler reports.

The DOJ is reviewing whether the special prosecutor’s office that investigated former President Nixon over Watergate committed misconduct during the investigation, sources told the Wall Street Journal. Former Nixon aide turned Watergate historian and revisionist Geoff Shepard recently gave a two-hour presentation at DOJ headquarters that laid out his theory that the deep state took Nixon down. The title of his 78-page slide was “Watergate As Lawfare.” Philip Wegmann and Sadie Gurman report.

Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency Bill Pulte this week moved to slash the inspector general’s office that scrutinizes his actions. It was the second time that Trump administration officials have taken steps to limit scrutiny of the FHFA, and the inspector general’s office has remained without a permanent leader. Luke Broadwater reports for the New York Times.

The Democratic National Committee yesterday filed a lawsuit accusing the Defense Department of trying to disenfranchise overseas voters by altering a form used to register vote and request mail ballots. The suit argued that the changes, which included removing a check box from the Federal Post Card Application form, were made in an attempt to block overseas voters. Tim Balk reports for the New York Times.

Hegseth on Wednesday said he is launching an office of religious affairs which will report directly to him. The office will help offer “first-class religious support” to members of the Pentagon. Tiffany Stanley reports for AP News.

The federal judge of the ‘Broadview Six’ case yesterday said she will create a list of issues she wants further evidence on amid claims of a ‘cover-up.’ Federal prosecutors in April assured the judge that they had no contact with the White House or DOJ officials about their pursuit of six Operation Midway Blitz protestors, but the judge yesterday said further “under oath” fact-finding is needed, with the possibility that she will name a special prosecutor to investigate U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros and others. Jon Seidel, Sophie Sherry, and Tom Schuba report for the Chicago Sun Times.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier yesterday filed a lawsuit in state court against Pfizer and its CEO Albert Bourla. The suit accused the drugmaker of misleading consumers about the safety and effectiveness of its Covid-19 vaccine. Kamal Choudhury and Christy Santhosh report for Reuters.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ACTION

Trump yesterday did not rule out demolishing the Kennedy Center during his interview with Eric Cortellessa from TIME magazine. Trump said he would not commit to anything, but that “if I build it, and if I agree that for the rest of my life, I’m going to be putting up $100 million to have it open to people… then I think the Trump administration should be recognized.” Mallory Wilson reports for The Hill.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LITIGATION

A Washington D.C. judge yesterday barred the Trump administration from any future attempt to charge former Olympian David Hearn with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. The ruling called the circumstances in Hearn’s case “exceptional” and said allowing the government to reinitiate a prosecution would put him at risk of being charged for a crime prosecutors have determined he didn’t commit. Lydia Wheeler reports for the Wall Street Journal.

A federal judge yesterday reinstated Roger Rogoff as the U.S. attorney in Seattle. The ruling found the Trump administration overstepped its authority in firing the prosecutor minutes after he took office earlier in the year, and barred the administration from attempting to remove Rogoff again. The judge also denied the administration’s motion to stay his ruling, and said it was “in the public’s interest to have the executive branch follow the law.” Danny Hakim and Taylor Mirfendereski report for the New York Times.

A federal judge yesterday dismissed a case that accused a Jamaican national of illegally voting. The ruling found the law criminalizing noncitizen voting was unconstitutional, but the ruling is not binding for other judges in other cases. Tom Hals reports for Reuters.

description:

text:
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. (WOOD) — A nurse from eastern Michigan faces a federal misdemeanor charge for helping a man escape ICE custody at an Ann Arbor hospital.

A criminal complaint against 33-year-old Chloe Freeman was filed on Aug. 28 and unsealed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan on Tuesday.

Court documents claim the incident happened on May 28. Border Patrol agents “conducted a targeted operation” to capture a Mexican native who had been deported back in 2022 and had unlawfully re-entered the country.

After approaching the suspect, the man reportedly ran away, tripped on a curb and struck his head on the pavement. He was treated at the scene and brought to Trinity Health Ann Arbor Hospital for evaluation.

ICE agents accompanied him to the hospital. The suspect was taken back for a CT scan, but prosecutors allege Freeman intervened and, instead of having him returned to his room, used her staff key card to help him escape.

“Badge swipe data from Trinity Health Hospital showed that on May 28, 2026, at 11:31:51 p.m., Freeman swiped the 2nd Floor CT Room 2738 door to gain access to the CT room where (the suspect) was located,” the probable cause document says. “Security video footage then showed (the suspect) exiting the hospital through the ambulance bay doors on May 28, 2026, at 11:32:59 p.m. Law enforcement have been unable to locate (the suspect) since his escape from Trinity Health Ann Arbor Hospital.”

Freeman was questioned by investigators weeks later and admitted to letting the suspect leave the hospital but claimed she did not believe he was in ICE custody because the agents did not physically accompany him to the CT room.

Freeman also told investigators that she disagreed with ICE’s policies, separating people from their families and that she was “going to set him free.”

She also admitted that she let him leave before his care was complete and he was properly discharged from the hospital, breaking hospital protocol.

Freeman faces one misdemeanor charge of assisting the escape of a person in federal custody. It comes with a sentence of up to one year in prison.

She was released on a $10,000 bond.

BELLINGHAM, WA (MyBellinghamNow.com) – Bellingham’s top official will be speaking on the recent uptick in federal immigration enforcement.

Indivisible Bellingham says Mayor Lund will address the city’s responses to ICE activity on Tuesday, Oct. 6.

According to statistics from the Deportation Data Project, there were 60 ICE arrests made in Whatcom County between June 1 and Aug. 4. Of the 60 arrested over that period, nine were identified as convicted criminals.

It included a significant spike with 36 arrests in June, reflecting the most the county has seen in a single month since the group began tracking data in 2022.

The statistics come in the form of government data provided by ICE in a response to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request, processed by the Deportation Data Project and analyzed by My Bellingham Now.

Tuesday’s meeting takes place at 7 p.m. at the Bellingham Unitarian Fellowship on 1207 Ellsworth St.

Lund will take questions after she gives her address, which is free and open to the public.

Another Indivisible Bellingham meeting addressing the impact of immigration enforcement will take place at the Ferndale Library at 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 6, as well.

WHATCOM COUNTY, WA (MyBellinghamNow.com) – Have you felt a chill in the air? Did you check your thermostat this week? Do you find yourself putting on layers of clothes and blankets every night when you sit down to relax or to go to sleep?

We’ve reached the time of year when the weather we’re experiencing may feel like a switch has been flipped. Some days are sunny and bright, others are dark and dreary. But overall, the nights are getting longer and colder, with wind advisories picking up the pace in frequency and velocity.

October is here, and with it come those cool fall nights. Drafts in your home may become more apparent at this time, bringing attention to air leaks and spots where you can feel the outside environment a little too much.

When you find yourself bundling up inside the house, it may be worth looking into whether your heating system is up to scratch. Thick sweaters and socks are not meant to be the only way to be comfortable while at home.

Consider comfort when you think about investment this fall and upgrade or change out your heating system to pass those forthcoming long nights with ease.

“Home comfort is a huge thing that we take for granted most days, and you can quickly notice when it is not quite right. If something is wrong with your system, or you have been getting through year after year of ‘I’ll do it next year,’ this might be the fall you want to tackle the issue that would help increase your home comfort, or simply get it back to where it needs to be!” Heating expert Phillip Dye said.

It’s better to get ahead of it by contacting your local heating expert because wait times for a consultation or an install may push you too far out for comfort, leaving you with a cold home longer than you want.

“Worrying about the comfort of our homes shouldn’t have to add to the stress of the fall, alongside kids returning to school, cold viruses spreading wild and the weather changing. Getting your home heating system either tuned up or replaced/upgraded as we enter into the fall and winter months is something we try to help keep at the front of people’s minds, that way something that could have been avoided doesn’t turn into a disaster or emergency,” Dye added. “We would love to share what your heating options might look like, ways to possibly upgrade and save money on your utility bills and increase the overall comfort in your home! Just think warm and cozy, and stress-free living.”

The longer you wait, the more those nights will sneak up on you. Change is in the air, and cold feet are not anything to get excited about.

text:
A proposed six-figure fee on H-1B workers is so prohibitive that it likely violates the law without clear authorization from Congress, employers warned in comments, offering a glimpse of potential arguments in future litigation.

An array of healthcare providers and other groups told the Department of Homeland Security its planned $103,265 fee would harm innovation and patient care during a public comment period that closed last week. Many of them also outlined the rule’s legal flaws similar to an earlier H-1B fee blocked by federal courts.

The Trump administration has made multiple bids to impose massive new costs to hire through the specialty occupation visa program, which has become the central focus of President Donald Trump’s foreign worker crackdown. Unlike the $100,000 charge added via White House proclamation last year, the DHS proposal relies on statutory authority to recoup the costs of services.

But the projected $8.7 billion in annual revenue raised by the latest fee and the long-term effects on care are so significant that it violates US Supreme Court precedent known as the major questions doctrine, the American Medical Association said in comments submitted ahead of the Sept. 24 deadline.

“This will lead to a sicker population overall which will have significant political and fiscal ramifications reaching from Medicare, to Medicaid, to private payers, and beyond,” wrote John Whyte, the group’s CEO and executive vice president. “The long-term effects of a lack of access to adequate medical care are enormous and likely unquantifiable both in terms of the impact on the health of patients and the cost associated with treating sicker individuals.”

Those effects mean the changes present a significant shift that would require approval from Congress, he said.

Lawmakers have set H-1B quotas, advanced degree exemptions, and a detailed cost structure, including fraud prevention fees, wrote Patrick Shen, vice president of immigration policy at the US Chamber of Commerce. They didn’t authorize another $100,000 charge “on top of that structure to finance unrelated federal programs,” he said.

DHS said it would address concerns about the proposal through the public comment process.

Initial Fee Litigation

The White House proclamation issued last year applied to H-1B hires from outside the US, which it said was necessary to limit alleged fraud and abuse in the program. Multiple groups — including the Chamber — sued to overturn the policy.

A federal judge in Boston vacated the proclamation in June, finding that it unlawfully wielded tax authority exclusive to Congress without delegation by lawmakers.

That decision handed a win to a coalition of Democratic attorneys general who challenged the proclamation. In a Sept. 24 letter, officials who joined that suit said the DHS proposal seeks to resurrect the same policy with no explanation of how the new fee wouldn’t also be an unconstitutional tax.

The new charge’s purported objective to recover immigration-related costs for DHS and other agencies appears to be an impermissibly broad application of fee provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act, the National Association of Manufacturers said in submitted comments.

Although it relies on a different legal authority than the 2025 proclamation, the proposal is another unlawful tax, the American Immigration Lawyers Association and American Immigration Council told DHS.

But the Institute for Sound Public Policy, which backs restricting foreign workers, said fee-setting authority in the INA doesn’t limit fees to incremental costs of particular applications.

“Congress created a fee-funded adjudication system, authorized full-cost recovery within that system, and allowed reimbursement of qualifying appropriations,” wrote Kevin Lynn, the group’s executive director.

Provider Impact

Medical groups told DHS that without an exemption to the fee, rural and safety-net health providers will be priced out of a key recruitment tool, imperiling patient care.

Rural hospitals and clinics already struggling with staffing shortages rely on the H-1B program because domestic supply of healthcare professionals doesn’t meet the needs of underserved areas, wrote Alan Morgan, CEO of the NRHA, in a public comment letter.

With physician shortages expected to worsen, demand for internationally born workers is only likely to grow, he said.

“In many communities, particularly rural and underserved areas, internationally born and trained physicians are not simply part of the workforce, they are the workforce,” Morgan said.

Health centers would find hiring for specialties as common as dental care infeasible with the six-figure charge, according to the National Association of Community Health Centers.

And the fee will steer hiring sponsorship away from hard-to-fill but needed primary care, said Mark D. Schwartz, president of the Society of General Internal Medicine.

“Our primary concern is that institutions may increasingly prioritize subspecialties that generate the greatest revenue to recoup the required investment, rather than focusing on primary care clinicians who can meet the needs of the communities they serve,” he said.

text:
NORTHWEST TALLAHASSEE, FL (WTXL) — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is releasing new details about what led to the detention of three Chile and Chili’s employees in northwest Tallahassee — two men and a woman — all from Guatemala who remain in ICE custody.

WATCH FULL REPORT BELOW:

ICE reveals what led to detentions at Chile & Chili's Taqueria in Tallahassee as legal expert weighs in

An ICE spokesperson said the agency and the Florida Highway Patrol were conducting targeted immigration enforcement activities when they attempted to stop a white truck carrying someone suspected of being in the country illegally from Guatemala.

When officers initiated the stop, the driver pulled onto Chile and Chilis property, and everyone inside the vehicle immediately started running.

The ICE spokesperson said the agency did not target the restaurant.

Owner Marco Tenorio told me Wednesday the incident sent staff into panic, and a spokesperson for the business said the detainees were finalizing paperwork at the time.

"I found out through a call from a worker who was in hiding— even though he had work papers. It’s the kind of panic that grips everyone, because seeing patrol cars making violent arrests, makes people scared and sends them into a panic, and they called me: 'Marco, Marco, what is happening?' Oh my God. All I did was try to reassure them: 'Calm down, calm down, nothing is going to happen, calm down, calm down,' but I felt a sense of utter helplessness," Marco Tenorio said, translated from Spanish.

ABC 27's Brieanna Smith asked Immigration Attorney Elizabeth Ricci about each detainee's case.

She said none of the three have a serious criminal history.

According to ICE, one male was issued a final order by an immigration judge last March, and his removal is pending.

The second male is requesting a voluntary departure.

The woman is facing pending immigration proceedings.

All detainees in the meantime will remain in ICE custody.

"These are examples of people who should, at least the latter two, find out. Do they have any options available to them? Talk to an immigration attorney or an accredited representative and find out rather than signing a way that you don't want to find out and just agree to leave," Elizabeth Ricci said.

Ricci said bond hearings could be scheduled on the same or next day, depending on where the detainee is held.

Bond could only be granted if there is no history of serious criminal history and if detainees pose no flight risk.

However, where detainees are held can make it difficult for attorneys and family members to contact them.

"This was a collateral situation, right? These three people were not targeted but because of the profiling, ended up fleeing,” Ricci said. “But what people don't realize is the people who were not in the video were legal and they all quit, so this has a chilling effect.

The ICE statement came days after the incident and after immigrant rights groups mobilized in Tallahassee.

T-CARE held a protest at the Tennessee Street location Wednesday, calling for the end of 287(g) agreements.

However, the Tallahassee Police Department, Leon County Sheriff’s Office and Florida Department of Law Enforcement denied involvement.

We reached out to Tenorio for an interview to get clarification on what his employees were doing to be in the U.S. legally.

Tenorio responded to our request for comment but did not set a date to discuss the matter further.

text:
The US State Department directed millions of dollars originally earmarked to promote human rights to promote far-right causes including Afrikaner rights in South Africa, safeguarding “Western civilizational norms,” and documenting “backsliding” in Europe related to mass migration, a source familiar with the matter told CNN.

The funds, which come from the nearly $177 million in Democracy Funds, were obligated despite concerns and holds by the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, the source said. They were due to lapse on Wednesday, the last day of the fiscal year.

The proposed causes align with the Trump administration’s broader shifts away from traditional human rights to focus on causes like alleged free-speech suppression and mass migration in Europe as well as “natural rights.” Two of the proposed grants are focused on Brazil and South Africa – countries where the administration has clashed with the governments – and a third is focused on Nigeria, where the administration has alleged “mass slaughter” of Christians.

It marks another instance of the administration bypassing Congress on funding matters, following its move to cancel $810 million of funding that has been appropriated by Congress for refugees, immigrants and other services.

Typically, the money from the Democracy Funds is used to support programs in authoritarian countries or those with limited democracies, the source said. Instead, the proposed grants, which were first reported by The Guardian, include funding for programs in Europe and the United Kingdom.

Asked about the funds, an unnamed State Department spokesperson said they had completed congressional notification requirements.

“The President promised to combat the destructive woke agenda that has done so much damage to our country and to the world,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said. “We will never apologize for defending Western civilization, opposing censorship, ending the era of mass migration, and taking action against government-sponsored race-based discrimination in South Africa.”

According to the source familiar with the matter, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had signed off on a memo to obligate the funds despite the ongoing holds. Senate Foreign Relations Committee ranking member Sen. Jeanne Shaheen had put holds on 10 proposed awards worth a total of $22 million.

The grants have buy-in from the highest levels of the White House, including Vice President JD Vance, the source said. The White House referred to the State Department for comment.

“Congress appropriated money for the Democracy Fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” Shaheen in a statement.

“In bypassing Congress, the Trump Administration is now using taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies,” the New Hampshire Democrat said. “This is a waste of resources and undermines American values and our relationships with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”

The proposed grants that had holds include one to combat alleged judicial overreach and censorship in Brazil. The Trump administration has clashed with the Lula government and had imposed sanctions on Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw the trial of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally. The sanctions were lifted in December. However, the US has also revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US and President Donald Trump has met with Flávio Bolsonaro, Jair Bolsonaro’s son who is running for president in Brazil.

Other proposed grants focus on Europe, including a $5 million award to support the development of “a civilizational alliance in Europe through research, public debates, and policy reform to safeguard freedom of expression, political competition, and national sovereignty.”

Top administration officials, including Vance, have lambasted European nations over allegations of free speech backsliding while also meeting with far-right European political figures.

Samuel Samson, a top appointee in the State Department’s Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor, argued last year for the need for “civilizational allies” in Europe.

“Our hope is that both Europe and the United States can recommit to our Western heritage, and that European nations will end the weaponization of government against those seeking to defend it,” he wrote.

The Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor has undergone significant changes under the second Trump administration.

text:
WASHINGTON – The family of Renee Good, an unarmed US citizen shot dead by an immigration agent during a sweeping federal crackdown, sued President Donald Trump’s administration on Oct 1, alleging wrongful death and civil rights violations.

Good, 37, was killed in Minneapolis on Jan 7 when an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent fired three shots into her car during Operation Metro Surge, the administration’s mass deployment in Minnesota.

Her family filed two lawsuits in federal court.

One names the United States and seeks damages under the Federal Tort Claims Act, alleging wrongful death, negligence and other misconduct.

The second names the killer, Jonathan Ross, along with senior Trump administration officials including then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Both Trump officials baselessly accused Good of terrorism, with Noem falsely claiming in a press conference that the victim had “attempted to run a law enforcement officer over”.

The second lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to violate civil rights under provisions of the 1871 Ku Klux Klan Act, arguing that the immigration operation deliberately targeted Somali and Hispanic communities and sought to intimidate people who protested or monitored federal agents.

“Renee’s death was not an accident,” lawyers for the family said, calling it the “predictable result” of policies that encouraged aggressive confrontations.

The Trump administration has defended its immigration crackdown and the conduct of its officers, maintaining that Ross’s use of deadly force was justified.

Video of the shooting showed Good calmly speaking to officers from inside her vehicle shortly before she tried to drive away.

The family’s lawsuit says she was unarmed, suspected of no crime and steering away from Ross when he fired.

Good’s killing triggered protests in Minneapolis and intensified scrutiny of the administration’s deportation campaign.

Two weeks later, federal immigration agents fatally shot another US citizen, intensive-care nurse Alex Pretti, during a confrontation in the city.

Good’s death also prompted turmoil inside the Justice Department after federal prosecutors in Minneapolis were prevented from investigating the agents involved, with several resigning in protest.

It has not charged any agent in connection with either killing, although Minnesota authorities are investigating both for possible violations of state law.

“What happened to us should never happen to any family. No child should grow up without a parent because of it. No one should lose their sister or their daughter. No one should have to live without their soulmate,” Good’s wife Becca Good said.

“Accountability – real accountability – is the only way to make sure that no other family has to go through what we have.” AFP

text:
Dive Update:

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday appealed a court ruling temporarily blocking the agency from implementing new regulations that would cap student visa stays to four years.

In mid-September, a federal judge put the regulations on pause just one day before they would have taken effect. In his ruling, U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor said a lawsuit from the higher education groups and unions over the cap was likely to succeed on several grounds.

The plaintiffs have argued that the rule violates the Administrative Procedure Act. Saylor agreed in his ruling, writing that the Trump administration’s justifications for the new regulations — namely, defending national security and preventing visa abuse — didn’t hold up to meaningful scrutiny.

The impact: DHS appealed the ruling to the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

The pipeline of international students that many colleges depend on is showing signs of cracking. Several major public universities have already reported steep declines in their international student populations this fall amid the Trump administration’s efforts to tighten visa policies.

The fate of these regulations could majorly impact those trends. In their lawsuit, the higher education groups warned that the effects would be “catastrophic for universities, international students and scholars, and the Nation as a whole.”

The background: The contested regulations would overhaul the nation’s longstanding international education system, which allows foreign students to stay in the U.S. for the duration of their studies.

Although international students could apply for extensions, the plaintiffs in the lawsuit have argued that there would be no guarantee that those would be granted. Saylor also voiced concerns with this process in his ruling, writing that DHS has provided little guidance and that decisions were left up to individual agency officials.

“In other words, a DHS official — based on limited and vague criteria, and with no possibility of appeal — will have the power to cut short the academic, research, or teaching activities of any non-U.S. citizen for no reason or any reason,” he wrote.

What we’re watching: Comprehensive data on international student enrollment is expected later this fall, potentially shedding more light on the impact of the Trump administration’s policies. In the meantime, the court fight over the rule is ongoing, as Saylor has not yet decided whether to vacate the regulations.

text:
Supreme Court lifts deportation block, Treasury automatically enrolls children in Trump Accounts, and more…

IN THE NEWS:

The U.S. Supreme Court issued a 6-3 order allowing the Trump Administration to resume deportations of migrants to countries not identified in the migrants’ removal orders. The majority did not state a reason for pausing the order issued by Judge Brian E. Murphy of the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts, who had found that the deportations violate due process rights by failing to give detainees meaningful notice. The Court also did not decide the legality of the deportation policy. The Court ordered a full oral argument on whether the policy violates the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution or international treaties on torture.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury issued a temporary rule automatically enrolling more than 60 million children in Trump Accounts, a tax-deferred savings and investment account, starting October 1, 2026. The automatic enrollment replaced the previous opt-in structure that required parents or guardians to submit an IRS form with a tax return or apply through the website. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that more than 7 million children have signed up for Trump Accounts as of late July and roughly 86% are from families earning less than $200,000. The Treasury Department has not provided full details on how parents or guardians can claim automatically created accounts to make their own contributions.

A federal court ruled that states can apply sports gambling laws to sports-related wagers on prediction markets. Kalshi and other prediction market platforms argued that the federal regulatory authority of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) preempts state regulation. The court, however, determined that the sporting event outcomes that customers place bets on remain outside the CFTC’s exclusive jurisdiction and that states may enforce their sports gambling laws against prediction market platforms. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit’s decision conflicted with a ruling from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, prompting some experts to anticipate further litigation at the U.S. Supreme Court.

The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) issued a final rule expanding notice requirements for people who store regulated explosive materials, such as dynamite and detonators. Existing regulations require people storing these materials to notify local fire safety officials when storage begins and report the type of explosives, the storage capacity, and the site location. The new rule requires people who store explosives to provide an updated notice every 12 months, a notice when storage ends, and keep copies of each notice for five years. The ATF explained that keeping officials informed about explosives storage helps firefighters plan safer responses to emergencies.

The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System proposed rules under the GENIUS Act for companies under its supervision that issue payment stablecoins, digital assets used for payments that issuers promise to exchange for a fixed amount of money. The proposal would require those companies to hold assets worth as much as their stablecoins still in circulation and keep those assets separate from their other holdings. Issuers would generally have to pay customers within two business days after receiving a request to exchange stablecoins for money. The Board explained that the proposed safeguards would help protect stablecoin holders from financial losses.

The U.S. Postal Service (USPS) changed the environmental review processes it uses to adhere to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). The USPS stated that it made the amendments to reduce regulatory burdens and bring its operations into compliance with recent legislation and judicial decisions establishing that NEPA is a procedural law not meant to subject agencies to substantive environmental responsibilities. The changes placed most of the USPS’s routine and administrative actions outside NEPA’s scope, narrowing the set of circumstances that trigger environmental review.

Connecticut implemented a new law that regulates artificial intelligence (AI) companies and chatbots. The law prohibits the sale of consumers’ geolocation data to prevent personal data from being used to set prices. The law also protects employees who report AI outputs that pose a “catastrophic risk” to the public from employer retaliation. Companies that offer “AI companions” are also required to have protocols for detecting when user interactions indicate a risk of suicide, self-harm, or imminent violence, and for referring users to mental health resources.

The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission initiated an investigation into the operations of the Northern Indiana Public Service Company after recent storms caused extended power outages for thousands of residents. The commission indicated that the investigation would seek information about the thoroughness of the utility’s extreme-weather preparedness and its use of third-party contractors to mitigate storm impacts. The commission acted after residential customers, consumer advocates, and Indiana Governor Mike Braun demanded accountability from the utility company, which received approval for $2 billion to upgrade transmission and distribution infrastructure in 2026.

WHAT WE’RE READING:

In a recent article in the Energy Law Journal, Uma Outka, a law professor at the University of Kansas, and Danielle Stokes, an associate professor of law at the University of Richmond, argued that centralized, state-level permitting for renewable energy projects could address development bottlenecks while incorporating input from local communities. Outka and Stokes contended that recent efforts by state governments to reclaim permitting authority from counties, municipalities, and townships would remove regulatory obstacles for renewable energy producers. Outka and Stokes evaluated policy changes in Michigan, New York, Illinois, and Massachusetts and concluded that states preempting or limiting local government authority can allow new development while maintaining opportunities for communities to negotiate financial and infrastructural benefits.

In a recent report, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) examined how the U.S. Department of Education oversees federal K-12 education programs and tracks chronic absenteeism, defined as missing at least 10 percent of school days. GAO found that the Education Department stopped its most comprehensive compliance reviews in 2026, increasing the chance that the misuse of federal education funds would go undetected. GAO also found that absenteeism rates could be inflated because the Education Department measured enrollment on day, excluding students who enrolled at a later date. GAO recommended that the Education Department reinstate broader compliance reviews and require states to use compatible methods for reporting enrollment and chronic absenteeism so the Education Department can calculate accurate absenteeism rates.

In a recent New America report, Daniel Kimmage and Darjan Vujica, fellows in the Future Security program of New America, argued that the most urgent AI threat is not a future autonomous system but the present-day erosion of democratic institutions and reinforcement of authoritarian repression. Kimmage and Vujica examined how authoritarian regimes are deploying AI to fabricate reality and silence dissent through deepfake pornography and surveillance. They noted that publicly available models have placed these capabilities in the hands of anyone with a laptop. Kimmage and Vujica contended that the United States has disarmed offices fighting information manipulation at agencies such as the Federal Bureau of Investigation, even as AI-generated content infiltrates domestic politics. They recommended that policymakers document AI’s harms and impose disclosure requirements.

EDITOR’S CHOICE:

In an essay in The Regulatory Review, Suzanne Eckes, the Susan S. Engeleiter Professor of Education Law, Policy, and Practice at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, and Charles J. Russo, the Joseph Panzer Chair in Education in the School of Education and Health Sciences at the University of Dayton, explained that although states and local school boards control and regulate public schools, courts can intervene when decisions about what schools teach violate constitutional rights. Eckes and Russo described how a federal court found that school officials in Arizona violated constitutional rights by targeting a Mexican American studies program for racially discriminatory reasons. Eckes and Russo also noted that a Virginia state court rejected parents’ challenge to an anti-racism curriculum, concluding that parents could not veto lessons because the content conflicted with their beliefs. Eckes and Russo questioned whether President Donald J. Trump’s executive order addressing school curricula could survive court challenges, given federal laws restricting what public schools teach.

text:
Japan has revised its permanent residence rules. The move is a response to concerns about abuse of the process. The problem is that Japan needs more immigrants to help fill the expanding shortages in the labor force.

An important driver of these revisions is a sense that the growing number of foreign immigrants is changing Japan for the worse. This is an impression, more than a reality. Japan, like every other nation, should aim to ensure that foreign immigrants obey the law, have the tools to fit into society and be prepared to make contributions — but that does not mean that it should necessarily be harder to immigrate. The Japanese government must focus on the long-term need for immigrants rather than the short-term political payoffs that come from exploiting unfounded fear.

Japan has long been ambivalent about its foreign-born population. For more than 200 years, it embraced an official policy of “sakoku” that resulted in an isolationist foreign policy and the creation of ghettos for the very few foreign residents who lived here. The country’s identity has been based on a myth of homogeneity — diversity is natural to a country of this geographic size and population — and a resulting insularity, expressed at a fatal moment as “100 million hearts beating as one.” Foreigners remained foreign, an identity that was often thrust upon them no matter how much they tried to integrate.

text:
The American Civil Liberties Union and several other immigrants’ rights advocates sent a letter to the Department of Homeland Security Thursday condemning “deplorable” conditions inside the Diamondback Correctional Facility in Watonga.

The letter cites widespread reports of medical neglect, insufficient food, severe social deprivation and failure to provide detained people with reasonable access to their legal counsel.

“We have received dozens of harrowing reports about life inside Diamondback,” the letter states. “These accounts are strikingly consistent in the concerns they raise.”

The 2,160-bed Diamondback Correctional Facility was built in 1998. Before it reopened this year as an immigration detention center, it sat empty for 15 years. In October 2025, the Oklahoma Department of Corrections and the federal government signed a 1000 million dollar contract with the private prison company CoreCivic, allowing the company to “hold noncitizens in immigration detention” at Diamondback. Two months later, the facility became operational.

“The uniformity and gravity of these complaints signal to us that ICE and its contractor CoreCivic are operating the facility with blatant disregard for the safety and legal rights of the people in their custody and care,” the letter states.

The facility’s infrastructure is potentially unfit to facilitate attorney-client visits, according to the letter. The advocates also say immigration detention is civil and not criminal in nature, meaning people at Diamondback are constitutionally entitled to conditions that do not aim to inflict punishment.

“People detained at Diamondback have also alleged that ICE officials systemically deny them reasonable access to counsel and the law library,” the letter states. “These barriers to basic legal resources undermine detained people’s constitutional rights, depriving them of fundamental fairness in their immigration proceedings.”

Travis Handler is a legal fellow for the ACLU of Oklahoma. In a press release, Handler said the Trump Administration’s policies have disregarded due process and the rights of those detained.

“We encourage all Oklahomans to hold the Department of Homeland Security and CoreCivic accountable,” Handler said in the statement. “Access to necessities like food, medical care, and legal counsel aren’t mere suggestions — they are constitutional protected rights to which all detained people are entitled.”

The letter details reports of deficient medical treatment. One detained man reported going without his prescription HIV medication for over two weeks, making him more vulnerable to HIV “progressively destroying his immune system.” Another woman reported having a urinary tract infection for over a month, despite requests for assistance.

Detained people also reported being deprived of sufficient food and clean drinking water, leading to significant weight loss, according to the letter.

The 14-page letter was signed by people from the ACLU of Oklahoma, the ACLU National Prison Project, Latitude Legal Alliance, YWCA Tulsa, Rivas & Associates law firm, University of Tulsa College of Law Legal Clinic and Council on American-Islamic Relations of Oklahoma.

It was directly addressed to two people at Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the warden at Diamondback Correctional Facility, requesting a meeting with officials to discuss concerns. The Oklahoma Department of Corrections was copied on the letter, along with six federal committees and offices.

“We urge ICE not to process in any new detained noncitizens at Diamondback until it has conducted a comprehensive review and ensures the public that the facility has adequate systems in place to provide for constitutional health care, attorney access, access to outdoor recreation, and processes for swiftly effectuating voluntary departure orders,” the letter states.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court announced it will hear arguments in a lawsuit over the Trump administration’s practice of indefinitely detaining migrants who allegedly crossed the border illegally.

In the past, accused illegal immigrants were often granted a hearing before a judge about their detention, but President Trump had been keen on ending so-called “catch and release” practices due to concerns that the migrants won’t show up to court.

The lower courts have splintered over whether the Trump administration’s policy on mandatory detentions violates federal law.

Now a key aspect of Trump’s immigration agenda will be in the Supreme Court’s crosshairs.

The decision to grant certiorari comes after the high court agreed this week to take up another case involving deportations.

The Supreme Court allowed the administration to continue deportations to third countries, nations that are not the illegal immigrants’ place of origin.

The indefinite detention case revolves around Brazilian citizen Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, who officials alleged entered the country illegally some two decades ago and has since sought asylum.

His attorneys have noted that he was never charged with a crime.

An immigration judge concluded he needed to be kept in detention, despite his push for a bond hearing.

An estimated 70,000 migrants are currently being holed up in immigration detention facilities, according to data from Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The Supreme Court is set to kick off its new term on Monday. A date for oral arguments in the case on indefinite detention, Rhoney, Acting Dir. v. Barbosa Da Cunha, Ricardo A., has not yet been scheduled.

US Solicitor General John Sauer has argued that indefinitely holding illegal immigrants residing in the country “prevents those aliens from evading hearings and helps ensure their removal from the United States.”

Immigrant rights groups have argued that under federal law, noncitizens are also afforded the right to have a bond hearing and that the policy has undermined that.

Trump faced a mixed bag on immigration cases before the Supreme Court last term, famously losing the birthright citizenship case, but prevailing on others, such as his attempt to yank temporary protected status (TPS) for thousands of Syrian and Haitian migrants.

Still, his losses before the high court have seemingly put a bad taste in Trump’s mouth, even toward some of his handpicked justices.

“They voted against me too often. I was very—I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often,” Trump vented to TIME magazine in a recent interview, when asked if he regrets some of his appointments. “The Democrats stick like glue—those three, they virtually never vary.”

“It’s unfortunate what they did.”
