text:
Amna Nawaz:

We start the day's other headlines in Washington, D.C., where the Supreme Court agreed to review the Trump administration's mandatory detention policy for migrants.

The justices will consider whether the government can legally deny bond hearings to immigrants who've been living in the U.S. after crossing the border illegally. The court's new term will kick off next week.

Separately, the family of Renee Good, the 37-year-old who was shot and killed by an ICE agent in Minneapolis, is suing the U.S. government. At a press conference, Good's loved ones, including her partner, Becca, said they're seeking accountability and change.

Becca Good, Partner of Renee Good: What happened to us should never happen to any family. No child should grow up without a parent. No one should lose their sister or their daughter. No one should have to live without their soul mate.

Brent Ganger, Brother of Renee Good: Since Renee's death, no meaningful change has occurred. The deaths of innocent Americans by taxpayer-funded government agents should not be a partisan issue, and it should alarm every American.

Amna Nawaz:

The two lawsuits also name former and current Trump immigration officials, as well as the agent himself. Renee Good was killed back in January amid massive protests sparked by the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Minneapolis.

President Trump is traveling to Texas and Oklahoma today as part of a midterms push to rally his party. But broadcast outlets are choosing not to show footage of his travels after the White House abruptly removed CNN from its press pool duties for the trip. Just days earlier, CNN was also barred from flying on Air Force One for a visit to Tennessee.

Last week, a judge blocked the administration's ban on CNN and two other media organizations from covering Mr. Trump, but only on the White House grounds. In a statement provided to the "News Hour," the lawyer representing the outlets said -- quote -- "The White House is persisting in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing the president's unconstitutional ban on the free press."

Driving storms across the center of the country broke daily rainfall records, and flash floods prompted water rescues and evacuations. What was Hurricane Polo has combined with a massive storm system trudging east, stretching from Colorado to Iowa. Roughly 40 million people were under flood alerts today, including in Texas.

Floodwaters overnight in Abilene submerged cars, and at least one person had to be rescued, while, in Nebraska, harrowing moments as a tractor trailer jackknifed in the driving rain. Some downpours, like in Omaha, dropped more than five inches of rain in just 24 hours. Forecasters say a considerable flood threat will last through tomorrow.

In the U.K., police say they have arrested a British-Iranian citizen on suspicion of planning a terror attack following a security incident at an air base. Authorities say the 27-year-old was taken into custody today in Central London. Another British national was also questioned by police, but not arrested.

Five men who were detained near RAF Fairford this past weekend were later released on bail. The air base has been used by American bombers in the war against Iran. '

Yesterday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he sees -- quote -- "strong indications" that Iran is linked to the incident, though Tehran has denied this.

In Ukraine, a Russian drone slammed into a school in Kyiv today as the capital endured yet another day of aerial attacks. Street camera footage shows the moment the drone hit the building and knocked out part of its wall. Students and staff were sheltering in a bunker and no injuries were reported.

The school's principal says it's the second time the building has been damaged in a strike.

Valentyna Chorna, School Principal (through interpreter):

The Russians spare no one. In order to destroy a nation, of course they need to destroy children. That is why they keep striking educational institutions. But we are holding on. We are working. We are teaching children.

Amna Nawaz:

Meantime, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy posted a video on social media today saying it shows the first combat use of a domestically made ballistic missile. And in a separate post, he said that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian ship in the Black Sea, while, in Moscow, President Vladimir Putin renewed threats to use, as he put it, "all weapons in our country's arsenal" if European nations attack Kaliningrad.

That is Russia's exclave between Lithuania and Poland. His comments follow an earlier warning by Russia that nuclear weapons could be deployed.

On Wall Street today, stocks largely held steady amid the latest swings in the bond market. The Dow Jones industrial average added just 20 points, so basically flat. The Nasdaq also ended little changed, and the S&P 500 managed to break a three-day losing streak.

And, in Florida, SpaceX launched four astronauts to the International Space Station this morning.

Man:

Three, two, one, ignition, and liftoff.

Amna Nawaz:

Their 230-foot-tall Falcon 9 rocket powered off the ground for an estimated eight-hour journey to the ISS. That is faster than any prior U.S. journey to the station. The crew is made up of two Americans, a Canadian and a Russian cosmonaut. And it's led by Commander Jessica Watkins, the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit.

Their six-month mission is meant to focus on human health and performance while in space.

text:
As the Trump administration continues to accelerate the deportations of immigrants — including to third-party countries — artists and comedians alike are jumping into action.

On Saturday, creatives will gather at the La Cita Bar in downtown L.A. to release “Contra-ICE Vol. 1: ICE Out,” a new album released under the label SoundsGood Records that rallies against the inhumane onslaught of immigration enforcement and amplifies the humanity of immigrant communities.

“The fire was there, the urgency was there,” said Dali Colorado, a longtime DJ and Los Angeles native who helped curate the 47-track project. “ I really want people to listen to it as a calming space, to sit and feel the vibration by all the artists.”

The Saturday event, which kicks off at 8 p.m., will double as a benefit show. Proceeds will go to nonprofits like Build Art Make Change, which spearheaded the compilation, as well as community defense organizations Unión del Barrio and the National Day Laborer Organizing Network (NDLON).

While somber at times, the compilation kicks off with “I Refuse,” an eerie spoken-word track composed by Filer Coleman, who pieces together anonymous testimonies of civil rights violations. Coleman later joins forces with HopesAndDrums for a house mix that calls for abolishing ICE.

But the anthology also deploys humor as a form of protest. In the track “Al and Chris Vs. ICE,” comedians Al Madrigal and Chris Estrada call out Latino ICE agents in a country-punk standoff, by rescinding their invitations to the collective carne asada. Comedian Frankie Quiñones also reprises his role as Creeper from his web series, “CholoFit,” to lead a meditation.

Other notable features include Fred Armisen, Kathleen Hanna, Ad-Rock, Adrian Quesada, Ceci Bastida, Tom Morello, Richard Montoya, Tropa Magica and more.

The origin of the momentous volunteer project dates back to the day that President Trump was elected for his second term in 2024. Colorado felt uneasy after Trump vowed to carry out the “largest domestic deportation operation in American history” once in office.

“Things are gonna get really bad,” Colorado said to herself.

In the summer following Trump’s inauguration, his administration would conduct massive immigration raids and sweeps in Colorado’s hometown. She thought, “How can you do social justice when you’re an artist?”

Alongside her longtime friend, saxophonist Ulises “Uli” Bella of Grammy-winning band Ozomatli, the two recalled moments of political polarization under Presidents Reagan and George H.W. Bush between 1981 and 1993. They looked to the presidents’ response, or lack thereof, to the HIV/AIDS epidemic — which claimed an estimated 100,777 lives between 1981 and 1990, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

In 1990, the Red Hot Organization — a nonprofit raising awareness and funding to fight the global HIV/AIDS epidemic — released its first compilation album, “Red Hot + Blue.” The organization has release 21 compilations and raised over $10 million since; its subsequent television special on ABC became one of the first major AIDS benefits in the music business.

“[‘Red Hot + Blue’] really resonates with me — the silence equals death [idea],” said Colorado, quoting a protest slogan from AIDS activist organization ACT UP. “Because that’s how I feel about what’s happening here. We have to mobilize. We have to become active.”

Bella cited post-hardcore band Fugazi as inspiration for the album, as well as punk rockers Dead Kennedys, who used satire to call out corporate greed and politicians. They famously likened former California Gov. Jerry Brown to a hippie fascist in “California Über Alles”; Dead Kennedys’ former frontman Jello Biafra also contributed to the anti-ICE album.

“I was a teenage kid listening to this stuff and I was getting so much political education from all these bands,” said Bella.

There was one particularly gripping incident that occurred during the height of the ICE raids in L.A. that inspired the album cover for “Contra-ICE.” Designed by Lalo Alcaraz, the artwork features an ice cream cart under a spotlight, surrounded by loudspeakers.

Bella recalled the haunting image of the abandoned paletero cart, which belonged to Ambrocio “Enrique” Lozano, an undocumented immigrant who sold ice cream in Culver City for nearly two decades before he was taken by masked federal agents inside an unmarked vehicle.

“It’s almost like all of a sudden someone disappeared into thin air. That cart is just left there as a testament to their existence,” said Bella.

Kathleen Hanna, lead singer of all-woman punk band Bikini Kill, jumped at the chance to participate in the project.

“ We all obviously strongly believe that people should not be kidnapped off the streets,” said Hanna — who pioneered the “riot grrrl” feminist punk movement in the early 1990s. In the album, she covers “Let Me Love You” by DJ Snake featuring Justin Bieber, alongside Ad-Rock, Money Mark, Fredo Ortiz and Frank Figueroa.

It’s not a love song, she said in a call to The Times, but rather a track that counters the dehumanization of immigrants, who are made to feel undeserving of human rights and respect. “[They say] you’re not lovable, you’re not worthy, you’re not even human,” she explained.

“I sang it with that emotion in my heart, that feeling of telling someone else, ‘No, you are lovable,’” said Hanna.

There were some initial doubts over the relevance that “Contra-ICE Vol. 1: ICE Out” would have a year after the blitz of ICE raids in 2025, which Bella called “ political theater” — citing how former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem appeared publicly donning tactical gear, which critics called opportunistic.

“ Sadly, we’re still here and it’s as worse as ever,” said Bella.

Jim Coleman, who releases ambient music as Filer Coleman, believes the timing of this release is more relevant than ever.

The musician was a keyboardist and founding member of Cop Shoot Cop, a noise rock group that formed in New York City in 1987. Coleman recalled a recent New York Times article that highlighted how immigration raids this summer — which surpassed 50,000 arrests in July and August — received little public backlash compared to last year’s wave.

“[ICE] activities are becoming way more accelerated, but the visibility is decreased. A lot of people are like ‘Oh, is that still a thing?’” said Coleman. “This album is ‘Volume One,’ so I think there’s a road ahead where we can continue.”

Creative director Jake Trussell — the visionary behind HopesAndDrums, whose production is also featured throughout the album — felt called to contribute after witnessing Operation Midway Blitz in his Chicago neighborhood, an immigration enforcement plan that launched Sept. 8, 2025.

“They’ve killed people since then. They keep shooting people. They keep arresting innocent people. They’re going around in masks and unmarked vehicles without badges,” said Trussell.

There have been other moments of terror that lit a fire in Trussell’s soul, including the killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti on Jan. 7 and 24, respectively, by federal agents.

“It was inspiring for me to see the people of Minneapolis come out on the streets [protesting], and hopefully what we’re doing will be inspiring to others,” said Trussell.

Performances for “Contra-ICE Vol. 1: ICE Out” will begin at 8 p.m. Saturday with various contributors taking part — including Bella, Filer Coleman and HopesAndDrums.

They will be joined by L.A.-based acts like Fishbone, Los Abandoned, Daniel French of Las Cafeteras, Of Mexican Descent feat. 2Mex, Las Chorizeras and Nancy Sanchez. Comedians Richard Montoya of Culture Clash and Frankie Quiñones and cartoonist Lalo Alcaraz will also make cameos.

text:
As the Trump administration's sweeping illegal immigration crackdown draws pushback from some Republican lawmakers, White House border czar Tom Homan told CBS News that critics should "talk to ICE" and "educate themselves."

GOP Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida raised eyebrows last month when she taped a campaign ad warning President Trump the Hispanic voters who helped him secure a second term "feel betrayed." She said some of the administration's tactics have "gone too far," pointing to data that shows many ICE detainees lack criminal records. Other Republicans have also raised concerns, including Sen. Jim Justice of West Virginia.

In response to Salazar's comments, Homan said: "Give me an example of where we went too far. That's a pretty bold statement to make."

Homan said the Trump administration is still prioritizing people who it views as public safety threats, but anybody who is in the U.S. illegally is "deportable by federal law."

"If you're in the country illegally, you got a problem. You shouldn't be here," Homan said, later adding that "everybody we arrest has an opportunity to see a judge and plead their case."

He argued much of the criticism is "about hate on this administration and taking on Trump," pointing to ICE's high arrest and deportation figures during the Obama administration, when Homan was a senior official at the agency.

Pressed on the growing GOP criticism, Homan said: "I wish they'd sit down and talk to ICE. I wish they'd find out: What is ICE doing? How are they doing it? And educate themselves."

The Trump administration has drawn scrutiny not just for the rapid surge in arrests, but also for the government's immigration tactics — including a series of shootings by ICE agents during traffic stops, two of which resulted in migrants being killed over the summer.

Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti — were also fatally shot by immigration agents during a crackdown in the Minneapolis area earlier this year. Good's family filed lawsuits against federal officials this week, naming Homan as a defendant in one of them.

Asked about Good's death earlier in his interview with CBS News, Homan called the situation "tragic," but said he is not involved in the investigation into the shooting.

"I don't want to see any tragedies happen," Homan said. "I wish Renee Good was alive today. I wish that incident [didn't] happen, but it happened, and it's being investigated. I don't want to see anybody die."

Arrests haven’t disappeared entirely This ruling, however, does not mean ICE can never arrest someone at an immigration courthouse.

text:
The decision comes after more than a year of aggressive ICE enforcement at the facility and nearby 290 Broadway, during which masked agents dragged men, women, and even children through the hallways, many of whom had no criminal records. amNewYork documented tearful scenes and families being separated at the Manhattan immigration court, where people who came for what were supposed to be routine hearings found themselves facing detention.

Under the ruling issued on Oct. 1, arrests can now be made only in or near courthouses, and only under limited circumstances. U.S. District Judge P. Kevin Castel said he found the legal basis for the previous detentions to be “arbitrary and capricious.” This comes after ICE allegedly lied to the same judge in March regarding their legal right to make the arrests inside immigration courts.

In the filing, then-U.S Attorney for the Southern District of New York Jay Clayton and the New York Civil Liberties Union, which objects to immigration enforcement detaining respondents at locations such as 26 Federal Plaza and 290 Broadway, said the agency outright lied to prosecutors, immigration courts, and others about their right to make the now-infamous arrests. In fact, this jurisdiction only applied to criminal courthouses.

“The undersigned were specifically informed by ICE that the 2025 ICE Guidance applied to immigration courthouse arrests,” Clayton wrote.

“We deeply regret that this error has come to light at this late stage, after the parties have expended significant resources and time to litigate this case and this Court has carefully considered Plaintiffs’ challenge to the 2025 ICE Guidance,” Clayton wrote in the filing, according to The American Prospect.

The Oct. 1 ruling means ICE must again operate under a 2021 policy governing civil immigration enforcement at or near immigration courts. That policy permits arrests only under limited circumstances, rather than giving agents broad discretion to arrest at immigration courthouses.

“Today’s ruling is an enormous win for every noncitizen seeking to safely attend their immigration court proceedings,” said Amy Belsher, director of Immigrants’ Rights Litigation at the New York Civil Liberties Union. “For too long, we watched masked, often armed, ICE officers ambush noncitizens in courthouse hallways, throw immigrants to the ground, and tear sobbing children from their parents. But with today’s order, the Court made clear: ICE’s cruel, unjustified policy of conducting mass immigration arrests in courthouses is unlawful and cannot stand.”

The original lawsuit was filed by a coalition of immigrant rights groups, including The New York Civil Liberties Union, American Civil Liberties Union, Make the Road NY, and more on Aug. 1, 2025, which eventually led the court to issue a stay after ICE allegedly fabricated its authority to make the arrests. This final federal ruling affirms that order, and expands it to apply nationwide. It is effective immediately.

Arrests haven’t disappeared entirely

This ruling, however, does not mean ICE can never arrest someone at an immigration courthouse. Instead, it restores the 2021 policy, which permits arrests at or near immigration courts only under limited circumstances.

Nevertheless, advocates called Thursday’s ruling a victory.

“The court’s ruling is a monumental victory for immigrant families and the rule of law. It brings to an end the cruel and callous practice of arresting immigrants simply for showing up to their court hearings — something that no one should have to worry about, and yet so many were forced to live under that cloud of fear,” said Harold Solis, co-legal director at Make the Road New York.

During the summer of 2025, the 12th and 14th floors of 26 Federal Plaza saw what sources described as an almost conveyor belt of ICE arrests, with double-digit arrests occurring on some days.

While the number of ICE detentions at the building has slowed in recent months, arrests still occur, according to courthouse sources. One arrest took place last week, a source told amNewYork. Other arrests have reportedly shifted to other floors of the building, including during ICE check-ins, with enforcement increasingly affecting African immigrants in New York.

Courthouse sources also told amNewYork that the arrests caused widespread panic among immigrants, with some respondents choosing not to attend their immigration hearings out of fear of being detained.

Under federal law, people who fail to appear for their immigration hearings can be ordered removed in absentia. The judge’s opinion itself notes that fear of arrest could therefore create a dilemma in which immigrants risk detention by attending court or a deportation order by staying away.

Legal experts now say they hope the ruling will allow immigration proceedings to continue without people skipping their hearings because they fear arrest.

“Immigrant New Yorkers should not have to choose between attending a required immigration hearing and risking detention, or staying away and risking a deportation order for failing to appear,” said Katie Rosenfeld, a partner at Emery Celli Brinckerhoff Abady Ward & Maazel LLP. “This ruling restores important safeguards and makes clear that ICE cannot abandon those protections without a reasoned explanation. Due process requires a meaningful opportunity to be heard, and that means people must be able to come to court without fear.”

text:
Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage met for the first time on the debate stage Thursday night, where they continued their clash over healthcare and traded barbs over each other’s records in state government.

The state auditor and former governor are vying to replace outgoing Rep. Jared Golden in the U.S. House of Representatives for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District.The WMTW debate quickly settled on a familiar theme: the candidates’ opposing stances on healthcare and how to reduce rising costs.

Throughout the Democratic primary, Dunlap campaigned on his support for Medicare For All, placing him in stark opposition to LePage, who oversaw dramatic cuts to Maine’s healthcare programs as governor and vetoed several bills to expand MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program.

And while Dunlap acknowledged that universal healthcare would take time to implement, a more immediate solution he said he would advocate for in Congress is reestablishing marketplace insurance subsidies that congressional Republicans allowed to expire at the beginning of 2026.

Of the 61,000 Maine people who enroll through CoverME.gov, the state’s online marketplace, 85% relied on those premium tax credits to reduce their monthly costs. The lapse of the subsidies are contributing to spiking insurance costs in Maine and across the country.

“If you restore the subsidies to the Affordable Care Act, they’d see it immediately in January, as soon as we could enact it, and the president would sign it into law,” Dunlap said. “So I think that would be an immediate relief.”

In contrast, LePage said he would not support expanding Medicaid — even if it lowered the number of uninsured Mainers — and underscored his opposition to a universal healthcare system.

“The reason I have a problem with Medicare For All is they’re not telling you the truth,” LePage said. “If you’ve not lived in Canada, you don’t understand socialized medicine. What happens is your insurance coverage that you have now at work goes away. Bureaucrats make decisions on your healthcare, not your doctor.”

When Dunlap pushed back, LePage repeatedly questioned if he had lived in Canada and experienced the system to understand how it works. Dunlap said he had lived in Maine his whole life.

“I do understand how it works, and people in Canada are not flocking to Maine to get less insurance,” Dunlap said.

“No, they’re flocking to Maine to get cancer treatments and heart treatments,” LePage responded.

Fate of Medicare, Medicaid emerge as key issue in 2nd District race

Dunlap also criticized cuts to federal healthcare programs under President Donald Trump, and said they would only make things more expensive for Mainers. But LePage defended the president’s policies, specifically the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, which was passed to partially offset the dramatic cuts to Medicaid, though experts say it remains to be seen how those funds will be distributed.

“[Dunlap] says we’re going to lose Medicaid after the election,” LePage said. “No, you’re not. There’s $50 billion that’s going to be spent across the nation in rural communities to help sustain and have healthcare provided to those in need.”

“Which won’t replace the trillion dollars worth of cuts,” Dunlap interjected.

LePage also repeated the claim that there is extensive fraud in Maine’s benefit programs, which are currently being investigated by the state Department of Health and Human Services.

“I’m sorry to say that there’s fraud in Maine, fraud across the country in Social Security, and in our Medicaid and in our welfare programs and I experienced it,” LePage said. “I’ve been fighting this battle since 2015 and it’s only now coming to the surface.”

In the most recent federal review, Maine’s Medicaid payment error rate was 2.4%, lower than the national average of 3.2%. And only about 0.1% of total program spending was confirmed by federal reviewers to be definitively incorrect.

Dunlap pushed back on the claim, arguing that Republicans’ focus on fraud is a cover for cutting program funding.

“When J.D. Vance, however, talks about Medicaid fraud, I want to be clear: he’s not interested in rooting out Medicaid fraud,” Dunlap said. “They’re interested in rooting out Medicaid, and I think that’s something we should be very wary of in the Congress.”

Tackling affordability challenges

Healthcare wasn’t the only divisive issue on the debate stage. The candidates clashed over housing, affordability issues, foreign conflicts and even what has been said on the campaign trail.

“You said that just last week that if you’re elected, you’re not going to do anything for two years because you’re going to be impeaching the president,” LePage said to Dunlap.

“I did not say that,” Dunlap answered. “What I said was that people should have the expectation that even if the Democrats take control of both chambers, President Trump probably won’t be signing very much that comes out. But however, we can still maintain our constitutional role of oversight of the executive branch, and that’s what we should be doing.”

Along with emphasizing his record as Maine governor, LePage pointed to his relationship with Trump and his access to the president.

“I know him personally, and I will say right now, I will be able to get into the Oval Office,” LePage said. “My opponent will not.”

Dunlap countered that Congress is meant to hold the president accountable, not maintain close ties.

On the issue of affordability, LePage said one of his top priorities if elected is to ask the president to put restrictions on diesel exports, echoing a call from top congressional Republicans, and would advocate for the state and federal government to suspend taxes on fuel.

Dunlap said he had heard from many people in the district that rising fuel and heating oil prices were already straining their budgets.

“One thing that we could do to help lower the cost of energy very quickly is to pass a war powers resolution and stop this war in Iran, which my opponent won’t say whether or not he supports,” Dunlap said. “So if we stop the war in Iran, we’ll see the price of oil start to come down, and that’s something that will provide almost immediate relief.”

LePage said he did not believe in the War Powers Act and that the president has constitutional authority over the military.

“I do not support the war in Iran,” LePage said. “I do support not allowing Iran to get the nuclear power, nuclear bomb, and so I’m urging the president to work as fast, as vigilant, as possible to get this done quickly. Let’s get out of it.”

The lack of access to affordable housing was also something the candidates were asked about.

Dunlap said he has spoken to people in construction and development, and said a key way Congress can help Maine’s housing crisis is by making more financing available.

“When you talk to people who work in the field of affordable housing and construction of it, they have a hard time accessing capital and financing,” Dunlap said. “And this is something that Congress can do and has done in the past: make funding available on a rotating basis, a revolving loan fund, so that it’d be easier for some of these developers to do.”

LePage agreed that Congress should provide funding, but he said that it should be focused on housing for the elderly. He then quickly pivoted to immigration.

“Housing costs remain out of control, first and foremost, stopping the illegal aliens from coming into our state and taking what housing is available should be stopped,” LePage said.

LePage said that he believes President Joe Biden let “millions and millions” of people enter the country illegally. And while he said he doesn’t disagree that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has “run roughshod” over communities, he believes the agency can be improved with proper training.

“I think we need to have a robust law enforcement division of our country that deals with it,” LePage said. “However, we should be able to have transparency, and if there are robust investigations, and if there’s a problem, then we need to account and make them accountable.”

The federal government has so far declined to investigate or reveal any information about the fatal shooting of Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero, the Biddeford man who was killed by federal agents in July, a pattern seen across the country in response to violence and wrongful detentions by ICE.

Dunlap said that while ICE should exist in some capacity, it shouldn’t be in the way the agency is functioning today.

“Gov. LePage has talked very strongly about being tough on illegal immigration, being tough on the border, until of course somebody he knew very well ran into some immigration trouble,” Dunlap said, referring to LePage’s recent comments that his daughter-in-law’s father had immigrated legally but was deported.

“Then he kind of changed his tune a little bit,” Dunlap continued.

LePage said that was a personal situation, and has nothing to do with illegal immigration or ICE.

On the issue of trade, LePage said he does not support the tariffs as they are currently structured, but that the country has gotten a “bad deal” for many years with many countries.

“These issues are real, and they and they need to be addressed,” LePage said. “We need to de-escalate the rhetoric, and we need to get the president and the prime minister of Canada back to the negotiating table.”

The Canadian tariffs that went into effect Sept. 8, are expected to impact $170 million of Maine exports.

Dunlap said it’s Maine residents who are paying for the tariffs, and Congress should exercise more authority over the issue.

“Tariffs are a tool, they should not be used as a blanket policy,” Dunlap said. “And my opponent said that he was all for the tariffs when they first started being applied, and now apparently, now apparently he’s changing his tune a little bit.”

text:
Renee Nicole Good's family filed two federal lawsuits on Thursday, which marked nearly nine months after she was shot and killed during an immigration enforcement operation in Minneapolis.

The lawsuits, which were filed in U.S. District Court in Minnesota, were brought by Good's brother, Brent Ganger, and her partner, Rebecca Good.

"What happened to Renee was completely senseless. And the fact that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy, is completely mind-blowing. What happened to America?" Ganger said during a news conference.

"Something must change now," he added. "It is our family's hope that today's lawsuit will accomplish our goal for Renee: accountability. Our family has waited. Our country has waited. And we will not wait any longer. The time is absolutely now for accountability for the deep damage done by ICE and others. We will not be quiet. We will not go away."

One lawsuit, filed against "the United States of America," alleges the wrongful death of Good under Minnesota law predicated on claims of battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and negligence that caused her death.

The complaint alleges Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) deportation officer Jonathan Ross acted unlawfully. He fired three shots into Good's Honda Pilot on January 7 as she drove away from agents.

One bullet hit the 37-year-old in the left temple, according to the filing.

The lawsuit said Good was not the target of an investigation, had no criminal history, and had committed no act of violence. It alleged Ross moved out of the SUV's path before leaning toward it, drawing his gun and firing.

Good's partner had stepped out of the SUV to record agents with her cellphone and was standing nearby when the shots were fired, the complaint says.

The filing alleged that no agents rendered aid after the shooting and that an ICE agent turned away a bystander, who identified himself as a physician. Good was pronounced dead at Hennepin County Medical Center.

The Trump administration previously said Good tried to weaponize her SUV and harm ICE agents. Federal officials at the time said the agent acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in "an act of domestic terrorism."

The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights.

It names multiple defendants, including Ross, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem, former U.S. Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino, Corey Lewandowski, who is President Donald Trump's campaign manager, and several others.

text:
President Donald Trump's push to expand immigration detention is headed to the Supreme Court, setting up a major test for three justices he now says he regrets appointing.

The Supreme Court announced Thursday that it will review the Trump administration's policy of denying bond hearings to certain immigrants arrested inside the United States while they challenge deportation proceedings, a case that could affect millions of noncitizens and significantly reshape federal immigration enforcement.

A decision is expected during the court's current term, which begins Monday, October 5, and runs through mid-2027.

Read More on Politics

"DHS is glad that the Supreme Court will hear arguments regarding mandatory detention and opinions from the Board of Immigration Appeals and multiple federal courts of appeals that reflect the soundness of the Department's legal position," a DHS spokesperson told Newsweek.

The announcement arrives as Trump said in an interview with TIME that he regretted appointing Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett because they had ruled against him "too often" in several major cases during his second term.

What the Supreme Court Will Decide

The dispute centers on whether immigrants accused of entering the country illegally must remain in government custody throughout their removal cases or whether they are entitled to individualized bond hearings before an immigration judge. Most federal appeals courts have concluded that prolonged detention without such hearings violates federal law, while the Fifth and Eighth Circuits have sided with the administration's interpretation that detention is mandatory.

"They say the nation’s courts have been inundated with thousands of petitions filed by immigrants challenging the government’s legal interpretation," Trump's lawyers wrote. “The result is an unworkable patchwork of inconsistent immigration enforcement, where aliens present without admission are subject to mandatory detention in some circuits but are entitled to bond hearings and often released in others."

At issue is how broadly a 1996 immigration statute should be applied. The administration contends it covers immigrants who entered the country illegally regardless of how long they have lived in the United States, while opponents argue Congress intended the mandatory-detention provision to apply mainly to individuals encountered at or near the border.

The DHS spokesperson said the administration's implementation of the law "put the nail in the coffin" for former Democratic President Joe Biden's "catch and release policies" and argued that covered immigrants "are required to be detained."

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), which is helping represent the plaintiffs in the case, welcomed the Supreme Court's decision to hear the case and noted lower courts have rejected the administration's interpretation of the statute.

"The courts have repeatedly and resoundingly rejected the Trump administration's radical misinterpretation of the law," Michael K.T. Tan, deputy director of the ACLU's Immigrants' Rights Project, said in a statement shared with Newsweek via email. "Try as it might, the government cannot twist the law to detain immigrants for months or even years on end without a bond hearing."

Jennifer Lee Koh, a professor at Pepperdine Caruso School of Law who specializes in immigration law, told Newsweek the dispute extends beyond a technical disagreement over how federal immigration statutes should be interpreted.

"Outwardly, the point of disagreement amongst the courts involves a seemingly technical interpretation of the law: for instance, what the words 'seeking admission' mean," Koh said in an email response. "But the case is really about something far more fundamental, which is the scope of the government's power to detain people based on the allegation that they once entered the country without authorization."

Newsweek has reached out to the Department of Justice (DOJ) via email on Thursday morning for comment.

Trump's Clash With His Supreme Court Picks

The case arrives before a court Trump has publicly criticized in recent months despite having appointed three of its nine members during his first term.

Referring to Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett, Trump told TIME: "Yeah. Yeah. What can I do? I put them in. They voted against me too often. I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often. They vote for me, too."

Trump's frustration with the three justices follows several significant Supreme Court defeats during his second term, including rulings on tariffs, birthright citizenship and the independence of the Federal Reserve. While the president insisted to TIME that he was seeking "good decisions" rather than loyalty, he contrasted his appointees with the court's three Democratic-appointed justices, whom he accused of voting together more consistently.

"The Democrats stick like glue, those three, they virtually never vary," he told the magazine. "You can come up with the worst thing in the world and they'll vote as a group. And while I don't like it, there's something I admire about it: there's loyalty."

He added, in part: "They have loyalty to Barack Hussein Obama. They have loyalty to [Joe] Biden ... And me, I gave them the chance of a lifetime, and it's unfortunate what they did."

The newly accepted immigration case is the latest major dispute involving Trump's immigration agenda to reach a court he has increasingly criticized over rulings that have frustrated key parts of his second-term policy agenda.

What a Supreme Court Decision Could Mean for ICE and Immigrant Detention

The case comes as Trump pursues an aggressive immigration crackdown that has become a defining feature of his second term. ICE reported in July that it had removed more than 356,000 people during fiscal year 2026, putting the agency on pace for one of its highest annual deportation totals in decades. At the same time, Reuters reported that ICE made nearly 51,000 arrests in August, a monthly record, including many people who did not have criminal convictions or pending criminal charges.

If the Supreme Court ultimately backs the Trump administration, it would clear the way for ICE to continue holding many immigrants in custody while their deportation cases move through the courts, without first providing bond hearings. Such a ruling could resolve the conflicting decisions that have emerged across the country and give the administration a significant victory as it pursues a broader immigration crackdown.

A ruling against the administration, however, could require ICE to once again provide broader access to bond hearings for immigrants arrested inside the United States, including some who have lived in the country for years. It would also reinforce the position adopted by most federal appeals courts and likely force the administration to revisit guidance that expanded the use of mandatory detention.

Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.

The US Supreme Court handed Donald Trump a significant victory on Tuesday by letting his administration immediately resume rapid deportations of migrants to third countries, triggering outrage from critics who branded the emergency order 'evil' and the policy 'reckless cruelty'.

A federal court had blocked those removals unless migrants had a chance to challenge them, including over fears of persecution or torture. The unsigned Supreme Court order lets the administration resume the policy ahead of arguments scheduled for December.

The government sought emergency permission to restart those rapid removals while the legal dispute continues.

The three liberal justices said they would have denied the administration's request. The order allows the government to proceed while the court prepares to hear arguments on the policy.

The Trump administration has sent more than 25,000 people to third countries, including Liberia, Equatorial Guinea and the Central African Republic, the New York Times reported.

Those reactions appeared on X and Bluesky, with critics challenging both the administration's choice of destinations and the court's decision to let removals restart.

text:
By MICHAEL KUNZELMAN

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Thursday agreed to review a Trump administration policy denying bond hearings for immigrants as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown.

The justices will consider whether immigrants who have been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation.

The case will test a key pillar of the Trump administration’s hard-line immigration agenda.

Most appeals courts to have considered the issue have found that it violates federal law to detain immigrants, including those living in the U.S. illegally, without a bond hearing. Those decisions conflict with rulings by the 5th and 8th circuits, which held that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the U.S. must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.

The high court agreed to hear the case of Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a citizen of Brazil. Authorities say he entered the United States illegally two decades ago and applied for asylum in 2016. He sought a bond hearing after an immigration judge determined that his detention was mandatory following his September 2025 arrest.

He has never been charged or convicted of a crime, his attorneys said. The court is expected to hear the case in the coming months.

President Donald Trump’s administration had urged the high court to take up a different but related case that involves the broader constitutional implications of the new policy.

Attorneys from the Republican administration argue the circuits’ split is “disrupting the orderly administration of immigration law.” They say the nation’s courts have been inundated with thousands of petitions filed by immigrants challenging the government’s legal interpretation.

“The result is an unworkable patchwork of inconsistent immigration enforcement, where aliens present without admission are subject to mandatory detention in some circuits but are entitled to bond hearings and often released in others,” lawyers for the administration wrote.

The plaintiffs are immigrants represented by the American Civil Liberties Union, which says hundreds of district court judges have joined most circuits in rejecting the Trump administration’s new reading of the statutes. Plaintiffs’ lawyers say the administration is trying to deny bond hearings for immigrants apprehended anywhere in the U.S. — no matter how long they’ve lived in the country — rather than limiting the restriction to noncitizens stopped at the border.

“Millions of noncitizens could be affected by the government’s new interpretation,” ACLU attorneys wrote.

text:
EUGENE, Ore. (CN) — A federal judge declined to order the Department of Homeland Security to ensure migrants in Oregon have access to attorneys before they are transferred out of the state.

“Plaintiffs cite no case for the proposition that access to counsel before transfer to [Northwest ICE Processing Center] is required,” U.S. District Judge Ann Aiken wrote in a 32-page order.

Clear Clinic, a Portland, Oregon-based pro bono law firm, and Pineros y Campesinos Unidos del Noroeste, a nonprofit representing Latino farmworkers, sued the Department of Homeland Security in 2025, accusing Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers of blocking detainees from accessing lawyers. Leon X, a 32-year-old Mexican national with a pending visa application, joined as a plaintiff to represent a class of individuals who fear arrest and detention by ICE.

The nonprofits said detainees are held in ICE facilities for mere hours before being transferred to larger facilities out of state, which denies them access to lawyers. The government argued deferring meetings with potential counsel before transferring detainees is not the same as denying counsel.

Aiken denied the nonprofits’ emergency motion for a temporary restraining order last year and on Wednesday denied their motion for a preliminary injunction and class certification.

The Bill Clinton appointee found that of the three plaintiffs, only Clear Clinic had standing to pursue its claims and preliminary injunction.

Under the proposed injunction, the nonprofit wanted ICE ordered to arrange a meeting between pro bono attorneys and detainees as well as provide the plaintiffs with all paperwork related to detained individuals even before an attorney-client relationship has been established. The nonprofit also requested detainees be allowed to attend Pineros y Campesinos Unidos del Noroeste’s Know Your Rights trainings and that they not be transported if they request to attend one.

Clear Clinic next requested that Oregon Field Offices remain open on weekends and holidays and until 8 p.m. every night, and to be notified if anyone is detained outside those hours.

“These conditions do not restore the status quo,” Aiken wrote. “Plaintiffs have asked this court to create new operational rules — and many of them — for any building hosting ICE facilities in Oregon.”

Aiken also disagreed with the plaintiffs’ interpretation of the meaning of the word “examination” in the regulation entitling detainees to representation, finding they had ignored the context of the full sentence by selectively quoting it.

“Plaintiffs’ reading of the regulation would give immigrant detainees a more robust due process requirement at this stage than those being booked in jail on criminal charges,” Aiken wrote.

The plaintiffs compared their case to others in which detainees had been denied access to counsel; however, Aiken noted the extended length of detention in field offices played a crucial factor in those and that there had been no claim that detainees have been held for more than 12 hours at any Oregon field office.

“In fact, the allegations are the opposite: according to plaintiffs, detainees are being transferred from Oregon field offices to a long-term detention facility too quickly.” Aiken wrote. “Plaintiffs ask the court to require defendants to hold detainees at the field offices for longer periods of time.”

Aiken also expressed concern about the evidence the nonprofits presented.

“Plaintiffs make an assertion in their motion about what is happening inside Oregon field offices, but the five evidentiary documents they cite provide minimal, if any, support for the proposition,” Aiken wrote.

Clear Clinic claimed its lack of access at Oregon field offices violated its First Amendment rights to disseminate information and solicit clients, but Aiken was not persuaded.

“​​The record shows that attorneys have been able to access clients, though not to the degree or for the length of time that they wish, nor at all hours that plaintiffs wishes,” Aiken wrote.

The federal defendants noted there were operational, logistical and security considerations impacting detention procedures, which Aiken found to be important interests. Plus, the court pointed out attorneys have been able to meet with prospective clients, though it may be a burden.

“Plaintiffs have not shown that defendants’ practice burdens substantially more speech than necessary,” Aiken wrote.

Aiken also dismissed Customs and Border Protection and its acting commissioner Pete Flores from the suit, finding the plaintiffs failed to accuse either of specific claims.

Jordan Cunnings, legal director at Innovation Law Lab, one of the firms representing the plaintiffs, said the law lab will continue to challenge ICE.

“Due process is a fundamental right in this country, and it doesn’t stop at ICE’s gate,” Cunnings said in a statement. “There is substantial evidence that ICE is denying people the right to speak with attorneys before transporting them out of state or even deporting them.”

The federal defendants did not respond to a request for comment before press time.

authors: TIM SULLIVAN, KATHY McCORMACK and MARK VANCLEAVE

MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Renee Good's family sued the U.S. government and the architects of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown Thursday, saying "the time is absolutely now for accountability" for her killing in January by a federal agent in Minneapolis.
"She was the love of my life," Becca Good said at a news conference announcing the lawsuits.
Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver's seat, her car blocking part of the road, as she repeatedly honks the horn.
Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives.
"I don't hate the people that took Renee from us," Becca Good said.
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Renee Good's family sued the U.S. government and the architects of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown Thursday, saying "the time is absolutely now for accountability" for her killing in January by a federal agent in Minneapolis.

Good's partner, Becca Good, and her brother Brent Ganger on behalf of her larger family, accused the government and Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot into her SUV and killed her, of unjustified and excessive use of force.

The Jan. 7 shooting, captured on bystander video, was "the predictable and intended product" of the Trump administration's crackdown on Somali and other immigrants in Minnesota dubbed Operation Metro Surge, according to one of the two lawsuits.

"She was the love of my life," Becca Good said at a news conference announcing the lawsuits. "I'm here today because last January, the whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed — as the sunshine who was my amazing Renee was robbed from us, from her children, and from her community."

The lack of accountability stuns Good's family

The killings of Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during Trump's second term.

The crackdown, a pillar of Trump's second term, has prompted a slew of lawsuits filed by everyone from Chicago-area pastors to more than a dozen states and the cities of Minneapolis and St. Paul. Hundreds of protesters have been arrested, but few have been convicted of any crimes.

"What happened to Renee was completely senseless," Ganger said. "And the fact that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind blowing."

The lawsuits — one against the government, the other against Ross and officials including White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, ex-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and White House border czar Tom Homan — seek unspecified damages for wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations.

"Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens," the family's lawyer, Antonio Romanucci, told reporters.

The Justice Department has not responded to an email seeking comment.

Ross shot Good as she turned her car away from him

Renee Good was killed while driving with Becca on a street where masked federal immigration officers were conducting an enforcement operation. They had just dropped their 6-year-old son at school. Renee stopped their red SUV in the street and honked her horn to warn people about the operation while Becca got out and started recording video with her cellphone.

Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver's seat, her car blocking part of the road, as she repeatedly honks the horn. Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as an officer again demands: "Get out of the car."

Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: "Drive, baby, drive!"

The officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, by then very close to the open window on the driver's side, fires two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.

Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in "an act of domestic terrorism."

Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.

"I don't hate the people that took Renee from us," Becca Good said.

"But what I want them to understand: Every single day they get to look at their children and their wives and their sisters and know what they took from our family. They took a mother away from her children. They know that. And they will carry it forever."

Government tried to hide the truth, lawsuit says

The wrongful death lawsuit against the U.S. government seeks damages for "the immense suffering" Good endured in her final moments and her family's "profound and permanent" loss.

The other lawsuit, against Ross and top federal immigration officials, paints Operation Metro Surge as a conspiracy to trample the civil rights of immigrants, and accuses the administration of targeting Becca instead of thoroughly investigating Good's killing.

The government sought to hide evidence of what happened, it said, and officials worried that pursuing a civil rights investigation would undermine Trump's claims that Good had tried to kill an officer.

The operation, the conspiracy lawsuit said, was a "carefully planned, coordinated effort" to make Somali and Hispanic immigrants "the object of aggression and abduction." The crackdown used violence and the threat of arrest to intimidate neighbors and allies "who observed, documented and warned."

Other defendants include: Corey Lewandowski, a Trump campaign manager who also served as one of Noem's advisers; former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Todd Lyons; former U.S. Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino; and 10 unnamed federal agents.

The news conference announcing the lawsuits was held in the atrium of the University of St. Thomas School of Law, and dozens of law students looked on as the family and lawyers spoke.

"The time is absolutely now for accountability for the deep damage done by ICE and others," Ganger said. "We will not be quiet. We will not go away."

Lawsuits are 'uphill battles'

Good's lawyers acknowledged the complexity of the cases, and legal scholars said they could be challenging to win.

"They're going to face significant uphill battles," said Rachel Moran, a professor at the University of St. Thomas law school. "These are both complicated types of lawsuits, and so I can't predict how they will play out. But I'm sure the government will have many, many types of responses to why the lawsuits should not go forward."

But she noted the conspiracy lawsuit, in particular, could reveal many unknown details about the crackdown, including the involvement of some of the country's top officials.

"Yes, ICE agents on the ground acted problematically, but that was at the behest, in many ways, of people very high up in the administration," she said.

___

McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

text:
Representatives Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas), and and Greg Casar (D-Texas), today sent a letter to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Director David J. Venturella calling for answers and accountability following three Immigration and Customs Enforcement shootings in their congressional districts where agents failed to wear body cameras.

The full letter is available here.

The Members point to the shootings of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas; Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine; and Wilber Rafael Garces Perez in Austin, Texas. In the latest case, Garces Perez was shot in the back by an ICE agent in Austin on September 20. The agent had been issued a body camera but was not wearing it. A second agent was wearing a camera, but it did not capture the shooting.

The repeated failures come despite significant funding from Congress. Earlier this year, Congress appropriated $20 million specifically for procuring, deploying, and operating body-worn cameras for federal immigration enforcement officers.

That is on top of an unprecedented increase in funding for ICE. Congress provided ICE roughly $75 billion in supplemental funding in 2025, followed by another $38.5 billion in 2026 through the Secure America Act.

“Over and over again, we’ve seen DHS agents resort to deadly violence when conducting enforcement operations in our districts. And when we demand to see the body cam footage, they give us the same tired excuses. No more,” said Congresswoman Pingree. “The fact that DHS has failed to outfit its officers with body cameras—despite having hundreds of billions of dollars at its disposal and more than a year to procure and deploy this equipment—is totally unacceptable. There is simply no reason that a federal agency with more money than most countries’ entire GDPs is not held to the same standards as local law enforcement. We deserve the truth about why cameras weren’t deployed during these most recent shootings, including the one that took the life of my constituent, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, in Biddeford, Maine on July 13. Our demands are simple: Every immigration enforcement officer must have a working body camera, must be properly trained on how to use it, and be held accountable when that camera isn’t used.”

“ICE is not short on money. Congress has provided billions of dollars to this agency, and after Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed in my district, we were told body cameras were coming. The money is there. The deadlines have passed. So why does this keep happening?” said Congresswoman Garcia. “This is completely unacceptable. When federal agents use deadly force, the public should not be left in the dark. There must be transparency, accountability, and answers for the families who are left behind. Lorenzo’s family deserves answers. They deserve justice. DHS and ICE need to explain why their body camera system keeps failing when it matters most.”

"Wilber Garces Perez was shot in the back in Austin by an ICE agent who wasn't wearing a body camera, weeks after DHS promised every officer in the field would have one," said Congressman Casar. "Secretary Mullin keeps making promises while his agents keep shooting people. Secretary Mullin must release every second of footage from that scene, so we can know the truth.”

The letter also points to commitments DHS made following the July 7 killing of Salgado Araujo in Houston. During a July 15 phone call with Congresswoman Garcia, Secretary Mullin said all federal immigration officers would have body-worn cameras within 45 to 60 days. That deadline passed in September.

Salgado Araujo, a Houston construction worker and father of three, was killed without available body camera footage capturing the shooting. Days later, ICE fatally shot 25-year-old Colombian national Johan Sebastian Durán Guerrero. Agents involved in Guerrero’s shooting were also not wearing body cameras. Then, on September 20, Garces Perez was shot in Austin by an officer who had been issued a camera but was not wearing it.

Members are demanding DHS and ICE explain whether all federal immigration officers have been issued working body cameras and properly trained to use them. They also ask why the officer who shot Garces Perez was not wearing his issued camera, why the second officer’s camera failed to capture the shooting, whether other footage exists, and whether officers who fail to follow body camera rules will face disciplinary action.

The Members requested written answers from DHS and ICE by October 14, 2026.

text:
California and six other states sued President Donald Trump and Office of Management and Budget director Russell Vought on Wednesday, alleging the administration unlawfully impounded congressionally appropriated funds. The suit also seeks to block the administration’s proposed rescission of an additional $810 million in federal funds.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed the complaint in the Northern District of California, joined by Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Nevada, New Mexico and Oregon. They challenge the president’s authority to unilaterally withhold congressionally appropriated funds and allow them to expire, alleging that the administration failed to spend money it was legally required to obligate and spend.

The states argue that the president has a duty to follow Congress’ spending priorities and cannot rescind funds based on his policy preferences. They allege that impoundments violate the Constitution’s Spending Clause, which grants Congress authority over federal spending, the Presentment Clause, which prescribes the legislative process, and the Take Care Clause, which obligates the president to ensure that the laws “be faithfully executed.” These clauses together preserve the separation of powers by ensuring that Congress decides where tax dollars go.

The states warn that allowing the administration’s actions to stand would “reduce Congress’s statutory appropriations to mere recommendations” and eliminate core policy negotiations between Congress and the executive branch.

Attorney General Bonta criticized President Trump’s “blatant disregard” for the constitutional framework of government, adding that “Just because the President doesn’t like a program doesn’t mean he can defund it.”

The complaint also addresses the president’s proposed rescission of $810 million in federal funding. The administration said the proposal builds its use of “pocket rescissions” through the Impoundment Control Act (ICA) last year, when it also froze nearly $5 billion in foreign aid. The Supreme Court, without reaching the merits, allowed the freeze to continue.

Last year, the administration argued a “pocket rescission” allows a president to propose rescission of funds with fewer than 45 days remaining before expiration and withhold them until they lapse, so that the money goes unspent without congressional action. The Government Accountability Office rejected this view, stating that the ICA “does not allow the President to withhold budget authority through its date of expiration.”

The Trump administration says the rescission is for “harmful government spending.” The proposed cuts mostly targeted programs serving immigrants and noncitizens. More than half of the proposed cuts, approximately $567 million, target the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement.

The administration claimed other cuts were aimed at welfare programs for illegal immigrants, nongovernmental organizations that assist undocumented immigrants, education programs for immigrants, as well as funding linked to LGBT youth programs, race-based grants, and climate-related debt relief and research.

text:
The Supreme Court agreed on Thursday to hear a dispute over a policy by President Donald Trump's administration that subjects millions of immigrants who entered the United States illegally to mandatory detention during their deportation proceedings.

In this latest legal battle over Trump's hardline immigration agenda to reach the top judicial body, the justices face an issue that has divided lower courts as numerous lawsuits by migrants and advocacy groups challenging the policy have played out. The policy is one of a number of measures his administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump's goal of mass deportation.

The justices took up the administration's appeal of a ruling against the policy by the New York-based 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals in a case involving a Brazilian national. The Supreme Court will hear the case in its new term that begins on Monday.

The Department of Homeland Security in July 2025 issued new guidance to federal immigration officials announcing that immigrants in the United States illegally are subject to mandatory detention without a bond hearing for the duration of their deportation proceedings, which can take months or even years to conclude.

The guidance represented a departure from a nearly three-decade-old interpretation of federal law that immigrants already living in the United States could be released on bond while they pursue their cases in immigration court.

The Republican president has enforced a sweeping crackdown on immigration — among his top priorities — since returning to office last year. The Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, has allowed a number of Trump's hardline immigration policies to go into effect.

The administration's detention policy produced an avalanche of lawsuits from immigrants seeking to be released. Immigrants have filed more than 73,000 such cases in federal court so far this year, about a quarter of all civil lawsuits brought in federal court.

A Reuters analysis in February found that hundreds of judges around the country had ruled more than 4,400 times that Trump's administration had detained such immigrants unlawfully.

The 2nd Circuit decision arose from a legal challenge brought by Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, who entered the United States illegally around 2004 or 2005 and has remained since then.

He was arrested by immigration officers in September 2025 while driving to work in Norwood, Massachusetts, and initially was denied a bond hearing under the disputed policy. He was subsequently released on bond at a later stage of his case, according to court papers.

Michael K.T. Tan, deputy director of the ACLU's Immigrants' Rights Project and a lawyer for Barbosa da Cunha, said his legal team looks forward to making their case to the Supreme Court.

"The courts have repeatedly and resoundingly rejected the Trump administration's radical misinterpretation of the law. Try as it might, the government cannot twist the law to detain immigrants for months or even years on end without a bond hearing," Tan said. "Not only is it cruel and inhumane; it is unlawful."

Bucking a long-standing interpretation of immigration law, the Department of Homeland Security last year took the position that non-citizens already residing in the United ​States, and not just people ​arriving at the border, ⁠qualify as "applicants for admission" subject to mandatory detention.

Under federal immigration law, "applicants for admission" to the United States are subject to mandatory detention while their cases proceed ​in immigration courts and are ineligible for bond hearings.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson welcomed the court's decision to hear the case.

"Under President Trump, the Department of Homeland Security finally implemented the law as Congress intended it to," the spokesperson said, faulting the actions of former President Joe Biden. "This implementation put the nail in the coffin for Biden's catch-and-release policies."

Most federal appellate courts to review the Trump administration's policy have ruled against it. Decisions against the policy by the 2nd Circuit and Cincinnati-based 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals prompted the administration to appeal to the Supreme Court.

In the 2nd Circuit ruling, U.S. Circuit Judge Joseph Bianco, a Trump appointee, wrote that the administration's "newfound interpretation" of federal law was an implausible basis for implementing what he described as "the broadest mass detention-without-bond mandate in our nation's history for millions of noncitizens."

The Supreme Court already is set to hear arguments in another major immigration-related case during its upcoming term.

The court on Tuesday let the administration resume, for now, swiftly deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face. The justices scheduled arguments in that case for December.

text:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) is raising several immigration-related fees beginning October 16, affecting asylum seekers and some applicants for work permits, parole, and Temporary Protected Status (TPS).

The increases are inflation adjustments to immigration fees established under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, President Donald Trump’s sweeping tax and spending law that became law in July 2025.

The changes come as the Trump administration continues to tighten control over legal immigration and make it more expensive for some immigrants to file applications.

Read More on News

USCIS, an agency under the Department of Homeland Security, administers immigration benefits, including applications for immigration status and work authorization.

USCIS Spokesperson Zach Kahler told Newsweek, “USCIS is implementing the annual inflation adjustment to certain immigration-related fees as required by H.R. 1. These adjustments ensure USCIS continues to apply the law as Congress intended while supporting the integrity and sustainability of the immigration system. Applicants and petitioners subject to these fees should review the updated amounts and submit the correct fee for any request that is postmarked on or after the effective date.”

What Applicants Will Pay

Under the new fee schedule, the annual asylum application fee will rise from $102 to $105. The immigration parole fee associated with Form I-131, which covers applications for travel documents, parole documents, and arrival/departure records, will increase from $1,020 to $1,050.

The fee for an initial work permit for asylum applicants, parolees, and TPS recipients will increase from $560 to $570. The fee for Form I-821, used to apply for Temporary Protected Status, will also rise by $10, from $510 to $520.

TPS allows eligible nationals of designated countries facing conditions such as armed conflict or environmental disasters to live and work temporarily in the U.S., while parole can permit certain people to enter or remain in the country temporarily without granting them permanent immigration status. The administration has moved to terminate the program for several countries.

USCIS's September guidance specifically confirms that Sudan and Ukraine are set to terminate on October 19, 2026, while the latest September 30 guidance says El Salvador remains protected pending a DHS announcement.

The Trump administration has already terminated TPS designations for Afghanistan, Cameroon, Haiti, Honduras, Myanmar (Burma), Nepal, Nicaragua, Somalia, South Sudan, Syria, Venezuela, Ethiopia, and Yemen at various points during 2025-2026.

USCIS said immigration benefit requests postmarked on or after October 16 must include the new fee when the adjusted charge applies. Applications submitted without the correct filing fee will be rejected.

The increases are relatively small compared with the underlying fees. The annual asylum fee rises by $3, or about 2.9 percent, while the parole fee increases by $30, also about 2.9 percent. The affected work permit fee rises by $10, or about 1.8 percent, and the Temporary Protected Status application fee increases by $10, or about 2 percent.

The new amounts apply based on when a request is postmarked, meaning applicants filing before October 16 remain subject to the previous amounts, while those whose requests are postmarked on or after that date must pay the adjusted fees.

For an asylum applicant subject to both the annual asylum fee and the affected initial work permit fee, for example, the two charges would total $675 under the new schedule, compared with $662 at the previous rates.

Immigration advocates have argued that the new fees create additional financial barriers for people seeking humanitarian protections, while the administration has framed fee changes as part of an effort to cover increased costs of reviewing applications.

The fee changes come as the State Department releases its October 2026 Visa Bulletin, the first bulletin of the new federal fiscal year. Each October, new annual immigrant visa numbers become available, potentially allowing some employment-based applicants to move forward after months or years of waiting.

“What happened to Renee was completely senseless,” Ganger said. “And the fact that there’s been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind blowing.”

The lawsuits — one against the government, the other against Ross and officials including White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, ex-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and White House border czar Tom Homan — seek unspecified damages for wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations.

“Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens,” the family’s lawyer, Antonio Romanucci, told reporters.

The Justice Department has not responded to an email seeking comment.

Ross shot Good as she turned her car away from him

Renee Good was killed while driving with Becca on a street where masked federal immigration officers were conducting an enforcement operation. They had just dropped their 6-year-old son at school. Renee stopped their red SUV in the street and honked her horn to warn people about the operation while Becca got out and started recording video with her cellphone.

Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver’s seat, her car blocking part of the road, as she repeatedly honks the horn. Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as an officer again demands: “Get out of the car.”

Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: “Drive, baby, drive!”

The officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, by then very close to the open window on the driver’s side, fires two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.

Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism.”

Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.

“I don’t hate the people that took Renee from us,” Becca Good said.

“But what I want them to understand: Every single day they get to look at their children and their wives and their sisters and know what they took from our family. They took a mother away from her children. They know that. And they will carry it forever.”

Government tried to hide the truth, lawsuit says

The wrongful death lawsuit against the U.S. government seeks damages for “the immense suffering” Good endured in her final moments and her family’s “profound and permanent” loss.

The other lawsuit, against Ross and top federal immigration officials, paints Operation Metro Surge as a conspiracy to trample the civil rights of immigrants, and accuses the administration of targeting Becca instead of thoroughly investigating Good’s killing.

The government sought to hide evidence of what happened, it said, and officials worried that pursuing a civil rights investigation would undermine Trump’s claims that Good had tried to kill an officer.

The operation, the conspiracy lawsuit said, was a “carefully planned, coordinated effort” to make Somali and Hispanic immigrants “the object of aggression and abduction.” The crackdown used violence and the threat of arrest to intimidate neighbors and allies “who observed, documented and warned.”

Other defendants include: Corey Lewandowski, a Trump campaign manager who also served as one of Noem’s advisers; former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Todd Lyons; former U.S. Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino; and 10 unnamed federal agents.

The news conference announcing the lawsuits was held in the atrium of the University of St. Thomas School of Law, and dozens of law students looked on as the family and lawyers spoke.

“The time is absolutely now for accountability for the deep damage done by ICE and others,” Ganger said. “We will not be quiet. We will not go away.”

Lawsuits are ‘uphill battles’

Good’s lawyers acknowledged the complexity of the cases, and legal scholars said they could be challenging to win.

“They’re going to face significant uphill battles,” said Rachel Moran, a professor at the University of St. Thomas law school. “These are both complicated types of lawsuits, and so I can’t predict how they will play out. But I’m sure the government will have many, many types of responses to why the lawsuits should not go forward.”

But she noted the conspiracy lawsuit, in particular, could reveal many unknown details about the crackdown, including the involvement of some of the country’s top officials.

“Yes, ICE agents on the ground acted problematically, but that was at the behest, in many ways, of people very high up in the administration,” she said.

___

McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire.
